#8421. It Took Six People and a Tractor to Haul This Massive Black Bear Off the Mountain

Published Oct 29, 2026 9:29 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Cecil Jackson, age 69, climbed into his elevated Millennium platform hunting blind the afternoon of October 24. It was opening day of archery bear season in this area of the Appalachian Mountains in southeast Kentucky. Jackson didn’t know it at the time, but he was about to take one of the biggest black bears in the area.

Archery deer season was also open and Jackson was going to take whatever the mountain provided.

“I was hunting deer or bear, whatever came along,” the just-retired Kentucky Utilities worker from the town of Pineville tells Outdoor Life. “I had trail cameras set up and I knew there were a few bears in the area. But I never imagined shooting a bear, because I had no gun with me in case I shot one and had to track it.”

Jackson’s blind was situated on rolling private farmland, and late that afternoon a fawn deer strolled down a mountain trail toward Jackson shortly before nightfall.

“It stood there awhile, then snapped its head up and looked up the mountain trail where it had come from,” Jackson says. “Then the deer left the area running. I thought maybe a buck was coming, but about 30 yards away a bear showed up.”

“That bear looked at me, turned to head after where the fawn had run, and that’s when I shot him with my Ravin crossbow,” Jackson says. “The bear ran about 100 yards, then turned into a thicket and I never saw or heard it again.”

The veteran hunter knew he’d made a good shot on the bear. He waited about 10 minutes in his blind, then went out and found his arrow, but there wasn’t much of a blood trail.

“Without a gun I wasn’t gonna track that bear alone,” he says. “That’s when a friend of mine called me and I told him I’d shot a bear, and I asked if he had a pistol with him.”

His buddy Tanner Jackson (no relation to Cecil) said he did have a gun and shortly met Cecil to start tracking the bear that night.

“I’m colorblind and have a tough time on a blood trail,” Cecil says. “We had a light, but it was a hard go trailing that bear.”

After about 70 yards of following faint blood sign, they stopped and used a high beam flashlight to scan the woods.

“I told Tanner to keep that pistol of his handy, and about that time I spotted the bear lying just off the woods path,” Cecil says. “I tossed a stick at it, but it didn’t move so we figured it was dead. When we walked up to it we couldn’t believe how big it was. We tried to lift just its head up but couldn’t.”

They phoned a nearby farm neighbor and some more friends. Using country woods savvy and a low spot in the road, they rigged a rope on a block and loaded the bear onto the tailgate of Jackson’s truck. They were just able to manhandle the whole bear into their truck.

“I didn’t think we could get that truck up and away from the low road spot, but that old truck in 4-wheel drive made it,” Cecil says. “It took six adults and a tractor to finally get that bear off the mountain.”

The hunters didn’t get the bear home until 11 p.m. that night.

The following day, James Dixon from the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources checked Cecil’s huge bear, which field dressed at an estimated weight of over 500 pounds. The bear measured 105-inches (nearly 9 feet) from nose to tail. Its neck measured 33 inches in circumference.

“James said he’d not seen a bear that size and believed it was the heaviest one taken so far from Kentucky this year – its huge head may be big enough for a record,” Cecil says. “I’m not much for bear meat, but some friends are, and I gave it all to them.

“I also gave away its fur to a buddy. But I may keep its skull for a European mount – especially if the head is of record size.”

#8419. Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#8418. Swallowed by the Camino Green Tunnel

The room we slept in was the top floor of a centuries-old, three-story building with a modern interior. Tuck-pointed right under the roof, we slept soundly through the night as periodic thunder and a heavy rain provided peaceful white noise overhead.

Stepping outside the next morning, sunrise illuminated a surreal sky, backlighting the massive monastery. We paused at a local cafe for a quick breakfast before leaving Samos behind.

Our hike started with a few miles of road walk before the Camino veered onto a forested, ancient track. Thick rock walls lined the path, guarded by groves of massive chestnut trees.

As the morning sun broke through, the air naturally turned humid. We began a steady climb along a narrow path where pilgrims over the years had woven stick crosses directly into the fencing alongside the trail.

Highlight of the Day: We ran into Anthony from Oxford–who was walking his fifth Camino. He explained that this sunken section of path is called a Holloway. Worn deep into the earth over centuries of foot traffic, it creates a stunning green tunnel with 12-foot mossy walls and a dense canopy of ancient trees overhead.

Our “tramily” friends, Jill and Robert, caught up with us midmorning, and the miles flew by as we chatted. We meandered from one quaint hamlet to the next along quite country roads. By 10:30 AM, we only had 2.5 miles left for the day.

We soon reached Foxos, a tiny village with cute medieval farm houses, old barns, and a historic church. From there, the path climbed steeply toward Aguiada, where our trail merged back on the main Camino Frances route. We were completely out of water, but this small village didn’t have any water sources available.

Reconnecting with the main route brought a dramatic shift. Because you only need to walk the final 100 km to earn a Compostela certificate, and since it was the start of the weekend, the trail was suddenly packed with weekend hikers and new pilgrims starting their journey from Sarria.

It instantly felt like a different Camino–less intimate, much more crowded, and distinctly touristy.

We rolled into Sarria at 1:00 PM. Built into a hillside, Sarria is a charming medieval city full of narrow, winding cobblestone streets.

Our accommodation was easily one of our favorites so far:

While Knockers immediately crashed for a two-hour nap, I got to work planning our journey past Santiago.

Next Steps: We officially decided that after reaching Santiago, we will hike out to Finisterre—traditionally known as “the end of the world” on the Atlantic coast. From there, we’ll return to Santiago and head south along the Portuguese Caminos. (There are a few ferry connections and complex logistics to map out for that stretch!)

Later that evening, we walked downhill to a local grocery store and definitely bought too much food. Being hungry and finding fresh, real ingredients for the first time in a long while made it impossible to resist.

Back at the apartment, we cooked up a huge meal and ate until we couldn’t take another bite. By the time “hiker midnight” rolled around, we crashed hard for another peaceful night’s rest.

#8416. Here’s What All Hunters Should Know About the Rut, Weather, and Deer Movement, According to One of the Top Experts In the Country

Published Oct 29, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

During the whitetail pre-rut and rut, hunters should worry less about the type of weather that will “get deer moving” and focus more on weather conditions that will help us hunt more effectively. That’s one of my takeaways from interviewing Dr. Grant Woods, a renowned wildlife researcher and diehard deer hunter. Woods and his crew publish excellent informational hunting content on his website, Growing Deer TV.

I interviewed him on Halloween just as a spectacular cold front was sinking into the heart of deer country. But if you didn’t kill your target buck during that front, don’t worry. The hunting is still getting better, Woods says. You can listen to my full interview with Woods in the podcast episode below. And read on to learn Woods’ other tips for understanding the rut, weather, and deer activity.

Recent research has found that fronts, even big cold fronts like we just experienced, don’t increase whitetail rutting activity, Woods says.

“The research says that weather is not much of a [factor in regards to deer rutting activity],” he says. “And that’s caused a bit of an issue in the last few years between hunters and researchers in a lot of online chatter.”

This discrepancy stems from the fact that hunters tend to see more deer when cold fronts hit. So, what gives? Woods’ explanation is essentially that both researchers and hunters are right. Cold temps don’t speed up breeding activity, but they do mean that hunters are more likely to see deer from their stands.

“I’m going to tell you, during our cold front, we went from high 70s to 30 and under in 24 hours. And on my trail cameras, when that cold front hit, I got a big spike… So what I’m saying is there’s some miscommunication going on,” Woods says. “Putting my scientist hat on now, typically I can’t publish something unless … 95 times out of 100 it’s going to happen. Well there’s a lot of conflicting things [concerning weather and deer activity]. When did the barometer rise? How much of a temperature was it? What phase of the rut was it? There’s a lot of noise. And when there’s a lot of noise a good biologist that’s doing really good work is going to say ‘I can’t say X because there’s too much noise.’ They’re going to be a little more conservative if they’re doing honest science.”

So what’s the takeaway for the hunter? It’s important to know that in the pre-rut deer usually don’t go running far outside their home range, even on a big cold front. However, they might walk around more within their home range.

Also, it’s important to understand what the pre-rut really is. Woods defines the pre-rut as the time period during which less than 25 percent of does are receptive. Bucks are seeking or moving more. Every day, a few more does become receptive and that brings a frenzy to the bucks. All of this happens regardless of weather.

Read Next: The Best Cellular Trail Cameras: The Complete Guide to Cell Cams and Subscription Plans

Yep, deer will keep on rutting even when the weather warms.

“The rut is a bell shaped curve and we’re definitively climbing up that curve [right now]. We’re increasing in intensity. So even if it’s 80 degrees, but the prom only happens once where you hunt, it’s still going to happen [during a warm front],” Woods says. “Now hunters sometimes debate that but if you look [at spring fawning season], fawns are born at the same time in the same place every year. There’s going to be some early fawns, a big cluster of fawns, and then some late fawns. [That’s because] especially up North, if they’re born too early, they’re going to fall into a snowbank and they’re not going to make it. And if they’re born too late they’re not going to gain enough weight before the next winter and they’re not going to make it. So the system is pretty refined over a long time. The rut is going to happen at the same time [locally, every year].”

Most deer hunters love to focus on the big fronts, but small changes in temperature can make for productive hunting, too. Woods uses a rough temperature change rule when deciding when to hunt vs. when to work.

“When it’s been warmer than normal, I get excited when there’s a 10 percent temperature decrease.”

So if it’s been 80 degrees and the forecast is calling for a drop down to 72 degrees, Woods will plan on hunting. During the late season, when deer are moving during warmer periods, Woods will hunt during a 10 percent increase in temperature. That means a small bump, like from 30 to 33 degrees.

When the rut is increasing in intensity, like it is right now, typical and stable weather makes for great hunting days, too, Woods says.

If the conditions are hot and not favorable, it’s probably not the time to skip work for an all-day sit. But Woods suggests making a short evening hunt and sliding in closer to bedding areas (assuming you can do so without bumping deer). This is because deer are likely to move only a few minutes before the end of legal shooting light during hot days. So there’s a chance you could catch a buck just leaving his bed at the end of the day.

Don’t be fooled by that one trail camera photo of a buck you have moving during a rainstorm. Bucks actually tend to move less during a steady rain.

“Researchers, again using GPS collared deer, have seen that bucks tend to move less when it’s raining,” Woods says. He thinks this could be because they have a harder time detecting predators in the rain, with blowing leaves and other disturbances in the woods.

Strangely, however, does tend to move a little bit more in the rain, Woods says. No one is quite sure why.

Instead of worrying about how weather impacts deer, hunters should consider how weather affects our potential success as predators. Woods mentions barometric pressure as a good example. During high pressure and low humidity, hunters tend to see more deer. But that’s not necessarily because deer are moving more on high-pressure days (data say they don’t). Instead, it’s likely because high pressure days favor the hunter so we’re not getting busted by deer.

“On high-pressure days, our scent is actually rising. So we’re able to get closer to deer without them detecting our scent,” Wood says. “We’re not talking [enough] about a hunter’s ability to hunt. We’re totally focused on the deer and what’s making them move. We need to accept that they’re feeding and drinking and avoiding predators every day of their lives.”

“I don’t have any data on this, but understanding the science and being a diehard hunter, I believe the biggest problem is that we often don’t include the human element and we are alerting way more deer than we think we are.”

Read Next: The 101 Best Tips for Hunting the Whitetail Rut

Wind is the biggest factor in our ability to hunt whitetails effectively—we all know this. But Woods says to analyze not just wind direction, but also wind speed and consistency. Hunters have the advantage during a strong (but not gusting) wind that is consistent in direction and speed.

This is one of the reasons why hunters tend to have success during cold fronts, Woods says. He suggests using NOAA’s Wind Roses page, which shows predominant wind direction and wind strength. This will help you get a better idea of how to set stands in your area.

Considering that deer live by their noses, Woods has a logical theory about why deer are most active at dawn and dusk. The temperature changes during morning (warming) and evening (cooling), often cause the wind to shift and swirl. A swirling wind helps deer detect predators from all directions, which makes them feel safer while moving and feeding.

“At night and full daytime deer only get nasal protection, if you will, from about 180 degrees —just throwing a number out,” Woods says. “But at sunrise and sunset, because the Earth is warming the Earth is cooling, thermals are shifting, they’re getting protection from a much greater area.”

One tactic Woods employs is executing very short hunts in the evening. The less time you’re out there, the less time there is for your scent to disperse and for that big buck to potentially bust you. —A.R.

#8413. Xpedition NexLite 35 Bow Review: Accuracy and Speed Test

Published Oct 29, 2026 1:00 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Late October is a great time to be a bowhunter. The bucks are chasing, and new bows seem to drop every week. One of them recently showed up on my front porch. (I’m still working on getting a buck to do that.) This one is a 35-inch featherweight from Xpedition, and on paper, its long axle-to-axle length and low mass weight make it a strong pick for anyone who wants one bow for both targets and the whitetail woods. I spent the last two weeks shooting the new Xpedition Nexlite 35 to find out if it lives up to that promise.

A typical 35-inch bow weighs 4.6 to 4.9 pounds. The NexLite 35 weighs 3.95 pounds. That weight savings comes from the Magnite riser material, which is a nanocomposite alloy that’s about 30 percent lighter than 6061 aluminum. Xpedition says it’s also stronger and absorbs vibration better than aluminum and carbon.

Low-profile arrow rest and sight mounting are now standard on premium and even budget compound bows. You’ll find Integrate rest mounting and a machined Picatinny sight mount on the NexLite 35. Xpedition also offers its XLOK accessories, such as a low-profile quiver and a bow stand.

The NexLite 35 uses the Tip-Shift tuning system. It’s a simple shimming system that doesn’t require a bow press. All you need is an Allen wrench to swap the shims and move your cams.

Before I fired my first shot from the NexLite 35, I was impressed with how light it is for a 35-inch bow. It’s only 4.9 pounds fully rigged with an XLOK stabilizer, Axcel Armortech sight, XLOK bow stand, and QAD arrow rest. Its low mass weight gives you the flexibility to run it as a lightweight hunting bow or rig it with long stabilizers for TAC and 3D competitions.

I paper tuned the NexLite without any drama. I didn’t need to use the Tip-Shift tuning system, but I did use it during the 2026 bow test. It’s a fantastically simple system. All you need to do is remove a screw with an Allen wrench and replace the spacer with the one that will fix your issue. The spacers have one, two, or three dots on them. The number of dots you install should always add up to four. I like that the Tip-Shift is a rigid system, so you don’t run the risk of an adjustment screw walking or accidentally moving a cam too far.

The NexLite 35’s draw cycle is smooth, but you can tell the cams were built for speed. The bow hits its peak weight early, evens out, and then there’s a final effort right before the valley. To me, it feels similar to drawing a Mathews Lift. The wall is solid with no give, and the valley is relatively short. If you come off the stops, the bow will let you know you’re creeping. But I found it very easy to keep the stops pinned, and the bow felt exceptionally comfortable and stable at full draw. It’s easy to drop the pin on the target and keep it there. At the shot, there is minimal vibration, which is impressive considering the bow’s low weight.

I quickly got used to the draw cycle while sighting in. Then I stepped back to 50 yards for accuracy testing and —— buddy, this bow is a shooter. I shot five five-shot groups at 50 yards that averaged 3.19 inches.

For the speed test, I shot a 430-grain arrow with the bow set at 61.2 pounds and a 31.5-inch draw length. The four-shot average was 281.6 fps. That’s pretty fast for a 35-inch bow.

The NexLite has nearly all the features you’d expect in a modern flagship bow, but there are three features I’d like to see added.

If you’re in the market for a long axle-to-axle bow, the NexLite 35 is definitely worth trying out at your local shop. It’s a top contender because its low mass weight makes it versatile as a combination target and hunting bow. It also has good performance, an easy-to-use tuning system, and high accuracy potential. I also really appreciate the NexLite 35’s build quality. It’s beautifully finished and masterfully machined — the type of workmanship I love to see in a premium bow.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8411. 900-Acre Wildfire in White Mountains Likely Caused by Humans, Authorities Say

An unusually large wildfire in the White Mountain National Forest near Gorham, New Hampshire, has spread to nearly 856 acres and is 11% contained as of the most recent update. The Wild River Fire was first reported on November 1 in the steep, rugged terrain south of Gorham and spread rapidly, fueled by drought conditions. No residential structures are currently threatened.

While the fire’s cause is still under investigation, a Forest Service spokesperson told New Hampshire Public Radio that experts believe it was caused by human activity.

A closure order is in effect in the area around the Wild River Fire, as shown on the map below. The Appalachian Trail passes northwest of the fire and remains open, although the Appalachian Trail Conservancy urged hikers in the area to use caution, follow all instructions from fire crews and posted signs, and be aware they may see and smell smoke. The organization also cautioned hikers that the Kenduskeag Trail, which connects to the AT at northbound mile 1,894.8, is closed.

As recently as yesterday, the fire was estimated at nearly 1,000 acres, but that estimate shrank today as a result of updated mapping. However, 856 acres is still an unprecedented size for a wildfire in this region. “That’s very uncommon in our area,” Gorham Fire Chief Philip Cloutier told NH Public Radio on Wednesday. “The largest wildfire that we can remember was just under 100 acres, and that was over 20 years ago.”

Despite dry conditions on the ground and challenging terrain, the Forest Service said in a press release that firefighters are making steady progress on suppression efforts. “I am proud of the firefighters who responded quickly and continue to work tirelessly to contain the Wild River Fire,” noted Josh Sjostrom, District Ranger for the White Mountain National Forest’s Androscoggin Ranger District. “We will continue to work with our neighbors and local and state partners to contain this fire.”

Check the White Mountain National Forest Facebook page and the Watch Duty app for updates on the status of the Wild River Fire.

#8409. The Biggest Archery Mistakes You’re Making This Bow Season

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:22 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Over the past 20 years, I’ve shot, competed with and hunted with everything from selfbows to compounds. If there’s a mistake you can make while shooting a bow, I’ve done it. Luckily, I’ve also had the chance to learn from world-class coaches, Olympians, and the best archers in the world. So I’ve learned how to fix the worst errors and spot trouble in other bowhunters.

Here are five common archery mistakes that new and experienced bowhunters make that ultimately cost opportunities in the field.

The easiest archery flaw to fix is also one of the most common ones. When you grip your bow properly, it becomes easier to tune, and your accuracy will improve because you won’t induce inconsistent torque into the bow. To grip your bow, place your hand as high as it will go in the grip, turn your knuckles so they’re at a 45-degree angle to the riser and make sure the bow touches your hand only between your thumb pad and lifeline.

Read Next: How to Grip a Compound Bow for Better Hunting Accuracy

Have you ever used the wrong pin, forgotten to look through your peep or fired as soon as your pin was close to a deer’s kill zone? Those mistakes happen because you’re relying on your subconscious to shoot the bow.

In the backyard, you can let your subconscious run the shot. Heck, you could shoot half asleep and do all right. But shooting under pressure is a different story. You can’t trust your subconscious in those situations because it will take shortcuts to skip to the ultimate goal — firing the arrow. It’s a lot like AI: It finds the most efficient solution, and wiping you out might be mere collateral damage.

Instead of relying on autopilot, you need a firm shot process that you fully control. Make a list of the key steps of your shot and check them off one by one. This keeps you in the present and focused on the process, not the result.

Read Next: Target Panic! Joel Turner and Joe Rogan Talk Archery

With time and repetitions, your strings can move, which affects your bow’s tune and sight tape. Don’t be one of those hunters who misses an easy shot because their sight was off or their drop-away rest timing changed. Every month or so, check your sight and rest timing, shoot your bow through paper and make sure your broadheads are in tune.

When you first learned to shoot a bow, someone probably told you that you need a consistent anchor point. But that doesn’t mean you need to anchor the string into your face. Pressing your face or your nose against the string causes oscillation, which leads to left-and-right inconsistencies. The string can touch your face, but only lightly.

If you find yourself trying really hard to hold your bow steady, you’re approaching archery the wrong way. A steady aim is the result of your form and bow setup. There’s no muscling your way to it. You also can’t make your pin stop moving. The goal is for your pin to have a slow, consistent float around the spot. Once you achieve that, your next job is to focus on shot execution.

When you make a change to your archery form or your bow, it’s normal for your accuracy to suffer at first. Trust the process during that learning period, and shoot at a big target such as the Blackout Longshot 36. The goal during the period is to get used to your change and not care about accuracy until your shot feels good again.

#8407. Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Plan B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team said that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”

One of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

The situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet

There was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

Nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet

“We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza said.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

The Spanish team sent us the video below summarizing the climb.

#8404. ‘It’s Trailer Park Chemistry.’ A Hybrid Bighorn Sheep Is on the Lam and That Could Be Bad News for Wild Herds

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:47 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The two-paragraph Sept. 18 news release from Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks raised more questions than it may have intended.

The department “is seeking help from the public to locate a hybridized female rocky mountain bighorn sheep that went missing from a private alternative livestock facility near Vaughn in early September,” the release from FWP’s Region 4 office in Great Falls stated. “The bighorn ewe is described as weighing about 120 pounds and is primarily white in color with a red ear tag.”

The news release stressed wildlife officials’ concern that the ewe could come into contact with wild bighorn sheep in the vicinity. Domestic sheep are often vectors for pathogens that can fatally infect wild sheep.

What the news release didn’t disclose is that the “alternative livestock facility” in question is owned by Arthur “Jack” Schubarth, who was convicted in 2024 of violating the federal Lacey Act in his pursuit to create giant hybrid bighorn rams. Schubarth pleaded guilty to helping smuggle genetic material from Marco Polo argali sheep from Kyrgyzstan into the United States in order to clone the ram and create a “super sheep” with huge spiraling horns and resistance to the pathogens that infect North American wild sheep. His quest was enabled by Montana hunting outfitter John Lewton, who lopped off the testicles of his clients’ trophy wild bighorns, kept the gonads on ice, and later sold them to Schubarth.

The idea, Schubarth later told court officials, was to use the genetic material to incubate hybrid sheep with horns larger than any North American rams.

Lewton was sentenced last week in federal court in Billings and received a $20,000 fine and a year of probation for his part in the genetic alchemy. As a condition of his federal-court sentence, Lewton is prohibited from outfitting or guiding hunters for a full year.

The notion that a “Frankenram” could be produced with a combination of cloned embryos and artificial insemination isn’t an abstraction. In 2017, Schubarth actually produced what he called the Montana Mountain King, a pure cloned Marco Polo ram birthed to a surrogate bighorn ewe. Schubarth subsequently bred offspring of the Montana Mountain King to captive bighorn ewes on his farm west of Great Falls. It’s one of these ewes that has now gone missing, according to Fish, Wildlife & Parks.

Schubarth’s genetic hermetics has both baffled and impressed wildlife investigators, who told Outdoor Life that the sort of reproductive science that Schubarth practiced is normally limited to hospitals, universities, and other science centers with state-of-the-art facilities.

“The best way to describe his operation is trailer-park chemistry,” said a source familiar with the case who spoke on background. “He’s pulled off a pretty high-level genetics program with hardware-store gear and limited resources.”

Schubarth received probation for his guilty plea to the Lacey Act violations. In his petition to the federal court for leniency, Schubarth’s attorney, Jason Holden, noted his client’s contribution to the science of wildlife propagation.

“Jack is an 81-year-old non-violent man,” Holden wrote in 2024. “His crime, the cloning of a Marco Polo Sheep from Kyrgyzstan, has ruined his life, reputation and family. Jack did something no one else could, or has ever done. On a ranch, in a barn in Montana, he created Montana Mountain King. MMK is an extraordinary animal, born of science, and from a man who, if he could rewrite history, would have left the challenge of cloning a Marco Polo to only the imagination of Michael Crichton.”

Read Next: Montana Man Charged for Illegally Cloning and Breeding Marco Polo Sheep from Central Asia

The department’s all-points-bulletin asking the public to report a lone and roaming ewe may not produce any sightings. That’s because there’s a possibility that the ewe isn’t actually on the lam. She may have been sold to an out-of-state game farm, said sources who spoke to Outdoor Life on the condition that they wouldn’t be identified based on the speculative nature of their hunches.

Schubarth, who is on probation from the 2024 federal wildlife-trafficking charges, has been charged by FWP with failure to report the escape of an animal permitted in his commercial wildlife operation, according to charging documents at the Cascade County District Court in Montana.

The “game farm” permit requires that if anything escapes the permitted facility, owners must report within 48 hours to both FWP and the Montana Department of Livestock.

“According to our records, the ewe in question reportedly escaped on Sept. 2, and our game wardens heard about it the next week,” says Dave Hagengruber, FWP’s public information officer in the Great Falls regional office. “Wardens went out to talk with Schubarth in mid-September, and he basically said, ‘Oh yeah, I meant to tell you.’”

Schubarth told wardens the ewe likely escaped either over a fence damaged by a wind storm or through a gate accidentally left open at the end of his property, beyond lines of kennels of dogs that produce puppies sold in Schubarth’s pet store in Great Falls.

Assuming the ewe did leave Schubarth’s facility, it could pose a risk to the region’s wild sheep.

“Cascade is 30 miles from his farm, and there’s a sizeable band of [wild] bighorns there,” says Hagengruber. “The Birdtail Hills are 20 to 25 miles to the west, and there are bighorns in those hills. The Rocky Mountain Front, home to Montana’s most treasured bighorn sheep herd, is 60 or 70 miles west. Fortunately, this is not a ram, so it’s less likely to roam widely, but the threat of disease transmission is a significant concern. That’s why we want to hear of any sightings. It’s Jack’s property and his responsibility to locate and return to his facility, but we can’t have this hybrid sheep potentially contacting wild bands.”

Schubarth insists he did not sell the ewe, and suspects the fugitive sheep was killed by predators within a few miles of his facility in the Sun River Valley.

“I haven’t heard anything about her, and to my knowledge Fish and Game hasn’t heard anything for five weeks now,” Schubarth said in an interview. “With all the people out looking, we haven’t seen it and no one’s called me. I’m assuming, with her lack of experience with predators, that a coyote got her.”

“She’s mainly bighorn and probably three or four domestic crosses from the original cross that was 50 percent bighorn,” Schubarth said. “I added some more bighorn from that original [parentage]. So they’re probably 62.5 percent bighorn. They don’t have any experience of being wild. I’m pretty sure she would have watched coyotes walk right up to her” without trying to evade them.

Schubarth further confirmed that he still has “around 45 head of sheep, is all” remaining on his 200-acre game farm. “All my sheep are sold right now and just waiting to leave. I’ve kept them back because I just want the pleasure of birthing out the lambs. It’s something I like to do, and at 83 years old, I like to see new life.”

As for the descendants of the Montana Mountain King, Schubarth said that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service required him to destroy progeny of the cloned ram back in 2024. The federal court also required Schubarth to dispose of all hybrid bighorn sheep by Dec. 31, 2025, and to stop “from engaging in breeding activity of big game stock while on supervision,” according to sentencing documents.

“We had 190 head of the hybrid Marco/bighorn here at the ranch and none of them got pneumonia in the three years I held them while waiting for a forever home for them. All were slaughtered,” he says. “I did sell some, 15 in all. There are some down in Texas, and every so often I see on Facebook somebody advertising a Marco Polo, but there’s no way they are more than about a quarter Marco” based on genetic dilution, he said.

As for the Montana Mountain King himself, Schubarth says the ram ended up at a zoological park in upstate New York. Indeed, last summer the Rosamond Gifford Zoo in Syracuse, New York, announced the acquisition of “Tilek,” the cloned argali at the center of Schubarth’s case. The ram had been held at an Oregon wildlife rehabilitation center for over three years before being moved to the Syracuse zoo.

Schubarth says “Tilek” would be about nine years old, but observed that he has not yet expressed the most distinctive trait of the Marco Polo subspecies of argali: its spiraling horns.

“He’s basically still 54 to 57 inches,” says Schubarth. “He ought to have 75 inches of horn on each side. But this year they put him in a larger grass pen so maybe he’ll grow more. For safety’s sake, they should have castrated him so no more genetics could get out there. Maybe they did, for all I know. I’ll never see him again. I don’t ever leave my ranch.”

Schubarth said that statements from prosecutors that he was motivated to create a hybrid ram with giant horns in order to upsell to commercial shooting operations are wrong. He was more interested in cross-breeding to create a bighorn race that might be resistant to what’s often called “M. ovi,” a respiratory disease that often results in catastrophic pneumonia-caused die-offs in wild sheep.

“My thinking was that here’s this wild sheep that has evolved with domestic sheep for thousands of years,” says Schubarth of the Marco Polo, native to the high alpine plateaus of central Asia. “The feds and Fish and Game made it out that I was selling to the hunt community and only motivated to create bigger horns. In actuality, I was after the immune system, and the reality is that even after several generations, these Marco hybrids still seem to be immune to pneumonia. I think that’s the real story.”

If he regrets anything about the misadventures of the Montana Mountain King, it’s that he trusted the lab that created the clone from genetic tissue smuggled from Kyrgyzstan.

“I’ve been happy all my life except for this last foolishness about the Marco Polo,” Schubarth says. “I wouldn’t have done it had the cloning company not told me it was legal. They lied after they took $32,000 from me. That was the cost of stockpiling the tissue and making the embryos for me.”

The rest of the genetic work was a cinch, he says. The surrogate bighorn ewes, most of which Schubarth bought from zoos in Canada and Colorado, were selected for their ability to carry the hybrid lamb.

“Laparoscopic work is easy,” he says, and artificial insemination is an established livestock practice. The trick is creating a genetically manipulated zygote.

“You take the egg and suck out the product and you put the material from the Marco Polo into the egg and implant it in a ewe. A little electricity, and poof, the thing starts to grow.”

Schubarth says he will be entirely out of the game-breeding business by 2027.

“Fish and Game has accomplished what they always wanted: to drive me out of business,” he says.

Meanwhile, he says the captive-shooting industry is thriving. He cites high-fence operations in Kansas and Texas that would pay top dollar for his hybrid bighorns while also insisting that he sold to fellow breeders, not trophy hunters.

“The feds made it out that I was the center of this industry based on shooting animals in pens,” he says, before acknowledging that most of his animals probably met that fate. “Without the interest of the hunting community, these animals would be worthless and only sold for meat. So yes, the industry revolves around the harvesting of these animals by collectors.”

Fish, Wildlife & Parks is less interested in the commercial than in the pathological outcome of the case. The state has struggled to establish bighorn sheep populations in prime habitat in the Missouri River Breaks and in the mountains of southwest Montana. Bands that thrive for years are often wiped out in a single season by pneumonia epizootics that often originate in domestic sheep.

State game wardens are authorized to shoot on sight wild bighorns that contact domestic sheep. The fear is that a traveling ram could become infected by a domestic sheep, and then take that pathogen back to the wild herd.

“We have spent many years and sportsmen’s dollars to restore and transplant wild sheep into available habitat in Montana,” says FWP’s Hagengruber. “We’ve had recent restorations in the Belts and the Breaks, and disease is always a big concern, and so is the ability of this hybrid ewe to breed with either domestic or wild sheep. So we take the possibility that there may be a hybrid domestic/wild sheep running around central Montana very seriously.”

Anyone who sees a lone sheep with a red ear tag in central Montana is urged to call FWP’s Region 4 office at 406-454-5840.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8403. Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

The image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who plan to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#8402. To The Hospital — John Muir Trail Days 7 and 8

After a night in the Motel 6, I got up, took the car keys Sam left me, and went to the Northern Inyo Hospital.  It was a sunny day in Bishop, California.  My stomach was still full of barbecue from the night before.

My hospital! (Photo credit to India M. Clamp)

The people at the hospital were really nice.  They checked me in.  I thought I packed my insurance card but could not find it.  Fortunately, I had my insurance card on my phone and was able to email that to them.  The nurse took my temperature and other vital signs.

A moment later the doctor came in, and I told her about my health, and the John Muir Trail, and how I wondered whether my hike was finished.  Then she put her stethoscope on my chest for about five seconds.  I was puzzled, but she said, “Look, we’re going to take a chest x-ray to rule out pneumonia.  But regardless of the outcome of that x-ray, we’re going to put you on antibiotics.  The x-ray will tell us which particular antibiotic, but that’s about it.”

I agreed (what else was I going to do?) and they wheeled me off for the x-ray.  Then, after the chest x-ray, nothing happened for a long time. I waited in my little cubby in the Emergency Room for about an hour and a half.  I began to wonder what was going on.

In the meantime, I went to the bathroom.  I began to feel cold and asked them for a blanket.  Finally, the doctor returned and said my chest x-ray looked okay.  She said, “We are going to give you Z-pak.”

According to Google AI: “Z-Pak (azithromycin) is a common brand-name prescription antibiotic (Zithromax) taken over a 5-day course to treat bacterial infections like bronchitis, pneumonia, and ear or throat infections.”  Sounded about right.

She said, “Go to Duane’s Pharmacy in town.  You will get six tablets.  Take two today and then one a day for the following four days.”  She also prescribed some codeine cough medication as well as cough pearls.

Then I said, “Well, doctor, you know what my next question is going to be, right?”

She paused for a few seconds and then replied, “You want to know whether you can go back out on the trail.”

I nodded and she said, “I’ll tell you what.  Take off today and take off tomorrow.  See how you respond to the antibiotic.  If you’re feeling a lot better, I think you can go back on the trail.”

Sam and I checked out of the Motel 6 and drove south, stopping for lunch back at the Copper Top BBQ.  We each had the same order:  Tri-Tip hamburgers and chocolate cake.  Oh, it was so good!

Right at that corner in Big Pine was a sign for the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest turnoff.  Having the free time, we drove 45 minutes up into the White Mountains of Inyo County on the east side of the valley (the Sierras are on the west side).  I had never heard of “ancient bristlecone pines” but these trees are apparently the oldest living things on earth.

Bristlecone Pine (thanks to Wal Saravia and Pexels)

Some of these trees are over 4,000 years old.  They live at high altitude in rocky soil under arid conditions.  These factors make them incredibly hardy.  Some are able to continue growing even with just a tiny strip of bark left on them.

Sadly, the location of the oldest tree of all, “Methuselah,” is kept secret to prevent damage from vandals.  Who would do something like that?  But it is not a hypothetical fear.  According to Wikipedia:  “On September 4, 2008, an arsonist set fire to the Schulman Grove Visitor Center and several bristlecone pines. The building and all the exhibits within were destroyed.”  Appalling.

On our way back down, we tried searching for fossils.  We did not have much luck, but we did find a beautiful yellow flowering plant.

Can anyone identify this? Beautiful in any case!

Back in Independence, we checked into the Eastern Sierra Motor Lodge, where we had stayed before setting off the previous week.  It felt like it had been a much longer interval than that.  Sam’s room was for one night; my room was for two nights.

I started to think about unpacking and seeing what I had in the sealed resupply bucket I left in Sam’s car.  No surprise, I had too much food, though not as much as I feared.  The Mount Williamson Motel (of Lauralyn fame) was across the road and had a hiker box for excess food.  So, it would not necessarily go to waste.

That night we went south into Lone Pine and had a steak dinner at Seasons Restaurant.  They ran out of filet mignon, so I had to suffer through a sirloin steak.  What a sacrifice!  I stayed away from the wine for health reasons.  Instead, Sam and I each had a couple of Heineken Zeros.

Sleeping through the night was going to be the big test of the antibiotics.  I had codeine cough medicine and pearls but decided I would not take any – at least at first — because I had taken my two Zithromax at lunch and I wanted to see how I was responding.

Yes, I woke up several times in the night to pee.  But each time I did, I didn’t cough more than two or three times before falling back asleep.  Basically, I slept through the night.

Sam planned to leave for the Las Vegas Airport around mid-morning and asked me to set my alarm so we could go for breakfast together.  When it went off, I immediately asked myself, “How did the night go?”

The answer was promising.  Yes, I felt weak, but I produced much less mucus and coughed much less.  The improvement was dramatic.

Sam and I drove down to Lone Pine to eat at the Alabama Hills Café and Bakery again.  This time we had eggs Benedict with bacon and avocado.  Yes, delicious.  Then we took a drive through the namesake Alabama Hills, famous as the location site for many old Western movies and TV shows.  Many of the boulders are named for images they (ostensibly) suggest and one or two are actually painted.  You can learn more about this area (with pictures) here.

A sample of Alabama Hills (thanks to Allie Feeley and Pexels)

Then we drove back to Independence and soon thereafter, Sam left.  He was headed home.  I was on my own.  Despite my illness, I really enjoyed our time together and appreciated his kindness during my ordeal.  At the same time, I am very used to hiking solo, so there was no anxiety surrounding the change.

After that I loafed about trying to decide how I was feeling, how much impact the antibiotics were having.  I asked myself, “Should I go back on trail tomorrow, or try to take one more day before going back?”  It was a balance between being cautious with my health and being brave enough to get back out there.

I sat outside my room at the motel pondering my options.

The Eastern Sierra Motor Lodge with my socks drying in the foreground and the High Sierra in the background.

Before deciding, I elected to take a walk through town.

First, I dropped off my excess food and gear at the Mount Williamson Motel.  They told me they would not provide transportation to the trailhead for non-guests, but they gave me a name and number for “Mark.”   They said hikers often hired him for that purpose.

I continued down the road, past a stand selling “miel” (honey), and I fell. My first fall on the trail!  It was kind of weird.

The town’s configuration at street crossings entails bright yellow indicators painted on the ground to show where the crosswalks are.  These are at right angles (depending on which road you are crossing at the intersection) and, in between the two, there is a raised concrete block right on the corner.  That block has no marking on it at all, making it kind of invisible, particularly with sunglasses.  I didn’t see that there was a step.  Suddenly I was just  flying onto the ground in the bright sunshine on the hard concrete sidewalk and trying to protect my head to avoid hurting myself severely.

Although it was a dramatic fall, and somebody came running over right away from the miel-selling place, I was actually okay.  Maybe I bruised my elbow just a little bit.  But how funny that my first fall on the John Muir Trail should occur while walking without a pack in the bright sunshine of downtown Independence, California.

There are two places that advertise Mexican food in Independence, but the first one I visited was only open Monday to Friday and this was a Sunday.  The other was a taco truck pop-up next to the Shell station.  I had two carnitas, one asada, and one chorizo there, all really good tacos with a Jarritos de Mandarina (a Mexican tangerine-flavored soft drink) to wash them down.  It was wonderful.

Since I was still close to my motel, I ordered dinner and breakfast to go.  I got a dinner burrito of carnitas asadas, and a breakfast burrito of chorizo for the morning.  I put those in my hotel room and then headed out to the Eastern Sierra Ice Cream Company.

I swear the pure lime they sell there is absolutely the best.  I tried the orange one, which is supposed to be similar, but the lime was just better, so very tart.  This flavor was especially welcome because it was hot.

The temperature was “only” in the low to mid-90s, but the sun was just blasting down.  No one else was foolish enough to walk around town like I was.

Still, I enjoyed the chance to sight-see and I took some pictures of the town.  It was still the Inyo County seat, attesting to a former dynamism.  My picture of that distinguished building — the Inyo County Courthouse — tops this blog post.  But now the town was just dead.  It was weird.

It felt like a ghost town.  Here we were, in peak tourist season too, so it was very strange.  Though I did encounter an attractive young woman and almost persuaded her to come back to my room with me.  At least she let me take a photo of the two of us together which you can see below.

Back in my room (alone) I took stock.  No, I was not ALL better yet.  But I was much better than I had been and was finally trending toward recovery.  I had taken two ‘Zero’ days and would be falling out of alignment with my John Muir Trail permit if I took any more.  With some trepidation, I called Mark and arranged for a pickup at the motel the next morning at 6 a.m.

“Here I come,” I thought.  “I’m going back on the trail tomorrow.  At least, I’m going to try.  I have a 2,700-foot pass to climb right off the bat, so that will be a good test.  And if I can only make 2,500 feet of that, I can still turn around.  I can still come back down.”

I realized also that once I got over the pass, and headed into the High Sierra, I would be kind of committed to keeping on.  The “bail-out” points were few and challenging.  A couple of days earlier I did not expect to be on my way back to Kearsarge Pass, that was for sure.  But now I was going to try.

There was a lot to do before turning in.  I ate the dinner burrito.  It was enormous.  I guessed my hiker hunger was abating, because I couldn’t even finish it.

In assembling my gear, I could not find one of my canteens.  I looked everywhere.  Maybe it was in Sam’s rental car?  Sam gave me his Smartwater bottle, so I still had two water containers.  But I wanted to keep that canteen as it was easier to fill with a filtering squeeze bottle.

What else?  I took a shower, texted, sent emails, and called a bunch of people:  wife, son, friends.

I trimmed my nails a little bit.  They weren’t too long, but the shower presented an opportunity to trim them now.  Who knows whether or when I would be able to do it again the rest of the trip?

The hair tie holding my ponytail I did not even try to remove.  I accepted that my hair was already a complete rat’s nest and it was only going to get worse.

In my supply bucket was an alternate finger splint.  I wore a splint religiously on trail, trying to recover from a mallet finger sustained on my longest and hardest training hike.  In Independence I threw out the old splint and replaced it with the new one.

I packed my backpack.  That was challenging.  I love my backpack, but it was actually just a little too small for what I was carrying on this trip.  Adding the bear cannister crossed the tipping point.  Somehow, I was still making it work.

I tested my umbrella.  I thought, “If I can get that sun umbrella to work, it could actually help me a lot.”

With my new-and-untested 20,000 mAh power bank charged I had taken care of my electronics (except for the “untested” part).

I even spent a little time memorizing lines for my role in “Almost, Maine.”  Lee and I were slated to perform in that play after my return.

All this activity was exhausting me.  So, I completed these trail notes, set my alarm, and hit the mattress.  As I dozed off, I thought, “I hope my next set of trail notes convey a successful first day back on the trail…”

She and I had similar political views.  Indeed… “Make Pupusas, Not War”

#8400. How to Field Dress a Deer Like a Pro: The Ultimate Step-By-Step Guide

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:10 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Learning (or remembering) how to field dress a deer can feel overwhelming, but if you have a sharp knife and a reasonably strong stomach, you’ll be able to figure it out. If you manage to do so without nicking the guts or yourself, that’s ideal.

Removing the guts is the bare minimum required for dropping a deer at a processor, and an essential skill every deer hunter should learn. A field-dressed deer is also a lighter deer, which makes dragging and loading it less cumbersome. And the sooner you gut a deer after shooting it, the better the venison will be. So, here’s a guide on how to field dress a deer in a few easy steps.

All you really need to gut a deer is a sharp knife and, if it’s getting dark, a good headlamp. Other deer hunters carry the kitchen sink with them and won’t field dress a deer without some or all of the following items:

Many experienced deer hunters can field dress a deer in minutes, while it can take new or casual deer hunters a half hour or more. The best way to gut a deer is to work slowly, use a sharp knife, and have adequate lighting.

Keep these gutting rules in mind before you get started:

Start by rolling the deer onto its back. It should be belly-up and evenly balanced on both shoulder blades. Adjust the rump and hips to ensure they’re as even as possible. If you’re working on a slope, rotate the deer so its rump points downhill and its head is uphill.

Ask a buddy to hold a leg. If you’re solo and the deer keeps slipping sideways or downhill, try wedging a log or stick under its rump or using paracord to tie a hind leg to a branch. Personally, I find paracord to be overkill, but will sometimes use my knee, shoulder, or armpit to anchor a hind leg or keep it out of the way as I work.

This step and the next can be done now or after opening the abdominal cavity. Grab a handful of the mammary gland, or testicles with your non-dominant hand and lift away from the deer’s body. Keeping your blade mostly parallel to the deer’s body, slice away at the base of the stretched hide until you’ve freed the reproductive organs, and toss aside. The goal is to avoid cutting into the organs and instead cutting under them.

This step can be done later or not at all, but I prefer to do this now (particularly when working alone) since it relaxes the tension between the hind legs and prevents your deer from rolling on you. It also creates more space to work while removing internal organs. I butcher my own deer and this does not sacrifice any of the meat on the hindquarters when done correctly.

Cut the muscle between the two back legs to expose the center of the pelvic bone. Find what looks like dead center on the meat between the two back legs and cut down (usually a few inches) from the top of the pelvis to the anus. Stay as close to the center as possible to avoid gouging the roasts on either leg. Don’t saw the muscle. Slice it instead, letting the downward pressure of your blade do the cutting.

Insert your knife tip into the side (not the center) of the anus. Keeping your blade pressed against the bone that encircles the rectum, cut around the rectum rather than through it. The goal is to cut the connective tissue so you can pull the tube of intestines out rather than dice it up.

This abdominal cut is often the most difficult for hunters, and the key here is not to puncture the deer’s stomach or bladder because you don’t want to get any bile or urine on the meat.

Prevent stabbing the guts by turning your knife blade up (toward the sky) and tilting it so the blade is more parallel to the deer’s belly rather than perpendicular. Working close to the base of the belly, grab a handful of hide and pull it up to create some space between the layer of hide and the organs beneath. Insert the tip of your knife and make an incision until you see (or more likely, feel with the knife tip) empty space below it. Keep the incision shallow and make the slit long enough to work a finger or two of your off-hand in the space. Take care to not insert the blade too far into the abdominal cavity.

Now that you’ve made an opening incision, apply even upward pressure with your knife blade to “unzip” the abdomen, or make a lengthwise cut along the deer from pelvis to breastbone. This is similar to using a pair of scissors to slice a piece of wrapping paper in a single, fluid motion. Don’t saw with your knife.

The organs you’re ultimately trying to remove lie in two groups: the guts (liver, stomach, intestines, bladder, kidneys, fat if present, etc.) and the vitals (heart and lungs). These two groups are separated by the diaphragm: a thin wall of purple muscle between the abdominal cavity and the rib cage.

Note: If you plan to shoulder mount your deer, do not split the ribs. You should only make your cut to the base of the lower ribcage (above) and stop there, since your taxidermist will need all that hide from the ribs to the tip of the nose (this is called the cape).

If you are planning on a skull mount or you aren’t mounting your deer at all, you can split the ribs if you want. Your blade will encounter some resistance once you hit the rib cage. If you center your knife, you can slice through cartilage in the breastplate before hitting bone. Some hunters use a hatchet or saw to split the rib cage open, but a stout fixed-blade knife will also work. Splitting the rib cage makes it easier to see (and therefore remove) the heart and lungs, but isn’t necessary if you are having trouble cutting through it. This step is especially useful if you suspect a broadhead is lodged in the rib cage.

Personally, I just carry a slim field-dressing knife when I hunt and skip this step altogether during rifle season. I don’t mind reaching into the rib cage to remove the lungs, heart, and windpipe by feel.

To access the heart and lungs in the rib cage (and ultimately free everything) you need to cut the diaphragm. Use the tip of your knife to puncture this thin layer of muscle, then circle the entire rib cage, keeping your knife close to the ribs. Once the diaphragm has been cut away, blood and jellied bits of lung usually slosh into the abdominal cavity. This is perfectly normal (and a sign of a good shot).

Work from the top of deer down toward the pelvis. If you split open the rib cage this part will be easier; if not, you’ll have to do it more by feel.

At the top of the chest cavity, you’ll see or feel a large ribbed tube. That’s the windpipe. Cut it crossways (perpendicular to the spine), then use a finger or two to grab ahold of it from the inside and begin pulling it up and away. This will begin to loosen the heart and lungs.

Grab hold of the heart and/or lungs with your off-hand and pull while continuing to cut connective tissue along the spine. Keep going all the way down to the pelvis and keep working until the stomach and guts come loose, too. Because all the organs are attached to the deer along the spine, it can be helpful to tilt the deer on its side for this part so the organs roll out of your way and reveal their connection point.

As everything loosens, just roll the guts and intestines out of the deer and onto the ground. Note: If you haven’t yet separated the rectum from the anus, the guts will still connect to the carcass by a single tube — that’s the lower large intestines, or colon. To free the guts and toss aside, slice the colon crossways just above the pelvis and tie it off (if it’s full) so pellets don’t spill inside your deer.

Read Next: How to Skin a Deer, Step by Step

To field dress big game with a hatchet, use it as you would a big belt knife, opening the paunch with a small incision at the base of the sternum. Then, tip the blade at right angles to the animal, with the handle up and your fingers spreading the skin close to the blade as you run it to the rectum. Do not try to cut the skin down into the animal; hair will collect on and dull the blade. Dump the entrails.

To quarter the carcass, hang it or set it belly-up on the ground. Loosen hams with careful strokes tight against the pelvis and through the ball joints. Don’t chop; use the blade like a knife, your fist around the hatchet head (inset). Remove the shoulders the same way, leaving the skin on unless you must remove it to let a big animal, like an elk or moose, cool in warm weather. The hatchet (or, better yet, a slim double-bit ax) excels at splitting the backbone. Hang the animal head down, rear legs spread, to facilitate this task. —Wayne Van Zwoll

It’s always best to gut your deer as soon as possible, but the window you have depends on the weather and the shot you made. If the weather is hot or even mild, the sooner you field dress your deer, the better. Within an hour of the shot is ideal in these conditions. If it’s cold, a deer can last longer before it needs to be gutted — hours or even overnight if you have to back out while blood trailing. It’s always easier to dress a deer when it’s warm and pliable.

The best knives for field dressing are usually a fixed-blade knife with a sharp blade. A smaller, handier blade makes certain tasks easier, like removing the colon and avoiding puncturing the guts. A larger, stouter blade is easier for heavy-duty tasks like splitting the ribs.

Field-dressing a deer isn’t difficult once you get the hang of it, and it’s usually easier with a buddy to help hold a leg or a light. Use a sharp knife, make slow, deliberate cuts at connective tissue. Do your best to avoid puncturing the stomach or bladder, but don’t panic if you do. More important is to avoid cutting yourself. The process may be messy or unpleasant, but ultimately you’ll end up with a cooling carcass ready for the skinning shed or processor.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8396. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

While they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

The people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

Early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0

A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

Farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0

Leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

Locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

Elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India

In Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Company

None of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Company officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.
