#8395. ‘Squirrels as Big as House Cats.’ We Competed in the Greatest Squirrel Dog Contest in the Country

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

“Neighbor down the road had a squirrel dog,” said Larry White as he led a cast of dogs and hunters to the woods. “Got its legs cut off by a mowing machine. Had to hunt that dog from a wheelbarrow.

“One day a friend asked to borrow the dog, so the owner explained that you had to push the wheelbarrow in whatever direction the dog pointed his nose. If he barked, the track was hot, so you pushed faster. When he looked up and barked, he had the squirrel treed and you got a shot. The friend came back late that night with no squirrels. His clothes were torn to shreds and his skin was scratched up and looked like a road map. ‘What in the world happened to you?’ the hound’s owner asked.

“‘What’s it look like?’ the friend snapped. ‘Your fool squirrel dog hit a deer and we ran that thing all day long!'”

Larry White was judging a cast in the 1981 World Champion Squirrel Hunt. His tale got a laugh, but it also emphasized the importance of handler/dog teamwork in any form of hunting.

A good squirrel dog works for the hunter by locating squirrels through scent on the ground and on trees as well as by seeing and following bushytails moving through the treetops. The dog’s manner of barking signals its degree of progress to the hunter. A good hunter works for the dog by staying keenly and constantly aware of what the barking means and by following almost within sight so he can get to the tree quickly and shoot the squirrel before it escapes.

Good competition squirrel dogs are more decisive, accurate and consistent than average squirrel dogs. They do the job with less wasted time and motion.

Squirrel-treeing talent always has been wherever you found it, but these days some unusual dogs are showing up in the woods. Chuck Trehern’s purebred Doberman pinscher learned to bark up a tree by watching the family coonhounds. Ronnie Liles’ 6-year-old Australian shepherd, Smokey, was never taught: he just started treeing squirrels. T.C. Jones won the 1980 Championship with a registered liver and white English pointer! Trophies similar to bowling trophies are awarded. The statuettes portray a dog barking treed.

Most squirrel dogs are not pedigreed, however. Two Illinois dogs were described as terrier and feist crosses. Randy Pannell, who trains 15 to 20 squirrel dogs every year, came over from Blue Springs, Mississippi, with a redtick coonhound/mountain cur cross. Fola Hart brought a Norwegian elkhound/feist cross from Virginia. And the 1981 winner was Orville Hart’s “Whiskey,” a 4-year-old Norwegian elkhound/feist from Leesburg, Ohio.

Feists, those wiry little mongrels that are intelligent enough to learn any job on the farm, are becoming rare because most people prefer to keep purebred dogs. As a result, many squirrel hunters are making their own mongrels by crossing two different purebreds. There’s a constant search for the best dog, and that’s one reason why Dick Sheets thought up the World Champion Squirrel Hunt.

Sheets reasoned that squirrel-dog competition would not only preserve and enlarge the sport, but that the dogs would improve through breeding. Perhaps breeds of purebred squirrel dogs of consistent ability would emerge from such an effort. The Yockanookany Coon Hunters Association of Ethel, Mississippi, agreed with Sheets and sponsored the first championship in 1980.

Yockanookany is Choctaw for “crawls on belly like snake” and also applies to the way hunters must cross a spongy swamp. The 100-mile-long Yockanookany Swamp is just two miles from the club grounds.

By 1981, competition had already influenced squirrel-dog breeding. L.E. Goutierez came over from Louisiana with two pups out of the 1980 second-place winner. The pups’ dam was Spot, his own small Chihuahua/feist cross.

Goutierez arrived a day early, pitched his tent and drove his dogs down the old Natchez Trace to the nearby woods where they could become accustomed to hunting new territory. The original Natchez Trace, which was once an extensive trading trail between the Indian tribes, runs right past the Yockanookany club grounds. The entire area is well forested with both hill-country and creek-bottom squirrel habitat.

Little Spot ran through the woods with her nose slightly down, searching for scent on the ground, on logs and on fallen limbs. Every tree got a sniff as she trotted past. But the squirrels weren’t moving. When Spot finally barked, L.E. didn’t become excited. “She scatter-barked,” he said. “It’s a cold track.”

Scatter barking is barking here and there instead of barking enthusiastically in one place such as on a hot trail or at a tree.

By the end of the championship hunt, Goutierez had learned one more thing about breeding squirrel dogs. “Have to get more size in my dogs,” he said. “My dogs can’t compete with the longer-legged, wider-running dogs.”

Four dogs were cast together in the first running of the championship in 1980 and many handlers thought that that was three too many. By nature, squirrel dogs do best alone. They’re highly intelligent, very independent and more than a little jealous of their relationships with their human partners. In 1981, a compromise was struck: only two dogs to a cast—male and female, if possible—and in weight categories of under and over 35 pounds.

The only reported fight occurred when the Doberman’s handler decided to be gentlemanly and let his competitor’s dog smell the dead squirrel, too. Getting to smell the squirrel is an encouraging reward of sorts and the Dobe was not ready to share that with another dog.

An impartial judge accompanies each cast, but it is up to the handler to “call” his own dog—that is, notify the judge when satisfied his dog has treed. As in coonhound competition, 100 points are earned by the first dog at the tree, 75 by the second. Unlike coonhound scoring, no points are awarded for striking (finding) a trail. This is because sometimes the trail is short, sometimes there is none and too many squirrel dogs are silent trailers. Also unlike coonhound scoring, tree points are not subtracted if no squirrel is found in the tree because squirrels all too readily travel from tree to tree.

If the squirrel is not found, the tree points are circled and do not count on the final score. Judges are allowed considerable latitude, however. If the squirrel is seen several trees away from the one the dog is treeing on and the judge is satisfied that the squirrel could have gotten there through the treetops, he can give the dog credit for that squirrel.

Six or eight squirrels an hour is not impossible in well-populated timber when the bushytails are really active. Ronnie Liles’ Australian shepherd treed 700 for him and his friends during the past two years. “The trick,” said Liles, “is to catch ’em stirrin’. You might not see a squirrel today. But you can come back through the same place tomorrow and see 10.”

Ronnie believes that the old hunters’ barometer, “If the cows are lying down, so are the deer,” also applies to squirrels. And as he says, the dogs are helpless if they can’t see, smell or possibly hear the bushytails. The squirrel that hasn’t been on the ground and is lounging on a limb or in a vine tangle probably won’t be discovered by a dog unless falling air currents allow the dog to “wind” it. This would happen mostly during the cool of late afternoon rather than during early morning when the warming sunlight causes air to rise.

Liles prefers hunting little cat squirrels (grays) in the big, swampy, bottom timbers. Shaking a vine spooks grays out of hiding faster and easier than it does fox squirrels. Other hunters choose the hills where more fox squirrels live because they don’t like the way grays often chase off through the treetops when a dog barks.

Randy Pannell minimizes that problem by staying fairly close to his dog and then getting to the tree fast. In competition, however, that’s not always possible. The second dog has five minutes in which to join the first dog at the tree. During that time, handlers and the judge stay clear.

Both Pannell and Fola Hart demonstrated the wisdom of walking apart from other hunters. At 79, Fola appeared to be walking far behind because of age. But he was the first to hear his dog bark treed while other members of the cast were busy talking.

The perceptive rapport between hunter and squirrel dog is nothing less than amazing. During a Friday afternoon cast, Orville Hart was reluctant to say that Whiskey had treed. “Them two dogs are looking at us,” he observed. “If they believed they had the squirrel, they’d be looking up the tree!”

When a squirrel was shot in Ronnie Liles’ cast, Smokey grabbed it and ran off with the second dog in hot pursuit. As Smokey raced past his master’s leg, Ronnie grinned. “That dog expects me to catch the other dog as it goes by. Then Smokey will bring me the squirrel. He won’t let the other dog have it. But if another dog gets to the squirrel first, Smokey won’t bother it.” Retrieving is an added nicety, but it isn’t rewarded with extra points during the Yockanookany competition.

Some dogs won’t bark if their masters happen to be present when the squirrel is treed, strongly suggesting that they have enough reasoning power to recognize that, in such a case, the boss doesn’t have to be called.

Read Next: The Ultimate Guide to Buying and Training a Squirrel Dog

One Mississippi hunter recalled a boyhood dog that would always dance around the opposite side of the tree, yanking and shaking every vine or sapling it could find. Invariably, this commotion chased the squirrel around to the gunner’s side. Since such a dog is quite rare, hunters often go in pairs, taking turns circling the tree and shaking the bushes after the dog has treed.

What’s it take to train a dog that shows interest in squirrels? Mostly, lots of time in the squirrel woods. But trainer Randy Pannell speeds things up with a slingshot and steel pellets. “Just hit the tree near the squirrel, and it will bail out or take off,” Pannell said. “The dog gets a sight chase through the treetops or maybe a short ground chase. This works best with gray squirrels, especially the young ones. And there’s no problem with game laws while training dogs because you’re not killing or hunting the squirrels.”

Never study treetops when the dog is in sight and isn’t treeing. A perceptive dog believes you see the squirrel and will start treeing. And never bring the dog running by shooting at something other than a squirrel. Fooling a squirrel dog ruins it fast.

The Yockanookany fox squirrels are flat out the most colorful in America. Some are rusty orange, as expected, but others are decorated with white noses, feet and tail tips and, occasionally, black scalps. Others are solid black. Two taken during the 1981 Championship were black with white tips. Southern grays are smaller than Northern grays, but the fox squirrels are bigger. Some, according to reliable reports, grow half again as big as their Northern counterparts and range—according to very unreliable exaggerations—up to the size of house cats, groundhogs and raccoons.

Yankee squirrel hunters are treated so many different ways during the Yockanookany event that they have to like some. They travel from as far away as Michigan to enter the event. “We welcome Yankees; it’s only the Damn Yanks we don’t like,” said one young Southern belle with a wink.

#8393. Young Climbers Bag New Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

An energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two new routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

As soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

“Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

Cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” said Bazon.

The ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

Since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

The climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

It took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below shows that the new French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

Left: the new route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain

Meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

“It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”

But this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

Kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni

#8391. 6.5 Creedmoor Vs. .300 Win Mag: Here’s the Truth About Cartridge Selection

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:09 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

One of the most common arguments we hear in favor of choosing larger cartridges for hunting big game is that a magnum cartridge will offer margin for error. When considering cartridges like 6.5 Creedmoor vs. .300 Win. Mag., the .300 has more energy, drives a bigger bullet faster, and, we assume, will do more damage than the 6.5. That means that if we don’t hit exactly where we are aiming, we are more likely to still kill the animal cleanly by choosing the magnum. At face value, the logic is sound. But how does it hold up when we start examining what the bullets actually do downrange? You might be surprised.

There are two schools of thought that commonly divide hunters when it comes to choosing cartridges. One opts for milder cartridges that have lower recoil and are generally easier and more pleasant to shoot well. The other wants the extra power to cover their bases. Everyone, of course, falls somewhere on a spectrum, and the categories aren’t mutually exclusive.

I’ve written a lot about why I think smaller cartridges are often the right choice for big game, and it generally boils down to two observations. First, with thoughtful bullet selection, I haven’t noticed a dramatic difference between the wound characteristics of smaller and larger cartridges — and the smaller rounds have produced consistently satisfactory results. Second, milder cartridges are more pleasant to shoot and, despite having no real limitations on the cartridges I have access to, that’s what I reach for consistently. I have the rifles and ammo to torch a hundred rounds of .300 PRC in a range session practicing positional shooting but, realistically, I’m going to pick a 6.5 Creedmoor, 6 Creed, or 22 ARC to do that. Practice with smaller cartridges can also benefit how you’ll shoot magnums, but there’s a lot of value in hunting with the cartridge that you train with.

You’ll commonly hear hunters argue that you should choose the largest cartridge that you can handle without flinching — especially for larger game. Lots of hunters consider this basic conventional wisdom, and it’s rooted in the belief that a larger cartridge, bullet, or more kinetic energy will result in a larger wound and will kill the animal more quickly. This makes up for some degree of shooting error, or will allow more forgiveness on less-than-ideal shot angles. Essentially, choosing a more powerful cartridge is viewed as cheap insurance.

There are many ways that bigger cartridges like the .300 Win. Mag. outperform smaller ones like the 6.5 Creedmoor. When choosing something for yourself, you need to know what the real benefits are, and decide whether they actually apply to you and your hunting. What does that look like in terms of margin for error? That’s exactly what we took a look at in the video above.

I took a 6.5 Creedmoor and .300 Win. Mag. to the range and fired the same line of factory ammo — Federal Fusion Tipped — from each into identical blocks of Clear Ballistics gel. This gel isn’t a one-to-one representation of flesh, but it is a homogeneous, consistent medium in which we can get a side-by-side comparison of two bullets. The blocks were placed at 200 yards with a Garmin chronograph positioned about 15 yards in front of the target to record impact velocity. The Fusion Tipped bullets were 140 grains and 180 grains for the 6.5 CM and .300 Win. Mag., respectively. The rifles were the same except for different barrel lengths — 18 inches for the 6.5 CM and 22 inches for the .300. Impact velocities were recorded as 2,233 fps and 2,526 fps, with the advantage going to the .300.

As expected, the .300 Win. Mag. load delivered higher velocity and more energy at the target than the 6.5 Creedmoor. The block was knocked off the table and was clearly hit harder with the 180-grain slug than the 140. However, the actual wound cavities were not much different. The expanded diameters of the recovered bullets were within .015 inch when measuring both the extreme diameter of the jacket (which would typically be smashed down flat in an animal) and the diameter of mushroomed bullet bodies. The .30-caliber bullet left a slightly wider overall wound cavity across its traverse, disrupting slightly more tissue, but the wound channels aren’t perfectly cylindrical either. The overall diameter of the wound channels and penetration were nearly identical.

To more closely estimate the difference in wound size, I measured the width and height of each wound channel every half inch from entry to the end of the expanded cavity — both were about 14 inches. Because I’m no longer spun up on my calculus, I plugged the data into Claude AI, and it calculated the estimated volume and generated simulated models. The wound channel cross sections are star shaped, not complete empty space, so this is only an estimate of the volume of gel affected by the permanent wound channel.

This demonstration shouldn’t be taken to mean that the 6.5 CM and .300 Win. Mag. are completely equal. They each have their advantages and disadvantages. The results, however, do track pretty well with other gel testing I’ve done, and what I’ve observed on animals. Those are that, with the same bullet construction, results don’t vary too much across most common hunting cartridges. In fact, things like penetration and wound cavity size can be more greatly influenced by bullet selection than simply picking a bigger or smaller cartridge.

Some hunters place a lot of weight in having a cartridge that “hits harder.” While we can see some of the effects in the movement of the gel blocks during this demonstration, and that delta in impact force could possibly offer increased effect to the central nervous system, it’s not a reliable predictor of how fast an animal will die, or how much room for error you have. What we can rely on is the damage the bullet does.

One of the real advantages of a magnum cartridge, with a thoughtfully chosen bullet, is that it can deliver effective velocities over longer distances. A disadvantage of a 6.5 Creedmoor, in common shorter barrel configurations, is that it will produce lower muzzle velocities and result in a shorter effective velocity window. Ensuring that your impact speeds are high enough to make the bullet work properly is critical.

Our field shooting exercise did demonstrate that you might be able to shoot a magnum just as well as the 6.5. If you can, then you are better poised to take advantage of a magnum’s real benefits. Over time, most people will find that they shoot milder cartridges more consistently. It is most important to choose a cartridge that you can shoot well and will practice with.

Read Next: I Shot the First Elk With the New 6.5 Creedmoor Plus Peak Ammo. It’s an Undeniable Elk Hunting Cartridge

Along with better equipment and more refined shooting technique, we are constantly learning more about terminal ballistics. Many of our long-held beliefs are simply a product of lore and oversimplified logic. If you’re a successful hunter and your favorite cartridge works well for you, we’re not asking you to change. But if you’re feeling the pressure to choose a cartridge that you don’t think you’ll shoot as well, because you feel that it’s powerful enough to make up the difference, you’re barking up the wrong tree. The smaller cartridges will work just as well on the good shots, and the big ones will do just as poorly on the bad shots.

#8389. Missouri Fourth Grader Has Already Taken Two Giant Whitetail Bucks This Season

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:01 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Noah Baker isn’t your typical young hunter. The Pike County, Missouri youngster is a hunting prodigy most sportsmen would be proud to call their son.

“He shot his first deer at age six,” his dad, Jared Baker, tells Outdoor Life. “He lives to hunt and fish. And we’d have to think about just how many deer he’s taken since that first one when he was still in first grade.”

October 25 was the last day of the Missouri early two-day youth gun deer season. Noah and Jared chose a hunting spot over a cut corn field late that afternoon near their home in Frankfort.

“The wind wasn’t great, and we just set up in a hillside haystack that overlooked a cut corn patch that was well below us,” says Jared, a 37-year-old heavy equipment operator. “We set a tripod rifle stand in the haystack, put Noah’s 7mm suppressed Remington rifle on it, and watched and waited.”

They got on the haystack about 4 p.m. on a hot afternoon. They hadn’t waited very long before a few small bucks and does started filtering into the corn to feed about 60 yards from where they were positioned.

“We were waiting for a big buck we knew was around that I named ‘Dwayne The Rock Johnson’, because he was so big and strong,” Noah says. “The deer’s head was huge, and I wanted him.”

The father-son team had two big target bucks they’d watched and planned to take this year. They’d also found shed antlers from the deer. Noah had shot the smaller of the two bucks — a 155-inch 10-pointer — with his crossbow on Oct. 2.

Now they were after the second buck – “Dwayne The Rock Johnson,” and it just so happened that the deer showed at 6:20 p.m.

“It happened fast,” Jared says. “We saw him at 80 yards, and he went into a grass patch to look at a doe.”

“I saw him first, dad was looking farther away when I spotted him,” says Noah. “Dwayne started to walk away, turning toward some smaller bucks. But dad used his grunt call, and the buck turned and looked at us.”

Noah had crosshairs settled on the deer’s chest and fired at the buck standing 80 yards away. The 140-grain Berger bullet put the buck down quickly.

“Noah and I just started fist pumping in the air,” said Jared.

Read Next: Here’s Why This Giant Missouri Buck Was Still in Velvet in Late September

They called some friends for help getting the giant 17-point buck out of the field. They didn’t weigh it, but a taxidermist who has the buck rough green-scored the antlers at 187 inches.

Noah’s other 155-inch 10-pointer also is with the same taxidermist for mounting.

“I’m going to hang both of them in my bedroom,” Noah says. “One on each side of my TV screen so I can watch them whenever I’m in there.”

#8387. Class 4 Terrain, Cozy Huts, Cold Beer: The Northern Alps Are Japan’s Best-Kept Secret

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Author and photographer Andy Cochrane spent months crafting this route from home in Bend, Oregon, consulting with multiple Japanese mountain guides, before flying to Tokyo to bring it to life. Along with four others, he ran this 100-mile technical traverse across the Northern Alps in a week, staying at mountain huts and soaking in Japanese hospitality along the way.

It’s not often that a local guide recommends helmets for a hut-to-hut trail running trip, but it’s always a sign of a good adventure if you ask me.

A couple of months before flying across the Pacific to Japan, I was on a mid-afternoon Zoom call—my third such conversation of the week—when my jaw hit the floor. I was meeting virtually with guides in the Northern Alps to learn more about the trails and huts of the range, hoping to suss out if a line I had plotted on a map was actually a feasible endeavor to run.

At the time, I wasn’t sure if anyone had run the route before us. There certainly weren’t any blogs, articles, or posts I could find about it. Hut owners on the trip later confirmed my suspicion that our 100-mile, seven-day itinerary was pretty far out of the box. Connecting the outdoor hub of Kamikochi at the southern end of the range to the Sea of Japan in the north along a single ridge line was an unheard of idea to everyone we spoke with. That made it a lot more exciting—and far from certain it would work out. If it did, however, we would get to experience all that the Northern Alps had to offer in a single push.

Because the route required a mix of trail running, boulder hopping, ladder climbing, and Class 4 scrambling, our local guide Tatsuro was adamant that we bring helmets, even if their use wouldn’t be required every day. TL;DR: he was right.

Before I get into specifics of the route and experience, let’s set the scene. The Northern Alps, or Hida Mountains, are Japan’s most primal terrain. Although lesser-known than the mountain ranges of Europe, South America, or mainland Asia, the Northern Alps are just as technical and challenging, if not more so. The range is a jagged, granite spine that defies the country’s reputation for manicured serenity. Trails in the Hida are riddled with boulders, ladders, roots, scrambling, and thick brush. Located just a few dozen miles off the Sea of Japan, the weather is incredibly fickle in the Hida, too.

Geographically, the Northern Alps lie just a few hours drive west of Tokyo on the main island and stretch across Nagano, Toyama, Gifu, and Niigata prefectures. Most of the range is inside Chubu-Sangaku National Park, which protects around 670 square miles from being absorbed by the urban centers that surround it. The Hida are widely regarded as Japan’s premier alpine terrain and feature the country’s most developed hut system, Yamagoya. These staffed huts offer hot meals, sleeping mats, water, snacks, and beer, allowing for multi-day runs and traverses with lightweight packs sans camping gear—perfect for a trip like ours.

Three years ago I ran across the Southern Alps on an ancient postal route called Nakasendo. While the Southern and Northern Alps offer remarkably different terrain and technicality, my first trip taught me much about Japanese culture and logistics that was helpful while preparing for my return.

Perhaps my biggest takeaway from that initial experience was that the language barrier is a major challenge—especially in rural places, where many people don’t speak a lick of English. While apps like Google Translate can help to order a quick meal or get assistance with navigation in a pinch, planning a trip and booking mountain huts requires someone not only fluent in Japanese, but who also understands the mountain culture. For us, that liaison was Kota.

I was connected with Kota at Japan Adventures Co. through a friend, and I honestly can’t say enough good things about him. He is an incredibly organized planner, a great communicator, and an avid hiker and trail runner. He even helped negotiate our stay with a few huts that didn’t believe our route was possible, ensuring the entire trip ran smoothly. Kota and his team lead a variety of hiking, food, and cultural trips around Japan, and are currently rolling out new trail running itineraries in the Northern Alps and elsewhere.

With help from Kota and advice from guides like Tatsuro and Paul from Nagano Adventures, I was able to refine our route to stay at unique huts, run the best trails, and find a balance between challenging and doable for each day. It’s important to note that mountain huts in Japan are warm and welcoming, but they run on rigid schedules. Breakfast is typically at 5 a.m. and dinner is around 5 p.m. If you don’t check in by 4 p.m., they will notify search and rescue, so it’s important to start early and keep an eye on your pace throughout the day.

My goal was to start in Kamikochi and end at the Seas of Japan, creating a single linkup by connecting a number of popular two- and three-day hiking routes—the Panorama Ginza Route, Mount Yari, Ura Ginza Panorama Route, the ridgeline from Mount Eboshi and Funakubo-dake, the Hachimine Kiretto, the Kaerazu no Ken (ridge of no return), and Tsugami Shindo. It’s a mouthful to say, but when drawn on a map, the routes piece together nicely, forming a (mostly) straight line running from north to south.

Getting to and from the Northern Alps isn’t terribly difficult. After landing in Tokyo (either HND or NRT), a bullet train, or Shinkansen, will take you to Matsumoto in just a few hours. From there you can take a smaller train, bus, or taxi into the mountains to begin your adventure. Returning to Tokyo is just as easy by hopping on a bullet train in a coastal city like Toyama. There are plenty of stations to choose from and you usually can find seats just a day or two in advance.

There are a few ways to shuttle your luggage from the start to the finish, but I recommend Yamato Transport. Other options include dropping bags at the post office, the front desk if you’re staying in a hotel, or even convenience stores like Lawson’s or 7-Eleven. Though this might seem risky at face value, it worked flawlessly for us. We walked into a convenience store around 10 p.m., spent a meager ten minutes filling out the paperwork, and walked out. Our bags arrived at our final hotel just after we arrived seven days later.

Despite plenty of challenges, the trip ran as smoothly as I could have imagined. We dealt with heavy rain, 50 mph winds, and thick mist for our first few days, which forced us to slow down on the scrambling sections, layer up to stay warm, and take plenty of breaks in huts along the way. Some days had tons of vert (often more than 1,000 feet per mile) and rocky trails that made running difficult, so we embraced the shuffle. On day four, when covering our most remote section, we didn’t see a single other person. Fortunately the trails are well marked, even where they are less frequented and overgrown.

The crux of the route, the Kaerazu no Ken, is a long and serpentine downclimb on Class 4 granite slabs, offering a chain for protection in some areas while others did not. This was one of the dozen or so sections that having a helmet was a welcomed addition to our kits. For those comfortable with alpine climbing, this will feel like a fun change of pace. For those afraid of exposure, it’ll be challenging. The huts themselves vary considerably from small ridgetop outposts like Funakubo to much larger and busier outfits like Hakuba Sanso. Regardless of size, every hut owner we met was incredibly kind. Japanese hospitality is something they take very seriously.

Overall, our experience in the Hida was more than we could have asked for. Steep and technical trails, unique and cozy huts, fickle yet fruitful weather, and no other Americans or Europeans along the way. It’s an undiscovered gem for anyone outside Japan. With the help of Kota, Tatsuro, and others, I’m already planning a return trip next year.

One of the lightest climbing helmets on the market, the Vapor was perfect for our trip. We frequently had sections of running between scrambles and wouldn’t leave it on because it breathes so well. The Vapor fits over a hat and under a rain jacket hood, making it great for wet days, too.

The latest from Garmin is designed for routes like ours with a solar-powered display that ran the full week on a single charge. The maps were critical on wet days when I didn’t want to use my phone, and the flashlight was perfect for early mornings trying to not wake up other guests.

The perfect size pack for a trip like ours, the Adventure was able to carry everything we needed—spare clothes, first aid, snacks, camera, and ditty—with ease, plus poles, flasks, and a phone in the external pockets. It can be adjusted on the fly to reduce bounce and chafing.

On a week-long trip you end up eating a ton of snacks—gummies, chips, gels, and whatever you can buy at the huts—but nothing hit home like GU stroops. Whether it was with morning tea, on the top of a big climb, or preventing a bonk, stroops played a big role in our success.

With major improvements from the previous version, the Speedgoat 7 was the perfect shoe for this trip, offering plenty of grip on technical scrambles and ladders, a comfortable and cushy ride for the long days, and a lay-flat tongue that kept most rocks and dirt out.

The perfect mid-layer for cool mornings or windy days, the Dawner breathes well and is quite comfortable next to skin. The exterior is stretchy and durable, which is great for running through brush and rubbing against rocks— an inevitability in terrain like the Northern Alps.

#8384. Should You Hunt a Buck’s Bedding Area, Or Is It Too Risky?

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:42 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

A heavy-racked buck beds down for the day. Wind sweeping from behind, and eyes scanning down below, danger has little chance of finding him before he detects it. After all, that’s why the buck picked this spot in the first place.

If you scan articles on the best rut hunting spots, you won’t find many that highlight buck bedding areas as key locations to target. But often times in deer hunting, going against the grain can produce great results.

However, you can only hunt buck bedding areas well if you have a firm understanding of how bucks bed, where they bed, and how they learn to survive based on their bedding area choices.

If you are tired of hunting the same old rut stands with minimal success, consider a change. Hunting a buck bedding area during the rut could be your ticket to hanging an old bruiser on the wall. Here’s what you should know.

Let’s start by agreeing on terms. Of course, bedding areas are places where deer rest and sleep. However, it’s important to know there are different types of bedding areas. Deer have daytime and nighttime bedding areas. For this article, we’ll focus on the daytime beds.

On the surface, it can be difficult to determine the difference between buck and doe bedding areas. There are distinctions, though.

Bucks tend to prioritize security over convenience. Does usually take the opposite approach. Bucks rely on themselves to detect danger (because they typically bed alone). However, does usually bed, feed, and travel within family units. When bedding together, does bed down facing different directions. This makes it easier to detect danger from all areas around them. Bucks can’t do this so they are much choosier in their bed locations.

Furthermore, bucks might or might not bed within the same patches of cover as does. When they do, bucks tend to take the best quality bedding. For example, in hill country, that might be the upper third of a ridge line. In swamps, that might be the highest dry ground available. In big woods, it could mean interiors of timber or in spots with the thickest cover and highest stem counts.

Bucks also bed in areas that offer plenty of horizontal cover. They might bed up against a boulder, log, or other object that hides their profile. Oftentimes, from a hunter’s perspective, all you might see is their head, antlers, and maybe the neck. Other times, you’ll see nothing at all (until it’s too late).

Regardless of the habitat type or geographical layout, bucks almost always bed with certain consistencies. For example, they tend to bed with the wind at their back. This allows them to smell anything upwind (behind them) and see anything downwind (in front).

This is one reason leeward ridges are so attractive to deer. The prevailing wind brings scent from over the top of the ridge. Early in the day, thermals bring scent up from below. Oftentimes, this allows deer to smell danger from multiple directions.

Without question, savvy bucks learn how to detect danger within their environment. With time, they learn typical directions that danger comes from. With that knowledge, they bed in areas that offer visibility to see hunters or predators coming from these directions. Therefore, don’t be surprised to see bucks bedding right on the edge of thick cover within some of the areas noted above. This gives them plenty of cover to hide and allows them to see danger approaching from the open areas nearby.

It’s logical to think that once bucks become confident in certain bedding areas, they’ll go back and use the same beds over and over. In some ways, and in many places, they do. It’s especially common for bucks that live in more desolate landscapes or areas with poorer habitat quality to reuse the same beds with higher frequency.

According to the MSU Deer Lab, in areas with higher timber-to-open ratios and bigger woods settings, bucks are less loyal to specific beds. They will still bed within the same relative geographic locations. However, the absolute locations of their beds tend to vary.

Read Next: How to Hunt Cover During the Rut, with Dr. Craig Harper

It’s been said many times, but older bucks operate completely differently than younger bucks and does. They take on vastly different habits and tendencies.

A common thread through most mature deer includes the desire for seclusion. Older bucks don’t want a bunch of other deer bedded close to them. Additionally, it’s important to recognize that higher populations of does, and higher deer densities in general, can cause bucks to bed on the fringes. That’s especially true outside of the rut.

Because of everything noted above, it’s challenging to hunt close to buck bedding. It becomes even harder when the deer is 4.5 years old or older. These deer have learned to survive in part due to their bedding area choices. Therefore, it takes strategic planning and very deliberate approaches to thread the needle and get a big buck on the ground.

While it isn’t as popular as other rut-centric stand locations, it’s certainly an option. By continuing to focus on buck bedding areas (similar to early season and pre-rut plans), hunters can find a big ol’ buck.

By digging through deer research and personal experience, it’s clear that bucks express unique habits and tendencies that culminate into perceived personalities. One example is a really old buck that barely participates in the rut. That’s the exception, of course, but it would call for a unique approach. You would have to hunt such a deer as if the rut isn’t even on. You’d focus on travel routes along bed-to-feed patterns.

Some mature bucks that participate in the rut still return to their preferred bedding areas. If they don’t find an estrus doe under cover of darkness, by dawn, they cautiously slink back to one of the advantageous beds they know. When hunting this type of deer, set up between his bed and nearby food sources. Or between his bed and nearby doe bedding.

Hunting this deer is similar to hunting the fringes of buck bedding outside of the rut. Use good entry and exit strategies, and keep wind directions in mind during the approach, hunt, and departure. Don’t be aggressive with calling, rattling, or decoying since reclusive bucks rarely respond well to those aggressive tactics.

Hunting buck bedding requires a lot of planning and consideration. Hunting buck bedding during the rut requires even more. In many cases, this isn’t the right play.

Oftentimes, it’s less-dominant, uber-mature deer (5 ½-plus), or specific bucks that tend to be more reclusive across their entire lifespan, that require this hunting tactic.

Once you’ve determined you’re hunting a specific buck like this, you must hunt him carefully. Use the hunting strategies you’d typically use to hunt a whitetail bedding area with the immediacy of the rut in the front of your mind.

#8380. “I Wanted to Throw Up.” I Missed 7 Bucks In a Row Before Finally Learning a Hard Lesson

Published Oct 31, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The coffee cups were almost dry again, and so were the hunting stories. Milt’s electric clock showed 6 a.m.—time to go. Moments later, the six of us were swallowed up in the gloom of a dense fog. Four inches of fluffy new snow muffled our footsteps as we began the trek to our deer stands.

There was a nervous excitement in the air that morning. We knew we were going to see deer. Rarely had we been so confident on an opening day. Almost 200 acres of willow swamp and fields belonged to us that morning and the preseason scouting we’d done plus the new snow added up to nothing but good news. The anticipation was almost crackling in the air around us.

I reached my stand first. I brushed off the loose snow and stood listening for a moment. The absolute stillness meant that my ears would be about as helpful as my eyes for the first few hours—longer if the fog remained. An inch of frost covered every limb of the big willow I occupied. I backed into a collar-high branch and a handful of the frozen dew fell, shaking any remaining sleep from me.

To my left was a standing field of short corn. To my right, the edge of a brushy swale wound its way down to the big willow swamp 200 yards away. In front of me, a fallen willow limb blocked my view. I settled comfortably against the trunk of the big tree and surveyed the fields. Sometimes the fog would allow me 80 yards of view, at other times less than 40.

When at last, according to my watch, it was 8 a.m., I knew that the sun had to be up. The light through the fog, however, had changed little. From the cornfield to my left came sounds of movement—short crunching noises. My ears strained to identify them. A cock pheasant crowed not far away and I relaxed a bit. A few moments later I watched a bluejay working over a cob. Birds were making the sounds, I told myself.

For nearly 30 minutes I continued to hear the sounds: a few crunches followed by silence. Then I saw the outline of a deer’s back moving slowly through the rows. Head down, the deer came closer, quartering across the field. At last it raised its head. For the first time I could see its crown of antlers. Not again, I said to myself, a bit of dread mixing with my excitement.

Seven times before, I’d managed to get shots at trophy bucks and seven times I’d missed—sometimes with a bow, sometimes with a shotgun. I’d got my chance nearly every season I’d hunted, and I’d gone home empty-handed every time. My hunting companions marveled at my incredible knack for being in the right place at the right time and at my equally incredible bad shooting. Despite hours of practice, something always seemed to go awry at the moment of truth. Not again, I groaned inwardly.

When it seemed that the buck was coming no closer, I raised my shotgun. The iron sights of my new slug barrel came to rest on the target—still more than 60 yards away. I fired.

The blast shook frost from the willow branches. For a moment, the buck disappeared. When I could see again, he was on the move.

Again I fired and again and again—as the buck crossed from left to right. As the big deer quartered toward me, he was hidden behind the frosty fallen branches of the willow. Suddenly he reappeared before me and I shot once more. The buck stopped just 40 yards away, his wide, dark rack swiveling like a radar antenna.

My gun was empty. I had to reload. Frantically I fumbled deep in my pocket for the shells. They were still in the box. This one time I hadn’t opened a second box just in case. Almost hysterically I tore the cardboard and threw a slug into the chamber. I took aim at the buck’s neck and fired. I thought I saw the deer cringe before he loped away down the swale toward the big swamp. Then I lost sight of him in the fog and frosty willows.

I can’t adequately describe my feelings. Despair is as close as any named emotion comes. I was beside myself. I couldn’t believe I’d missed again. The deer was right there, at the range I’d sighted-in my new barrel for, and still I’d missed. I scrambled down off the stand and began to search for the deer’s trail in hopes of finding blood, hair, anything that might mean the buck was hit. I reloaded the shotgun then and, to my disgust, found two shells in the magazine. In the excitement, I’d evidently put more slugs in the gun than I knew. I could have shot again—more despair.

In the snow, I followed the buck’s tracks across the swale, along the edge of the cornfield on the other side, way past the point at which I’d lost sight of him. For more than 200 yards I moved slowly beside the tracks. Then I was close to the swamp and my friend Steve’s stand. He’d heard the shots, but hadn’t glimpsed any deer passing by. “Maybe it was hidden in the fog,” he said.

I walked the trail many times that morning, tracing and retracing the deer’s movements in the snow. A sad realization was weighing more heavily with every step. Grudgingly, I had to admit that I must have missed number eight.

The next day the hunt ended and I went home, but the memory of the hunt stayed with me. When I tried to sleep, that morning’s events played back like a worn instant replay. Again and again I saw the buck cross and again and again I watched my shots as if I were looking for my mistake. I tried to spot and correct my error, but even in my dreams the buck escaped.

Five days later, a friend and I took to those same willows in search of pheasants. He’d heard my tale and seemed to understand. As we approached where I’d last seen the buck, I took a breath to call my friend. I wanted to tell him where the deer had been when my shots had missed. But before I could form the words, Tim stopped dead in his tracks.

“Oh no,” he said with a groan. “Oh no! There’s a huge buck lying over here.”

My first thought was that he was joking. But he wouldn’t have been, couldn’t have been. I was trembling as I waded the deep grass toward him. A sick sort of feeling began to knot my stomach. The sight of a shining antler almost put me to my knees.

There in the thin yellow grass lay my buck.

He lay there as he must have lain after the final shot that Saturday morning. He was crouched like a sleeping dog, facing the trail that I’d mistaken for his. My last shot had gone very low, into the left hindquarter and up into the body cavity. The wound hadn’t bled. That was why I’d found no blood in the snow.

I stood there in the silence thinking quickly, eyes burning. Tim shared the silence. He understood. I must have passed within a dozen yards of the buck time after time. Why hadn’t I seen him? How could a buck grow invisible in knee-high grass? Maybe he’d been deeper in the swale and had crawled out later when death approached. But why hadn’t we seen him on the second day? The trail to two of our other stands ran close by.

If only I’d gone into the swale on a hunch. If only I’d had a hunch. If only there hadn’t been such thick fog on that day, surely Steve would have seen the deer from his lofty perch. If only the wound had bled so I’d have stayed on the right trail. If only I’d shot truer. If only, if only…

But such musings were no help. I was beside myself with self-loathing. I wanted to throw up. I wanted to cry. Everything I was striving for as a hunter lay in ruin like the buck.

Tim and I returned that afternoon to take the cape and antlers. They were all that we could salvage. Silence returned as I guided the knife, wishing away the green that had begun to color the ruined venison. Forcing myself to speak, I asked Tim to age the deer. He was wildlife manager for the area’s Department of Natural Resources. He estimated 3½ years, give or take a season. That, at least, was a comfort.

I took the antlers as much out of respect for the animal as for myself. I knew the head would be a most worthy reminder.

“Well,” the taxidermist said, “at least you got the horns. You can always buy meat.” He didn’t understand.

Now the head hangs in a place of honor in my home. Beautiful as it is, I get no joy out of looking at it. It remains, however, a lasting monument to that day. I still think of the rotting venison and the slow death the buck may have had. I learned something then, something of deer hunting and of myself.

Read Next: What It Feels Like to Miss the Biggest Buck of Your Life at 45 Yards — With a Rifle

Many evenings, after the head was first hung, I would sit looking at it and recall that day. I had decided that my gun was to blame for the poor shooting, that the barrel wasn’t tightened down properly on the stock. I knew, too, that the deer had been lost because of poor tracking skills, fog, bad luck, all of the classic reasons. But I was only half right at best.

Finally I came to understand that the tale was told in those first moments when the buck raised his crown and I began to doubt myself. I forgot my skills then, thinking only of the glory or the humiliation that I faced. The strain of the moment, my self doubt and consequent loss of concentration cost me that buck. I was not a competent enough marksman to rise to the occasion, under pressure. Only more practice could be the cure.

I haven’t faced a buck since then, although I killed a doe cleanly the following season just 100 yards from the spot where I’d seen that buck. Somehow the pressure had faded then, but does don’t carry antlers. I wonder about that day to come when I’ll face a buck once more. And I wonder if the lesson that began on a frosty morning not long ago will serve me then.

This story was originally published in the November 1982 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8376. The 15 Best Spots to Hunt During the Peak of the Whitetail Rut

Published Oct 31, 2026 3:45 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The big-racked, muscled-up brute crashes through cover. Operating like a pedigreed cutting horse, he carves out two rival bucks and sends them packing for distant hills. Quickly, he returns to the small patch of cover where the wide-eyed estrus doe waits. The pair will likely stay in that obscure piece of real estate for the next 24 to 48 hours. That’s well away from most other deer — and hunters, who are focusing on better-looking ground with better traditional habitat hundreds of yards away. But it doesn’t have to be that way.

While traditional rut stands work just fine during the peak rut, other unorthodox spots can, too. Hunters should be aware of both sides of that coin. The rut-hunting playbook isn’t as small as some might believe. That’s why I’ve ranked the best 15 spots for peak-rut deer hunting.

Funnels and pinch-points are among the most orthodox stand locations during the rut. These are simply natural terrain features that encourage deer to travel through confined spaces. Of course, these are crucial for bowhunters, but they serve as excellent stand locations for gun hunters, too.

Because they’re so effective, however, funnels and pinch-points draw attention from a lot of hunters. On public land and shared private properties, such spots can become pressured and overhunted. In these scenarios, study a parcel’s pressure levels to determine if these spots are worth your time.

Does usually use the same, or the same few, bedding areas throughout the year. Over time, bucks learn where these locations are. During the rut, they’ll visit these in search of estrus does. Hunters should know where these are located, too.

Hunting doe bedding can be tricky, though. As with hunting any bedding area, you must get in early — long before daylight. Settle in on the downwind side of bedding areas and intercept bucks cruising these edges as they scent check for does. If multiple bedding areas are connected by cover, set up along these routes as bucks travel from one to the next.

Topography plays a major role in deer movement. Specific features can influence how, when, where, and why deer traverse certain routes. One such feature is an upper-third bench. This is a bench that, as it sounds like, spans the higher part of a ridge — but not the top of the ridge itself. Because morning thermals rise, this is a common area to catch bucks cruising the first few hours of the day. They can smell potential does down below. Furthermore, bucks often prefer the leeward side of the ridge because they can smell from both directions.

Similarly, lower-third benches are important, too. These are more effective hunting locations later in the day. In the evening, and sometimes even earlier in the afternoon, thermals fall. As the evening air pulls downward, scent collects and pools in the lowest points of the landscape. That’s why bucks travel along lower-level benches to detect potential does that are traveling, or have recently traveled, along the ridge above.

Now, back to those leeward ridges I mentioned above. These are simply the downwind sides of ridges, and they’re excellent locations to intercept deer travel patterns. These serve as great bedding areas as well as travel routes for deer, which mean they’re especially great stand locations during peak rut. Whether deer are bedding there, or merely using these as travel routes, hunters can intercept them.

Another hill-country feature to hunt is the famous saddle, or a low spot between two ridges. It might be where the same continuous ridge dips down and rises back up. Or it might be where two ridges running in different directions taper and meet. Either way, a saddle allows deer to pass through from one side or the other without having to climb up and over. It’s a smart spot to lie in wait for when they do.

Throughout the whitetail range, early successional habitat is vital to deer. Overgrown fields can provide that necessary edge cover. Oftentimes, these fill up with briars, brambles, grasses, and even forbs. Such growth might not look like much to us, but it provides good bedding cover and food sources. During the rut, bucks might even push estrus does into such areas to get them away from rival bucks.

Deer drink water year-round, but bucks get especially thirsty during the rut. All the cruising and chasing develops a need to rehydrate, and they frequent watering holes. Isolated water holes are especially attractive. Deer have limited options for finding water, particularly in dry conditions, and that increases the odds of shooting deer over one. You can hunt natural water sources or create your own, although creating these in huntable locations can require some serious strategy.

Deer spend most of their lives within cover, and that’s the best place to find a big deer. But during the rut, don’t overlook the power of a quality field-based food source. Standing soybeans, freshly cut corn, or any other crop with waist grain on the ground can be great. So can food plots, especially those planted with timely species. Hunting deer over food sources that are directly adjacent to quality bedding cover can produce sightings of a lot of deer, including mature bucks that are checking does or replenishing their energy.

Buck bedding areas are incredibly productive spots throughout the early season, pre-rut, and late season. Don’t overlook these areas during the rut. Often really old bucks will continue bedding in the same areas they have been using all fall, and only search for does at night. If they don’t find a hot doe, they retreat to the bedding areas they feel safest in.

So, continue to monitor the edges of these areas with trail cameras, and move in to hunt as necessary if you think a buck is still bedding there. Keep in mind that bucks and does often bed within the same block, but bucks tend to bed at higher elevations or in areas that are more advantageous.

I know, scrapes, go cold during the peak, rut, right? Sure, scraping activity drops off. But they don’t completely shut down. Bucks continue to check scrapes, and so do does. Does, and bucks that are between does, continue checking scrapes. So it doesn’t hurt to consider their prcense as a secondary or tertiary element when weighing strand locations, especially if scrapes are nearby an area you already plan to hunt.

Bucks don’t like competition. Because of this, older deer that know what they’re doing tend to push does into random areas the remainder of the deer herd rarely uses. Often this includes random brushy areas. Maybe it’s a fencerow, thick sinkhole, patch of grass, or other obscure — but maybe visually obvious — location.

Similarly, other small pockets of cover can be good, too. Even a half-acre, or even quarter-acre of cover can hold a breeding pair of deer. If it looks like a spot at least two deer could hide from other deer, and hunters, they might just be there. It might feel weird or unproductive to hunt these spots, but if you have good reason to, it just might pay off. Perhaps you saw a buck run into such a spot, maybe you didn’t. But during gun seasons, you should at least glass these areas or consider doing a deer drive through  these small pockets.

Drainage ditches are always overlooked. After all, who wants to hunt a hole in the ground? But drainage ditches with the right characteristics can hold deer. At the very least, deer might travel across or through it. Ditch crossings can be good all season long, but during the rut, it’s not uncommon for bucks to push does into brushy areas within ditches.

This is another area you wouldn’t expect a deer, but one worth considering. Brush piles with enough cover can hold a couple deer, and breeding pairs often shack up in such spots. Finding ways to hunt these can be difficult, but don’t overlook potential activity in such areas.

#8372. Matt Robertson Just Won $1.25 Million In the Champions Tournament. It’s The Largest First Place Payout in Professional Bass Fishing History

Published Oct 31, 2026 6:48 PM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

With a final day tally of 20 pounds, 2 ounces, and a total 3 day weight of 56 pounds and an ounce, Matt Robertson won a first-place payout of $1.25 million in the Champions bass fishing tournament on Old Hickory Lake in Tennessee. This is the largest first-place payout in the sport’s history and it represents an interesting turn in pro bass fishing.

Before we dive into the rest of the results, here’s what you need to know about the tournament and how it all came together.

It’s been just over 8 years since the professional bass fishing world effectively split the best anglers in the world into two separate organizations, the Bassmaster Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. In that time, new names have risen to the top of the leaderboards, and the old guard has won their fair share of events as well.

But the question that seemed to circulate year after year was who really is the best angler in the world?

Since the two organizations don’t cross-compete well, the answer remained shrouded in speculation and uncertainty. Sure, Jacob Wheeler might be the best at catching the most fish under the MLF BPT format, but could he still sack up 5 giants for 4 consecutive days in an Elite Series format? Would the young gun, Trey McKinney, give Wheeler or Kevin VanDam a run for their money in an MLF-style event?

The bass fishing world figured we’d never know, that is, until February of this year when World Bass Enterprises introduced The Champions Tournament. CEO Brian Bird announced the tournament, and an eye-popping $3.25 million purse to go along with it. Bass fishing fans from around the world started to pay attention.

To qualify for The Champions Tournament, Bassmaster Elite Series anglers and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers fished their respective 2026 tours throughout the year. After each event, they were awarded Angler of the Year points. The Champions Tournament lineup consisted of the top 25 in AOY points from the Elite Series and the MLF Bass Pro Tour. The additional spots were filled based off of a “win and you’re in” ruling that applies to anglers who won one of the major events, but didn’t make the points cut.

Two additional anglers were selected through a random draw that WBE put on for those who pre-ordered the Pay-per-view streaming service.  Due to naming rights, the anglers were split into teams. Elite anglers were assigned ‘Team Stars’ and MLF Bass Pro Tour anglers were assigned ‘Team Stripes’. The two randomly drawn anglers are Eric Giessing (Stars) and Kyle Carr (Stripes).

At the end of the event, a trophy was awarded to the top performing team, also “settling” the debate of which organization has the better anglers. For the 2026 Champions Tournament, Team Stars (Elite Series) has won bragging rights for the year.

“There has always been friendly competition and banter between the anglers on each tour, but no way to actually settle the score on the water,” MLF Bass Pro Tour 2025 Angler of the Year Jacob Wheeler said in a statement. “The opportunity to crown a true world champion across the entire sport is something our anglers have wanted for a very long time.”

The Champions Tournament was held on Old Hickory Lake, launching out of Sanders Ferry Park in Hendersonville, Tennessee. The launch and respective FanFest was full of attractions like a petting zoo, kids fishing area, inflatable archery, cornhole tournament, boat demos, and more. They even had the legendary Bill Dance fire off a cannon during the shotgun launch on the first day of competition.

Unsurprisingly, forward-facing sonar was addressed for this event, and seemingly played into a 50/50 outcome. For the first two days of competition, anglers were able to select which day they’d fish with live sonar, and which day they’d go without it. Then for the top 15 anglers fishing the final day, they got to use live sonar for 3 hours of competition.

To add to the pomp and circumstance, as if $1.25 million wasn’t enough, the weights also reset for the top 15 anglers heading into the final day. Making it truly anyone’s ballgame coming into Saturday. Old Hickory Lake put on quite a show for the first two days of competition, with largemouth, spotted bass, and smallmouth all making their way to the scales. The smallmouth dominant bags carried the most weight due to the minimum keeper size being 18-inches, while largemouth and spotted bass only needed to be 14-inches to make the cut.

The final day featured the following anglers fighting for the first place prize.

Matt Robertson, Ron Nelson, Bob Downey, Fisher Anaya, Pake South, Jason Christie, Trey Mckinney, Takahiro Omori, Kyle Welcher, Cole Sands, Chris Johnston, Cody Meyer, Bryan Thrift, Michael Neal, and Wesley Strader.

And while they all certainly wanted the top prize, the second place through seventh place payouts weren’t anything to scoff at either. Here is a look at the top 7 anglers, their final day weights, and their payouts after the final weigh-in. 15th place made a cool $20,000 and the payouts increased in $5,000 increments up to 7th.

1st Place: Matt Robertson (20-02) — $1.25 Million

3rd Place: Wesley Strader (11-02) — $300,000

4th Place: Trey Mckinney (11-0) — $200,000

5th Place: Michael Neal (10-10) — $100,000

While we put the largest professional bass fishing payout ever in the rearview mirror, it’s worth considering what The Champions Tournament means for bass fishing fans everywhere. Personally, there’s a bit of a shock factor involved. The payouts for the Bassmaster Classic and MLF Redcrest combined don’t even sniff the purse that was just awarded during this three-day event. That’s truly awe inspiring.

But what it really has shown me is that the two major organizations need to do some soul searching. If World Bass Enterprises can come out of nowhere and pull this off, perhaps it’s time to look at how they were able to do it successfully. Would fans pay a yearly subscription to watch a Pay-per-view Elite or BPT event? If so, could that increase the purses for those events and help the professionals in our sport actually make a living? I don’t see why not.

I know change is difficult for outdoorsmen and women, it’s in our nature to hold on to traditions and the status quo, but this weekend has shown me that there is a way to actually grow the sport of competitive bass fishing in a meaningful way. Now we’ll see if either organization actually has the guts to give it a try and truly make their anglers’ lives better.

As a final thought, I was blown away by the live coverage and the fanbase that showed up in-person and online, especially with the seasonality of this event. The bass fishing world was hungry for The Champions Tournament, and World Bass Enterprises pulled it off in epic fashion. I’m already looking forward to the 2027 lineup.

Derek Horner is the manager of audience development for Outdoor Life where he manages OL’s social accounts and email campaigns, and shares our stories with the world. He was born and raised in central Pennsylvania where his father and grandfather taught him to hunt and fish. He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8369. Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to a Top Deer Expert

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:14 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Jeff Sturgis has the unique experience of living through dozens of deer seasons all at once. As the founder of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, he works with clients around the country to improve their deer hunting and private land habitat.

But before ever stepping foot on a property, Sturgis does in-depth interviews with these hunters to understand what they’d like to improve and what problems they’ve been having. Through this process, trends start to emerge.

Sturgis calls these problems “huntisms.” But they could also be described as misconceptions, misunderstandings, or straight up bad information. Whatever you want to call them, there are certain things that hunters get wrong when it comes to hunting mature bucks and managing habitat for those mature bucks.

So in this episode of the Outdoor Life Podcast, Sturgis will reference his decades of experience working on private land habitat as well as his time spent hunting on public ground to outline the most common and detrimental deer hunting mistakes. Heed his advice for a better season next year.

This common mentality of having to pound the woods and hunt all the time has saved a lot of big deer over the decades, Sturgis says.

“In some cases I can see this being partially true,” Sturgis says. “Maybe if you’re hunting public land, you’ve got ten spots and you’ve got the time to hunt freely.”

But if you’re hunting small parcels where you can’t afford to spook deer, then it’s usually smarter to stay home when hunting conditions are poor in order to not burn out your stands.

“There’s something to be said for minimizing your hunting, taking care of other priorities in life and expecting a higher rate of potential success because you’ve not over-pressured your stand locations.”

“It’s not just your stand locations [that you don’t want to burn out, it’s also your family, your career, your friends — it extends to an entire way to look at things. When I go out in the woods I want there to be a reasonable expectation that I’m going to shoot a deer for this reason.”

Sturgis says that if you have a “rutcation” planned where you know you’re going to hunt for a solid seven to nine days in a row, then it’s critical to reduce your impact. Instead of charging into a core area regardless of conditions, hunt spots where your scent cone won’t spook deer (because it’s blowing over a lake or off a cliff). And when conditions aren’t ideal, hunt transition areas where you could catch a big buck walking by, but you won’t spook deer near bedding areas or primary food sources.

Sturgis works with many clients who have the financial resources to grow and maintain sprawling food plots on their properties. Many of these clients believe that growing the maximum amount of food on the property will translate to holding the most amount of mature bucks in the fall.

But that’s not how it plays out most of the time. Growing too much summertime food — like big clover or bean plots — will increase the number of does and fawns on the property. During the summer and early fall, mature bucks don’t like to live on crowded food sources and bedding areas, Sturgis says.

“When you add summer food to good cover, you get a lot of does and fawns,” Sturgis says. “And those does and fawns that are here today are here to stay.”

These deer take up space and resources. Mature bucks will live on the fringes of these high-density deer areas but not establish a core zone there.

“Yeah, some bucks will come through during the rut. But bucks, the older they get, they don’t want that commotion and stress of a bunch of does and fawns. That’s why they live somewhere else.”

Sturgis says it’s better to focus on a comprehensive management strategy with proper deer cover, screening cover, sanctuaries, water holes, fall food, and yes, maybe some summer food plots, than it is to simply plant clover plots throughout the entire property.

“If you want to raise the population, add summer food. If you want to lower the population, get rid of summer food,” Sturgis says. “When I go to a client and see 20 acres of beans on their 200-acre property and we drive around and see over 100 does and fawns and only a couple bucks, they have a severe problem. I’d rather have those does and fawns be somewhere else in the summertime and shift over to the property starting in September and October.”

Don’t read this as an attack on food plots. Sturgis has written countless articles on the benefits of food plots, he’s got an online food plot class, he’s authored a book on the subject, and Whitetail Habitat Solutions sells food plot seed. So yes, food plots can be a critical element in consistently harvesting mature bucks.

But that doesn’t mean you should always hunt over them.

“This year I shot four bucks in four states with my bow … and not one of them was shot on a food plot,” Sturgis says. “Then I go to clients and they’re spending 90 percent of their hunts on food plots — and I’m not saying I never hunt on food plots — but the point is that the vast majority of my bucks are shot not in food plots.”

Sturgis tries to convince his clients to hunt away from food plots. Focusing instead on waterholes or funnels in the woods that might lead to food. This helps hunters spook fewer deer and see target bucks during daylight hours.

“Food plots have the greatest level of potential reward and the greatest level of risk,” Sturgis says. “If you spook out those food plots, you’ve just destroyed your property.”

Even though Sturgis has access to prime whitetail properties in the Midwest, he also hunts public land in Pennsylvania every year. In 22 seasons of hunting the same public area, Sturgis has shot 18 bucks.

It’s pretty common for him to bump into other hunters on these hunts, but he doesn’t sweat it. He just moves somewhere else. The key is being flexible and using tactics that match the conditions. For example, if it’s snowy and windy, Sturgis might still hunt through an area. If the woods are blanketed in crunchy leaves, he’ll opt to sit for the day.

One way that Sturgis makes sure that he avoids other hunters is by walking in at twilight (not in the dark).

“You don’t have to be to your spot before light,” Sturgis says. “When I’m walking into a spot like that, I don’t know what tree I’m going to be sitting under or in… So we’re walking into an area in daylight and still hunting [our way in].”

Read Next: 35 Deer Hunting Tips to Read Before This Season

It’s also important to remember that other hunters will bump deer long distances, not just a few hundred yards.

“Public land deer will get pushed a long way,” Sturgis says. “Especially in open woods. Where we hunt we can get 200-yard shots in the woods in some places. So when people push deer out there, they’re moving three quarters of a mile. So don’t think about just one little thicket. Think about how deer are moving in the big picture [across the landscape].”

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.
