#8365. I Shot the World Record Archery Elk While Hunting in Montana’s Belt Mountains

Published Nov 2, 2026 9:46 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Imagine yourself in a tree stand in Montana’s Belt Mountains. You know a bull elk is approaching because you’ve heard him bugle several times. The bugles were high-pitched one-tone squeals, indicating an immature bull. You’re after a trophy-class animal, but still you can’t help but get excited and you tighten the grip on your 73-pound compound bow.

A twig cracks behind you. You turn slowly and get the surprise of your life. There, not 30 yards away, stands a monstrous bull elk. His antlers are so massive that you wonder how he can hold up his head. This might be the next world-record elk!

You slowly twist the upper half of your body to your right. Trying hard to control your excitement, you try to draw your bow. You can’t! You’re in such an awkward position and your bow is so powerful that you can’t shoot!

That’s exactly the situation in which Dave Snyder, a Las Vegas fireman, found himself last year. But Snyder was no stranger to the frustrations involved in hunting trophy-size elk. He’d bowhunted the Belt Mountains seven previous times and each time he’d killed an elk. Two of those had been large enough to be listed in the Pope and Young Club record book of bow-killed big game. But this bull was larger than any other he’d seen.

Big-game hunting has been in Snyder’s blood ever since he was 12 years old, when he killed his first deer with an old .25/30 rifle in Nevada. Since he took up bowhunting 20 years ago, he has traveled all over the West in search of game. Among his trophies are an Alaskan moose and caribou, wild boars, bears, whitetail deer, Catalina goats and more mule deer bucks than some hunters see in a lifetime.

But elk hunting has been his first love ever since he killed his first bull, a five-pointer, in Colorado in 1972. From each hunt, he has drawn knowledge that has improved his skills. As he admitted to me last summer, his success at bowhunting elk has not been an accident.

For three years running, he bet friends as much as $500 that he’d kill, with his bow and arrow, a bull elk with at least five points on each antler. He won every time. Now he can’t find anybody to bet with him.

“It might seem pretentious for me to bet like that,” Snyder said, “but it’s really not. I’m just confident. If you know what you’re doing, a bowhunter has just as good a chance as a rifleman of taking a big bull—maybe even a better chance. Most gun hunters do well only if there’s a lot of snow. Bowhunters have the advantage of being able to hunt in September during the rut when elk are most vulnerable.”

Snyder’s Montana elk hunting success started almost by accident in 1974. He and another Las Vegas fireman, Mike Freeman, were having trouble with their truck’s carburetor, so they stopped by the side of the road and opened the hood. Dressed in full camouflage, they soon attracted the attention of a local logger, Dee Hills, who stopped to offer help. Hills had been very successful while rifle hunting for elk, but he was a novice bowhunter and had doubts about the killing power of arrows. Snyder and Freeman assured Hills that, yes, arrows kill elk very effectively.

“Why don’t you show me?” Hills suggested. “I know where the elk are and I’d be happy to take you there.”

After fixing the truck, the three hunters drove to Hills’ hunting area in the Belt Mountains. The next morning they hiked into a deep bowl and found a herd of elk almost immediately. But it wasn’t until afternoon that they got close to the animals. Soon a calf came ambling by Snyder and Hills.

“Aren’t you going to shoot?” Hills asked.

Soon the biggest cow in the herd walked to within 25 yards. Snyder drew his bow, aimed and released the arrow. It was a perfect hit and the animal dashed into the trees.

Snyder stifled a laugh. Hills didn’t understand that most arrow-shot animals streak away for 25 to 200 yards before piling up.

“No, that was a good hit,” Snyder said. “We’ll find her. But this will be a good chance for you to learn how to track.”

Snyder had to eat his words when they followed the cow. A wide trail of blood plainly led to where the elk lay dead only 75 yards from where she had been hit.

During the next few years, Snyder and some of his friends made a tradition of hunting together with Hills. They had remarkable success for bowhunters, something they attribute to careful observation and study.

One afternoon, Hills, Snyder and Larry Crim were fanned out on a ridge when a bull bugled. Snyder trotted directly toward the sound. Soon two bulls began bugling back and forth. Stalking carefully, Snyder soon got to within 40 yards of a small five-point but he guessed that the other bull was bigger by the sound of its voice. Suddenly the big bull bugled again within about 60 yards. Snyder sneaked closer but stopped when he saw several cows feeding. Knowing that herd bulls often circle their harems to keep intruders away, Snyder knelt and waited. Within seconds an exceptional six-point bull appeared, walking directly toward him. When the elk was about 25 yards away, he stopped and looked back toward his cows. Snyder quickly drew and released. The Satellite-tipped arrow smacked into the chest. The bull threw back his head and galloped through a barbwire fence before crashing to the ground. The bull’s antlers scored 357⅞ points with the standard measuring system used by the Pope and Young Club. The rack still ranks No. 17 in the club’s record book.

Most hunters probably would have taken a shot at the five-pointer, ruining their chances for the record-class bull. Snyder well understands the importance of passing up opportunities while trophy hunting. His other elk listed in the Pope and Young records was shot under similar circumstances.

Snyder was watching a big herd of cows when a five-point bull came within 20 yards, offering an easy broadside shot. The elk didn’t seem large enough to keep such a large harem to himself, so Snyder decided to pass up the shot. In seconds, a big six-point streaked around the cows, stopped within bow range and looked at the small bull. Then he looked toward Snyder, who was crouched in some undergrowth. When the elk turned again, Snyder shot. The arrow buried itself in the animal’s lungs. The bull covered less than 50 yards before dropping dead. Its antlers later scored 248⅞. A minimum score of 240 is required for listing in the record book.

Taking two record-book elk might satisfy many hunters but not Dave Snyder. He knew there were elk big enough to break the Pope and Young world record in Montana, a state that yields more truly exceptional bulls than any other. He felt his experience gave him just as good a chance as anybody else to find such an animal.

The Belt Mountains offer ideal habitat. Covered mostly by lodgepole pines, Snyder’s hunting area is broken up by dozens of logging clearcuts where elk find a good supply of the grass and low brush they need. Although the Belts aren’t as rugged and remote as some other elk-rich ranges in Montana, they offer plenty of cover in which crafty old bulls can hide from hunters and attain the old age necessary for growing outsize antlers.

The hunter had learned that elk are much more set in their habits than many sportsmen realize. In 1981, Snyder decided to take advantage of that by hunting from a tree stand near heavy elk sign.

On the first day of the season, Snyder carried a portable tree stand to a drainage about two miles from camp. He’d taken one of his record-book bulls there and had seen larger ones. Partway there, he walked to within 35 yards of an unusual spike bull with antlers at least two feet high. Snyder already had decided to shoot nothing smaller than a six-pointer for the first five days of the season but he was tempted to take the spike. After all, it would yield a freezer full of delicious meat and would make an unusual trophy. He finally decided to hold to his resolution and so watched the spike feed out of sight. But he had second thoughts about doing so.

Snyder set his stand in a tree overlooking a recently used elk wallow and several rubs—small trees had been debarked by elk preparing their antlers for the fighting and breeding season.

The next morning, Snyder rose before dawn, confident that he’d have action. But he couldn’t find the stand in the dark. By the time he finally found it, the sun was high and he decided to return to camp for lunch.

That afternoon, he and another Las Vegas bowhunter, Lynn Williams, decided to glass clearcuts and meadows. After half an hour or so, they saw an unusually large bull in a clearcut about 1½ miles away. The men decided to move closer to study the size of the antlers. By the time they reached the cut about an hour later, the bull was gone.

“I’m coming back here in the morning,” Williams said. “I know he’s a monster and, if he came here once, he’ll come again.”

The next morning Williams returned to the cut, Snyder to his tree stand, and Hills and Crim to a drainage that had yielded four elk in previous years, including Snyder’s biggest bull. The four hunters saw only one spike among them.

“I don’t think the rut has started,” Crim said during lunch. “We might as well hunt deer this afternoon. Elk hunting will be a lot easier after the rut starts anyway because the bulls will be bugling.”

Williams and Hills agreed, but Snyder couldn’t get the big bull out of his mind, so he decided to hunt elk while the others hunted deer. By 3:30 he was in the pines above the cut where he had seen the big elk. The elk sign was encouraging—fresh tracks and droppings and several newly destroyed saplings. Obviously elk had been feeding in the cut during the evenings. Normally, Snyder doesn’t like to hunt in or near feeding areas because the animals are extra-wary there, just as they are in bedding areas. Instead, he finds routes between feeding and bedding grounds and ambushes the animals as they pass. But daylight would soon run out, so he decided to find a good place to hide.

A game trail that led from the trees into the clearcut showed signs of heavy use. A spruce sapling, freshly mangled by a bull elk, stood next to the trail. Snyder happened to glance up. An old tree stand, made of two boards nailed between two trees, overlooked the trail. One board was hanging loose, nailed at only one end.

Snyder took a rope from his camouflage fanny pack, climbed the tree and tied the loose board tight. Gingerly, he put his whole weight on the stand to test it. In half an hour it would be too dark to shoot.

Less than 15 minutes later, he heard a faint bugle. It was more of a one-tone squeal than a bugle—typical of the sounds made by spike or raghorn bulls.

In reply, Snyder blew his own bugle, a simple tubular plastic whistle. The bull answered.

Snyder considered climbing to the ground where he’d have good mobility, but he knew he’d be harder to see 15 feet above the ground and that his scent would be more likely to drift high above the bull’s sensitive nose. The bull bugled again. Snyder bugled back and the elk immediately answered. Knowing that too much bugling can spook elk, he decided to wait for the bull to bugle on his own. A minute or so later, the elk squealed again, probably from within 200 yards.

Apprehensively, Snyder whistled for the third time. Again the bull answered with a high-pitched whistle. Snyder was certain the bull was a small one but he decided to prepare for a shot anyway. The bull bugled again, this time within 100 yards. Soon some limbs broke about 50 yards away and a faint sound of hooves on the ground could be heard. Snyder checked his bow and arrow one last time. The sound of his pulse in his ears made it difficult to hear the approaching bull. He fully expected the animal to offer an easy broadside shot on the trail to his left.

Suddenly, less than 30 yards away, a twig cracked behind him. Turning slowly, Snyder saw a magnificent bull with heavy mahogany antlers walk into the clearcut. Twisting to his right, Snyder started to draw his 73-pound Martin Cougar compound. Because of the awkward angle, he could draw it only partway.

The animal began walking slowly to the left. Snyder realized he’d have to twist back to his original position to shoot. He shifted his weight and the thing he had feared happened—the old tree stand creaked. The bull instantly stopped, swung around and stared right at him. Snyder didn’t dare to move. During that tense instant, another bull bugled no more than 200 yards away. The big elk turned and looked toward the sound and resumed walking to the left. Snyder prepared mentally to take a 25-yard broadside shot.

When the bull was behind some branches, it stopped and bugled the call of a spike elk.

“Come on, baby, just three more steps,” Snyder thought. “Just three more steps.”

The other bull bugled again. For no apparent reason, the heavy-antlered bull turned 180° and began walking back into the woods. This time Snyder drew his bow and then twisted around. He could see the bull between two trees that were perhaps 12 inches apart, so he crouched low to shoot under some branches, judged the distance at 45 yards, aimed and released. The orange aluminum arrow was visible during the first part of its flight but then disappeared. The bull hunched over as though he’d been hit and galloped across the clearcut, kicking up such a great cloud of dust that he was hardly visible as he fled. Moments after the bull disappeared into the trees, Snyder heard a crash. Had the magnificent animal fallen?

Snyder climbed to the ground and looked for blood and tracks. Already there was very little light and he could find no sign that he had hit the animal.

He returned to camp to get help and a Coleman lantern. Finding nobody there, he left a note and returned to his stand. He looked for his arrow or blood and found neither, so he searched a logging road that encircled the area but could find no sign that the animal had crossed it. Right then Crim, Williams and Hills arrived. The four men, carrying lanterns, spread out in a line and walked through the trees where Snyder had heard the crash. They knew they had to find the elk within a few hours or the massive animal’s body heat would ruin the game meat. They’d gone about 50 yards when Hills shouted, “There he is!”

The group walked up to the dead bull in silence. He’d fallen so hard that his antler tines had dug several feet under the sod. The antlers were so massive and his body so huge that the four hunters just stood there staring in awe. Finally Hills broke the silence: “Well, we better get to work or we’ll be here all night!”

To get the antlers out of the ground took the combined strength of all four men. The elk was so heavy that just dressing the carcass and dragging it 100 yards down a grassy slope took from 9 p.m. until 3 a.m.

The hunters decided to try winching the carcass off the ground so that the meat could cool. Fortunately, Williams had a powerful winch on the front of his four-wheel-drive pickup. They threw the winch cable over a branch in a large pine, attached the cable to the antlers and lifted the animal clear of the ground. Hanging this way, the bull looked as big as a full-grown rhinoceros.

Later, the bull yielded 560 pounds of boneless fat-free meat. Snyder estimates that the animal weighed well over 1,000 pounds, even after it had been field-dressed.

Read Next: The Real Story Behind the Casey Brooks Bull, the Pending World Record Elk

The 45-pound antlers were a bonus surprise. Though they had looked huge, none of the hunters had guessed that no bowhunter had ever killed a bigger bull. After a required 60-day drying period to allow for shrinkage, the rack was conservatively measured at 389⅞ points with the measuring system used by the Pope and Young Club.

That exceeded the score of the world-record elk taken by Jay Elmer of Arizona in 1980 (“Back-To-Back Bulls,” OUTDOOR LIFE, November 1981). The actual score verified by a panel of judges at the Pope and Young Club’s award banquet last spring was officially put at 391⅞. Snyder’s bull is now recognized as the world record. Even Dave Snyder should be satisfied with that.

He’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

#8362. How to Beat the Worst Case of Buck Fever, According to This Archery Pro

Published Nov 2, 2026 11:29 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

When John Dudley was a kid, still learning how to hunt in Illinois, he had an encounter with a big buck that changed the trajectory of his bowhunting life. Dudley was hunting with a compound bow that was set too heavy—though he was able to draw the bow fine during practice.

When a stud buck casually walked into range, Dudley pulled with all of his might but he couldn’t get the bowstring back.

“He literally walks like 10 feet underneath my treestand … and I freakin’ pulled and tugged on that bow while my knees were clacking together,” Dudley says. “I had that thing pointed straight up in the air trying to pull it back. My heartbeat was hitting so hard I honestly thought I was going to need some stents or something by the time it was done.”

At first Dudley thought there was some sort of malfunction with his bow. As the buck walked off he examined the cams and the string. Then, with the deer (and the nerves) long gone, he simply grabbed the bow and drew it back without issue.

“You know when you have that nightmare that you can’t scream, well this was a living nightmare of John Dudley not being able to pull his bow back because he had buck fever that bad,” he says.

Fast forward a couple decades and Dudley is now an accomplished pro archer, a veteran whitetail hunter, and perhaps the most popular archery instructor in the country. Since that fateful Illinois bowhunt Dudley has learned a lot about shooting well under pressure during hunts and competitions. His hard-earned knowledge (which you can hear all about in the podcast episode below) will help you shoot your best when that big buck steps into your setup this fall.

When Dudley is sitting in his treestand he visualizes all the good scenarios that he hopes will happen. But this is far more than daydreaming about a giant buck turning broadside. Just like an athlete preparing for all the motions of a game, he visualizes each specific movement he’ll make under each possible scenario.

“I visualize myself getting a couple good ranges on him [as the buck comes in],” Dudley says. “I visualize making sure I grab my release the right way. I’m pivoting my feet the right way. And [the buck] is doing his thing as I’m able to slowly draw. And then I think about my shot process.”

With all the waiting we do in a treestand, there’s plenty of time to visualize and plan for a variety of shot scenarios.

“Sometimes I’m in a stand for two weeks before I have an opportunity and I’m constructing these things in my mind,” Dudley says. “You literally end up creating a vision. And when that happens, your conscious mind is already thinking about all the processes [you need to execute].”

In other words, when that giant buck finally does show, you won’t feel shocked, because you’ve already visualized it hundreds or thousands of times.

It’s almost a guarantee that every professional shooter in any shooting discipline has a shot process. As Dudley describes it, this is simply a series of words he says in his mind that coincide with actions he executes in order to make a perfect shot. Dudley’s shot process is this: 1) Stance; 2) Grip; 3) Shoulder; 4) Anchor; 5) Peep; 6) Pull and Finish.

Dudley learned the importance of having a process from Olympic medalist Lanny Bassham who wrote the book “With Winning in Mind” (which Dudley recommends for any shooter). The key is that saying the words and executing the movements is the work of the conscious mind. Activating the conscious mind helps prevent a shooter from “going on autopilot,” rushing the shot, punching the trigger, or simply blacking out.

You can and should adapt a shot process for your own needs. For example, OL gear editor and competitive archer Scott Einsmann’s process is: 1) Anchor; 2) Get it there (his cue to just get the aiming portion done with); 3) Feel alignment; 4) Okay, my shot can break anytime.

If you have a bad habit of getting excited and drawing back wildly, you might want to add a word like “smooth” to your shot process. If you have a tendency to get anxious about your pin floating around the target then you might want to add the word “float” to your process—reassuring yourself that it’s ok to let that pin float. The key is to have a shot process that works for you and to follow it on every single shot. Especially that shot on a giant buck.

Reciting a mantra is similarly useful. Just like running through a shot process, a mantra gives control to your conscious mind. You must choose to say your mantra.

For competitions, Dudley’s mantra is: “I shoot Xs because they make me feel good.”

When an animal comes in during a hunting scenario Dudley says the word “checkmate” to himself.

“When the animal presents that shot … I’m thinking ‘checkmate’, you know, game over,” he says. “Because that’s a positive affirmation that really reinforces your conscious thought process rather than sitting there thinking ‘Oh man this is the biggest buck I’ve ever seen.’”

But these tactics don’t eliminate the excitement and subsequent pressure you’ll likely feel when you see a shooter buck. The real key is training yourself to get comfortable while shooting under pressure.

“Think of buck fever like a hot bathtub,” Dudley says. “It might be scalding hot when you first put your toe into it. But if you just breathe and ease into it, eventually you’re going to acclimate and that water is going to feel OK.”

This is why Dudley recommends shooting in archery tournaments so you can “put yourself in a situation where you feel like you’ve been in the boiling pot before.”

If you have a high deer population where you hunt, or you just need to fill the freezer, shooting a few does with your bow is also a great way to get used to shooting under pressure. Your potential case of buck fever will likely be less extreme if you’ve cleanly killed a few does earlier in the season.

On the flipside don’t crank up the pressure on yourself during a hunt. In the treestand you want to feel positive, confident, and mellow.

“Don’t apply self-induced pressure,” Dudley says. “That’s the only pressure you really have control over. Most of the time buck fever or target anticipation is from pressure that you’re applying to yourself. It’s not like the animal is shooting [pressure] up at you. The best thing you can do is just positive self affirmation.”

In the days leading up to a big deer hunt Dudley makes sure to get in some practice sessions from a seated position and from an elevated position. This is because most whitetail shots will be from a ground blind or a treestand.

It’s important to know that shooting downhill or shooting from a seated position will induce more pin movement while you’re holding on target. But that’s OK if you’re used to it.

“It’s about mentally getting over that [pin movement],” Dudley says.

But there’s also value in practicing at long range even if you won’t be shooting at long range during a hunt. This is because flaws in your shooting will be more apparent at longer distances, and recognizing those flaws will help you correct them.

“I actually practice more at 80 than any distance I shoot at,” Dudley says.

Dudley believes in Chuck Adam’s theory that your effective range as a bowhunter is half the distance of your effective range in the backyard. In other words, if you’re able to shoot 8-inch groups at 80 yards in the backyard, you’ll be able to shoot 8-inch groups at 40 yards under a hunting scenario.

Plus, practicing at long range will boost your confidence when you move in for those realistic 20- and 30-yard shots. And really, at this point in the season, all practice is about building confidence for that moment of truth.

“Always practice at distances where you have confidence,” Dudley says. “Especially when you’re trying to instill confidence.”

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8361. Des Linden’s Simple (and Somewhat Shocking) 100-Mile Fueling Plan

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Boston Marathon champion Des Linden will toe the line at her first 100-miler on October 31, 2026, at the Javelina Jundred near Fountain Hills, Arizona. To prepare for the distance and hot desert conditions, she worked with a team of sports scientists, including Olympic-marathoner-turned-ultrarunner-champion Magda Boulet, to dial in her metabolic needs and a fueling plan. She will primarily rely on liquid calories, with the addition of some more out-of-the-box products like “cooling” menthol gels, while understanding that mid-race adjustments will be key.

For Boston Marathon champion-turned-competitive ultrarunner Des Linden, one question keeps driving her forward: “Can I do this?”

After years of racing some of the world’s most prestigious road marathons, the two-time Olympian is shifting her focus to off-road competitions. On October 31, she’ll attempt her most ambitious athletic endeavor yet when she toes the start line of the Javelina Jundred, a 100-mile trail race through Arizona’s Sonoran Desert that also serves as a Golden Ticket race into the 2027 Western States 100.

“I feel like part of me is just missing being afraid of something; the unknown,” Linden tells Trail Runner. “What is this going to pull out of me? What is this going to ask of me? That’s all really fascinating.”

In addition to the distance—nearly 40 miles more than Linden has ever covered in one go–Javelina presents a slew of unfamiliar challenges. One of the biggest is fueling and hydration over the course of 13-plus hours in desert conditions. Linden got a small taste, literally, at the Black Canyon 50K in February. It was her first ultramarathon and she acknowledged after the race that all of those years of fueling on the roads was only so helpful.

“I went into Black Canyon 50k with a loose fueling plan—to have a Gu at each aid station and sip on an electrolyte beverage between stations,” Linden said. “I wasn’t diligent about it during the race and certainly didn’t account for the time required for trail miles versus road miles. After the race, I realized it was a very easy place to make improvements, and getting it dialed before MDS would be important.”

It’s a relatable learning curve that Linden has taken seriously in the eight months since. Together with a team of sports scientists, including Olympic-marathoner-turned ultrarunning-champion Magda Boulet, Linden has tested her metabolic needs under hot ultramarathon conditions to develop a (somewhat surprising) fueling plan for October 31.

Linden retired from professional road running in 2025 after an illustrious career that included two Olympic Games, two runner-up finishes at both the Chicago and Boston Marathons, and an iconic win at the 2018 Boston Marathon—becoming the first American woman to do so in 33 years. Rather than hanging up her running shoes, Linden is targeting some of the world’s most prestigious trail races.

“I think a lot of this part of my career is getting away from comparing myself to my former self. So this is uncharted territory for me,” Linden says.

This past April, Linden, 43, competed in only her second ultra-trail event, finishing third at Marathon des Sables (MDS), a six-day stage race in the southern Moroccan Sahara often referred to as the “Toughest Footrace on Earth.” While Linden has spent her career refining how she fuels for peak performance and recovery, her MDS experience reinforced just how critical nutrition is to sustaining her endurance and rebounding after hours on her feet. She adds that ultrarunning has pushed her to reevaluate her approach to nutrition as she continues to take on longer and more demanding challenges.

“The distance itself makes nutrition so much more important,” Linden says. “You can’t cover that distance if you’re skimping or shortcutting getting the calories in throughout the day.”

The Javelina Jundred is an open and exposed course. The race is defined by heat: the average high is around 82 degrees Fahrenheit and the average low is roughly 58 degrees. Managing more time on her feet also creates more opportunities for things to go awry. Research has long suggested that heat stress can reduce appetite: A 2018 study in Nature found that exercise suppresses appetite by heating up a region of the brain responsible for regulating eating. Of course, this appetite suppression is counterproductive since you are expending lots of extra energy while running, and create a negative feedback loop that self-perpetuates.

Along with dehydration, racing in the heat creates a unique set of challenges. Linden has been working hard to prepare for them.

To prepare for the challenge, Linden enlisted experts from Gu Energy Labs, based in Berkeley, California, including Roxanne Vogel, Ph.D., nutrition scientist, exercise physiologist, and director of research and education, and Magda Boulet, Gu Energy Labs president and one of the world’s most accomplished ultrarunners. Boulet’s own evolution from Olympic marathoner to Western States 100, Leadville 100, and Marathon des Sables champion has made her a valuable resource for Linden’s own ultramarathon journey.

“I imagine most ultrarunners will look and be like ‘you’re not ready at all.’ But they don’t necessarily know that behind the scenes I have the ultrarunner,” Linden says.

Ahead of MDS this spring, Linden underwent laboratory testing at Gu’s Performance Lab with the goal of understanding her energy expenditure, hydration needs, and fueling tolerance during ultramarathon efforts. As part of the assessment, Vogel set out to measure Linden’s sweat rate and sodium losses under heat stress, her caloric demands at race pace, and how her body uses carbohydrate versus fat in simulated desert conditions.

The data helped Vogel develop an individualized metabolic and hydration profile for Linden. Vogel discovered that Linden isn’t a very salty sweater, and she also learned that Linden needs approximately 10 grams of carbohydrate per kilogram of body weight per day. (For a 120-pound person, that’s roughly 550 grams of carbs.)

Going into MDS, the team developed a precise nutrition strategy for Linden, which included Gu Roctane Drink Mix along with gels and chews for her on-course fueling. After each stage, Linden leaned on nut butter and Roctane Protein Recovery Drink Mix to supply the necessary carbohydrates, electrolytes, and 20 grams of whey protein. Her dinner included a savory dehydrated potato mash with added protein and sodium. Linden also integrated Gu Roctane BCAA capsules before and after the stages to support muscle repair and reduce soreness.

Vogel says those core principles will be part of Linden’s approach at Javelina, but the demands of a single day 100-mile race in the Arizona desert will require some adjustments. For Javelina, liquid calories will be the backbone of her nutrition strategy. The target is to consume approximately 16 ounces (500 milliliters) of Roctane Drink Mix per hour. Per 16-ounce serving, it offers 250 calories, 60 grams of carbs, and 320 milligrams of sodium. Linden also plans to integrate some products that remain under development, Vogel says, including Roctane MC-318, a patented menthol-based energy gel designed to help athletes feel perceptually cooler. The product is not yet commercially available, but has already been tested by athletes at races such as Badwater 135, Western States 100, and Marathon des Sables.

The Javelina course consists of five loops along rolling desert singletrack. It’s a format that allows for both Linden and her crew to accurately anticipate her arrival at aid stations, where she’ll be able to replenish supplies and, crucially, will allow for crew to frequently assess how she’s managing the nutrition and hydration plan.

The terrain will help determine when Linden takes in different forms of fuel. Uphill sections, when she’s moving more slowly, provide an opportunity to take gels or chews. On downhills, when she wants to let her legs unwind and rip down as fast as possible, she’ll focus more on liquids. Her approach also reflects a shift from road marathon racing, where fueling opportunities are often more structured and brief.

“In the marathon, [every] 5K you grab the bottle, you want eight to 10 ounces and you want to get rid of the bottle as quickly as possible. We have the luxury of carrying it and sipping on it, and also strategizing,” Linden says.

Temperature will be one of the most significant variables. Research has found that during prolonged exercise in the heat, gastrointestinal symptoms are greater.

“People think it has to be really hot for them to need to make changes to their nutrition or their electrolyte plan,” Vogel says. “The cutoff is somewhere around 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Above that, you’re certainly going to be at an increased level of needs in terms of your hydration and electrolytes, plus also potentially your carbohydrate needs. Even in somewhat moderately warm temperatures, athletes can be needing more than what they would normally take in.”

As the temperature rises throughout the day over the course of the race, Linden anticipates leaning more heavily on liquids. The drink mix can provide fluid and carbohydrates while helping her meet her electrolyte needs, and gels with water will fill any gaps.

“She’s never done a [single day] race this long. The longer you’re out there, the more likely your gut is going to have some issues,” Vogel says. “When you’re exercising, blood flow is going to your working muscles. Less of it is going to your digestive track. So that’s one thing that’s putting stress on the system that makes it harder to digest and absorb [nutrition]. Hence the whole reason for things like gels. They’re easy to digest.”

During the hottest part of the day, Vogel says the team may decrease Linden’s carbohydrate intake to account for changes in digestive tolerance. But as temperatures fall into the night, they’ll look to increase her carbs. Vogel says caffeine will require similar consideration.

“During very hot weather events, caffeine can actually be triggering to the gut in a bad way,” Vogel says. “Rather than following a fixed schedule regardless of conditions, we might actually pull back on caffeine during the heat of the day and start to strategically add it back in as it cools off later in the day.”

Another factor to consider: flavor fatigue, when sensory receptors on your tongue that detect flavor become less responsive with repeated consumption.

“Flavor fatigue is something we know and understand. In hot environments, you don’t generally want to have things that are what we call indulgent—chocolates and caramels and vanillas that are going to stay heavy on the palate. We want more things like citrus and light fruity or even sour, tart flavors that are going to clear the palate or stimulate some thirst,” Vogel says.

Ultimately, the goal is to make the strategy simple to execute, Vogel says. Linden’s success will depend not only on having a precise nutrition plan, but on adjusting on the fly when fatigue and discomfort begin to accumulate.

“I feel like it’s a race within itself. Did I try to execute as well as possible? Did I follow the plan? Did I make good decisions?” Linden says. “I want to finish, and I think there’s so many things that can go in so many different directions in that amount of time and that distance. So if I fueled enough to get myself through 100 miles, that’s a victory.”

#8360. The Best Climbing Skins for Skis of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: This gear guide covers the five best climbing skins for skis, tested last season by our experts. The best climbing skins overall are the Pomoca Tour Pro for their excellent glide and reliable tail clip. The most durable climbing skins are the Black Diamond Glidelite Tour for their longevity and lightweight construction.

Unless you’re one of the lucky few who go catskiing or have a helicopter at your disposal (give us a ring, if so), backcountry skiing almost always involves a fair amount of climbing. And while climbing skins—the adhesive-backed strips of fiber that glide up but not down (like fish scales), then get removed for the descent—might not feel like the most exciting piece of gear in our closet, they have the power to make or break our day.

Last winter, our testers took to the hills (worldwide) and put eight different pairs to the test to bring you our favorite climbing skins for 2027. We indulged in deep powder days in the Tetons, dropped pillows in BC, explored wide-open glaciers in the Swiss Alps, and traversed the rugged mountains of Kyrgyzstan, all the while evaluating each pair of skins for grip, glide, durability and packability.

Pros and Cons + Excellent glide + Reliable tail clip – Plush needs break-in period

If we had to choose one skin to accompany us on all of our backcountry adventures, the Pomoca Tour Pro is an easy choice. After big missions in Grand Teton National Park, short dawn patrols on Teton Pass, and quick skins out the gates at Jackson Hole, testers said the Tour Pro blends excellent grip, glide, and packability, checking all the boxes for a trusty pair.

The Tour Pro features Pomoca’s Power Hook metal tail clip, an update last season to their plastic tail clip that was frequently an early fail point on the skins. Testers who’ve been using Pomoca skins for years all commented on the small but crucial update—which “essentially added seasons to the life of these skins,” reported one tester in the Tetons.

Underneath, Pomoca’s dual fiber plush technology is designed to walk the line between grip and glide, placing grippier fiber blends at the edges of the skin (more nylon), and fiber blends with better glide (more mohair) in the center. The result is solid edgehold on firm, refrozen skintracks, while maintaining the energy-saving glide skiers have come to love from Pomoca. “A great choice for everyday ski touring,” said one tester after a season in the Tetons. “They’re no skimo skin, but they easily handled everything I could throw at them.”

While the plush layer proved to glide well on long days in the mountains, testers noticed they took a tour or two to break in. Still, give ’em a few days and these skins will be your companion for years to come.

Pros and Cons + Excellent glide + Super packable – Finicky tail clip – Hard to peel apart at first

Skins don’t have to be boring. Atomic’s MultiFit Bent Chetler skins feature tip-to-tail artwork by celebrated artist and professional skier Chris Benchetler, making a solid case for sprucing up skin design. But they’re more than just pretty: After rigorous testing in the Tetons, Alps, Kyrgyzstan, and Alaska, these skins, which feature a 70/30 mohair/nylon blend, boasted the best glide.

“After a few tours, they were super fast,” said one tester after three weeks of ski guiding a mixed bag of conditions in Kyrgyzstan, ranging from deep powder to alpine variable. “And they packed up neatly so I could stash them in a pocket.”

A few drawbacks: One tester said the tail clips felt larger than necessary and easily slid off his skis if he wasn’t careful. And while the glue was incredibly reliable, even on sub-zero days, it took some muscle to peel them apart for the first 10 or so tours before getting progressively easier. Despite the sticky nature of Atomic’s Hot Melt glue, they never left residue on the skin.

Pros and Cons + Excellent grip + Solid glide + No breakdown in stickiness over multiple laps – Glue needs a break-in period

There’s hardly a better testing ground for skins than a spring hut trip in British Columbia, and one of our testers put G3’s new Alpinist Universal skins through the wringer while ascending wide-open glaciers, heavy isothermal snow, and bulletproof re-frozen crud. “An awesome mid-point between pretty packable, extremely durable, and super reliable,” reported the tester after he returned from Blanket Glacier Chalet in the Monashee Mountains.

G3 completely overhauled their skin collection this season with a redesign of their ChannelBond glue adhesive, which you’ll find in the new Alpinist Universal, Alpinist Grip, Alpinist Glide, and Alpinist Speed. A vertical channel pattern of adhesive on each skin provided a super solid hold around the edges of the ski, which is where we typically see snow sneak in on long tours.

The glue was ultra sticky at first, but after four or five tours it got significantly easier to peel them apart. The updated glue also maintained performance during multi-lap tours, even in deep snow. It’s easy for skin glue to start to fail when you repeatedly pull them on and off but testers found the Alpinist Universal to be just as solid on lap five as lap one.

Pros and Cons + Highly packable + Durable design – Glue takes a few tours to break in

Our favorite skins for longevity, Black Diamond’s new Glidelite Tour skins replace the Glidelite Mix (our longstanding favorite for durability), with a lightened up version of the reliable construction skiers have come to know and love.

“The glue had excellent hold on skis, even during multi-lap days where the snow really starts to cake up,” said one tester after a week of skiing on Teton Pass. Testers noted that the Glidelite Tour felt lower profile than the previous Glidelite Mix skins, making it easier to fit them in a pack. “These skins folded up really nicely, so I could stuff them in a jacket pocket for quick laps where I didn’t need to do a full transition,” said one Jackson, Wyoming-based tester.

A solid metal tail clip provided a secure hold, while the wide reinforced metal tip loop fit a variety of skis, from fat powder sticks to narrower spring skis. While we still found the glue needed a tour or two to break in, it was nothing like previous iterations of the Glidelite Mix, which a few testers had found to need five to 10 days in the backcountry for the glue to mellow out.

Pros and Cons + Super packable + Reliable glue in a variety of conditions – Plush is less durable – Middle of the road glide

The Kohla Freeride Air Skins were a rock-solid midwinter companion this season. They were packable, lightweight, and easy to peel apart right out of the box. We were impressed with how well the glue held up on a seven-day hut trip in the Selkirks, where we’d frequently complete at least ten transitions while lapping short pillow runs.

Packability is thanks to a thin construction, which does result in a small hit in durability. “I usually wouldn’t throw skins in my jacket for laps since they are just so bulky, but I find myself shoving these in my jacket pockets since they lie so flat,” said a tester after a week of nonstop skiing in British Columbia.

The rubbery tail clip was our favorite of all the ones we tested this season, stretchy yet secure, and easy to slide between sizes for adjustments on the fly. The glide is solid, but nothing to write home about—it felt pretty middle of the road compared to the other skins we tested. We’ve had one pair for two seasons now, and so far the glue has held up, though we see the plush deteriorating a bit after 100 days on them—so you might look elsewhere if you tend to beat the crap out of your gear. You can get these skins from Kohla, but brands like Head, Faction, Fischer, and others also brand Kohla skins with their logo, pre-cut to specific skis.

When choosing skins, the first thing we look at is plush material. Mohair (a fiber made from angora goat hair) provides glide, while nylon provides grip. Skins heavier in nylon will feature more grip than mohair-heavy skins. Most of our favorite skins worked out to be in the middle ground range, with a pretty standard 65/35 blend of mohair and nylon respectively. If you’re newer to skinning and looking for extra grip, the Black Diamond Ascension Skins will provide extra security, albeit at the cost of weight and bulk.

We also look for packability, since there’s somehow never enough room in our packs as it is, and skins that fold up nicely (like the Kohla Freeride Air Skins) make it easy to stuff them in a jacket pocket for quick laps.

Some skins come pre-cut to your skis if you buy them as a package, which can be nice if you’re not into cutting them yourself. Buying skins to match your skis isn’t essential (most skins come with a skin-cutting tool), but will guarantee a precise fit and often a tail clip that lines up well.

Tail clips vary in shape and look but work mostly the same. Most backcountry skis already have a flat spot or notch for a tail clip to hold skins in place, but if you have rounded rockered tails it’s worth checking on how they integrate before buying.

Last winter, we put ski climbing skins to the test all over the world, seeking out the full gamut of backcountry conditions. Our testers put eight pairs of climbing skins to the test in Jackson, Wyoming, Victor, Idaho, the Swiss Alps, Washington’s Cascade Mountains, Kyrgyzstan, Alaska, the Monashees and Selkirks of B.C. and Mammoth Lakes, California, evaluating skins for grip, glide, packability and ease of setup. We sorted through which skins felt like trusty companions lap after lap, and which skins felt more finicky. While testers enjoyed plenty of backyard missions, we believe truly putting skins to the test involves taking them along on multi-day trips and missions, gliding along windswept ridges, refrozen chunder, through deep powder and across questionably frozen lakes—all the while taking note of how they did day after day.

Lily Ritter is a freelance journalist and ski guide based in Victor, Idaho with work featured in The Ski Journal, SKI, Powder Magazine, Freeskier, Teton Gravity Research, and Ascent Backcountry Snow Journal. She spends winters backcountry skiing in Grand Teton National Park and riding lifts at Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, with the occasional trip to the Alps (for the food, obviously).

Jake Stern is a writer and editor based in Mammoth Lakes, California. Formerly an editor at Outside and Powder, he fits boots and writes freelance. He spends his free time exploring the Eastern Sierra backcountry and perfecting his pizza dough recipe.

Morgan McGonagle first dipped her toe into the industry as a professional ski patroller at Crystal Mountain, Washington. These days, she balances her time as a patroller with work as a ski guide and avalanche educator. In the summer, Morgan is a full-time mountain guide working primarily on Washington’s glaciated volcanos, so she spends 12 months of the year walking and sliding on snow. One of her favorite things to do while in the backcountry is plunging into a pristine alpine lake or river.

Ariel Kazunas is a freelance writer based in the Teton Range on the Wyoming and Idaho border. Her favorite ways to recreate (on protected public lands) include skiing, biking, hiking, and backpacking. Ariel believes deeply in questioning the status quo and advocating for both people and planet. Other hobbies include baking sourdough, babying her houseplants, making tailgate cocktails, and scanning Zillow obsessively to see if the US’s wealth inequity problem has been addressed so she can afford a home.

#8358. ‘There Was No Controlling that Fish.’ Two Buddies Land One of the Largest Blue Marlin Ever Caught in Southern California

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:56 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

California fishing buddies Mike Mackenback and Matt Mackinga headed their 20-foot fishing boat into the Pacific at about daybreak on October 25. They were targeting wahoo, which had been hitting off the coast of southern California, but they were about to catch something much bigger.

“We ran south, looking for water temperature breaks where we believed wahoo would be found,” Mackenback tells Outdoor Life. “We were trolling by about 8 a.m., with three lines out – one a deep diving plug, a surface-skipping ‘Black Bart’ lure on another line, and a far back shotgun line with a lure.

“We were about 12 miles from San Pedro, trolling on a beautiful slick-ocean with clear water about 1,500-feet deep.”

Mackenback is a veteran marine boatman, having worked on tugboats and as a merchant marine. He knows boats and fishing and trolled fast at 8 knots for wahoo along a water temperature break from 73 to 75 degrees.

“The fish came up and smashed the surface skipping Black Bart lure about 30 minutes after we started,” says Mackenback, 29, who is now a real estate agent in Redondo Beach. “I thought at first it was a striped marlin until it jumped, then I knew it was huge – there was no controlling that fish as it ran 400 yards of line off a reel in one minute.”

Mackenback held the trolling rod which was set with a Shimano 30 Tiagra reel. It was spooled with 80-pound test Spectra braided line, with a top-shot of 50-pound test monofilament, and a 25-foot 200-pound test fluorocarbon leader.

Mackenback quickly realized they had hooked a huge blue marlin that was rapidly taking all the line off his reel, which was rigged for wahoo and much smaller striped marlin.

“I gave the rod to Matt, he went to the bow to fight the fish, and I turned the boat to chase after it,” Mackenback says. “The marlin was jumping and racing away, and I chased it with the boat for a few minutes while Matt tried to gain some of the line it took on those blistering runs.”

Matt kept the line tight on the marlin, and Mackenback got closer to the fish with his boat.

Then the marlin dove deep as it got a second wind during the fight.

“It almost spooled us twice,” says Mackenback. “Matt would gain line fighting the fish. I’d stay over it with the boat, and then it would dive deep again, and again, and again.

“We traded back and forth fighting the fish with the rod. We had no fighting belt or harness – just a small slide on the rod butt cushion. I didn’t think there was a 10 percent chance we’d catch and release it. My wahoo tackle wasn’t built for a giant blue marlin.”

One hour into the epic battle, the anglers decided to just follow the blue with their boat, trying to tire it out over time.

Almost two hours into the marlin battle they gained enough line on the fish that they could see its shiny blue color deep below in clear water. Then it dove deep again, and it was another 45 minutes before they spotted the fish near their boat.

“Suddenly the line went slack, and I thought it was gone,” Mackenback says. “We saw the swivel to the leader, grabbed it, and hauled on the leader to get it close.

“The fish was whipped, I knew it was gone as I was holding 600-pounds of blue marlin beside my 20-foot boat.”

They tried multiple times to revive the marlin for release. But the big blue fought until it was dead. There was no way they could get the marlin pulled up into their Grady-White boat. So, they lashed it to the side of their boat and ran slowly back to San Pedro’s Cabrillo Way Marina where they’d left that morning.

They notified the marina they were coming in with a huge marlin, and a crane was waiting for the anglers to haul the fish up and weigh it.

Their blue marlin measured more than 13 feet and weighed 595 pounds. It’s one of the largest blues ever caught off Southern California. Giant blues are believed to have moved into the region due to unusual water and weather conditions in this El Nino year.

In September 2015, a 648-pound blue marlin was caught 40 miles off San Diego by anglers aboard the boat Pegasus. A 692-pound blue was caught also during an El Nino year off the coast of Southern California.

Read Next: My Outboard Died — Just as We Hooked Up with a Giant Marlin

Mackenback and Mackinga cleaned and processed their marlin, and had some of it for dinner that night.

“We spent hours processing the marlin into steaks, and gave a lot of it to neighbors and friends,” says Mackenback. “We grilled marlin steaks that night and had a great cookout.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8357. Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:39 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

You’re five minutes into legal shooting with high hopes for your morning sit, then you hear it. A faint buzzing overhead. Eyes to the sky, you spot the drone hovering over your property. Suddenly, you’re less optimistic about your hunt.

[Insert neighbor] is up to no good again, you think. But is it actually who you think it is? How can you be sure? Basic, consumer-level drones can fly for miles. They can also spook deer and other wildlife on both public and private land.

Talk to landowners and deer hunters in Big Deer country and you’ll hear that drone usage has skyrocketed in recent years. Sure, there are a lot of folks flying drones legally during deer season. In many places it’s legal to fly a drone while attempting to recover a hit deer. Thermal drones are incredibly effective at this. But more and more, folks are using drones to scan other people’s properties in order to locate (and sometimes harass) big bucks.

Enter the drone defense system — a technology that defends against unwanted drones flying over a hunting property for all the wrong reasons.

Modern deer hunting and land management look vastly different than they did just a few years ago. Today, drones weave through several aspects of whitetail management and sometimes hunting and poaching, too. Drones are used for population surveys, property management, and deer recovery. These are common reasons deer hunters and land managers consult drone operators or fly their own drones. So long as laws are followed and ethical hunting is prioritized, there’s nothing wrong with any of that. In fact, when used properly, drones can be a net positive for whitetail herds, especially when sound management is the driving force.

But like with any new technology, some people are hellbent on using thermal drones for unethical purposes, namely, spying on the neighbor’s deer — and possibly even poaching them. That has sparked the need for the drone defense systems being promoted by Jack Huston, owner and operator of Midwest Deer Surveys.

“Most of the problem is people flying over property they don’t own or have permission to be on,” Huston says. “It’s not so much local landowners flying every day trying to know how to hunt a buck. It’s more people scouting the whole township, if you will.

“That’s a huge problem, and in my eyes, it’s trespassing,” Huston says. “People work so hard to have land to hunt. They work to make it ready for hunting season. Then, if somebody wants to just go fly a drone and buzz your deer, they can. And I don’t think that should be OK.”

The fast-growing popularity of drones in the hunting world creates a whole barrage of questions: What are the regulations around drones? Is it legal to fly over someone else’s property? Will wildlife agencies be using drone tracking tech to prevent poaching? Huston says the laws are very different from state to state.

“You know, Ohio is completely wide open — probably too much so,” Huston says. “Then there are some states that are what I call anti-drone.”

For example, Pennsylvania prohibits drone usage for any type of hunting, including tracking wounded deer.

Huston’s system allows a landowner to identify when a drone flies their property, and who the drone is registered to.

“I go all around the country doing deer surveys for landowners,” Huston said. “I talk to all of these people, and they are complaining about drones flying over their farms. A lot of times, these people are bigger landowners in the area, and people get curious.

“A lot of people pushed me to find a product that could essentially serve as a radar for drones. That is this product. People are setting them up at their house or barn and it just sits there and monitors the drone activity on that property, and all around it.”

The system picks up the transmission between the remote controller and the drone itself. It’s able to read that transmission and get the location of the pilot, location of the drone, the make of the drone, its serial number, and more. It records all of that and stores it for the user.

The collected drone detection information feeds back to an app on the landowner’s phone. It lets them know who’s flying, where they’re flying, and everything that’s going on in their airspace. It’s essentially a monitoring tool to alert landowners when someone is flying their property.

“With these drone detectors, we have real data of how many people are flying, and it’s certainly far more than I thought,” Huston says.

Huston says you can buy one of several drone defense system sizes and choose from options that cover roughly a 5-mile, 20-mile, or 40-mile radius.

“A lot of my customers are just geo-fencing their farm,” Huston says. “So, they’re creating a bit of a bubble around their property where they want to cover the skies.”

But as you can probably guess, setting up one of these systems isn’t cheap. Smaller stations start at about $5,000 while the bigger station will set you back about $12,000. Still, for a large property owner who has spent millions of dollars on owning the ground and implementing habitat work, the cost of a drone surveillance system is only a drop in the bucket.

While Huston doesn’t manufacture these himself (he works with a company on the manufacturing side), he helped establish and design the drone defense system.

Huston’s installations are already making positive impacts for some landowners who invest. He says there have been several instances where drones were detected, confirmations of illegal use were made, and law enforcement was called to intercept. Essentially, drones were being used to aid in poaching, and the drone defense systems assisted in prevention, and maybe eventual prosecution.

It does not take too much imagination to see how wildlife agencies and their game wardens might one day use similar drone detection systems to catch poachers and illegal fliers.

“Drones are the Wild West, right now,” Huston says. “I think, when the word gets out on these… It will push drones to be used how they’re supposed to be used.

Read Next: Drones Could Revolutionize How Hunters Recover Lost Deer … If They’re Not Banned First

“When I go out on my land, or my family’s land, I don’t want a drone bothering me,” Huston says. “And if there is one, I want to know who it is and solve that problem. This is the solution to that problem. Without it, people can get away with whatever they want.”

#8356. The Future Wild

In Spain’s emptying countryside, nature is moving back in.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

And they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

#8355. Montana Man Banned From Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull

Published Nov 2, 2026 6:36 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A father and son who pleaded guilty to poaching in central Montana have lost their hunting privileges for a combined 24 years. Their poaching activity goes back years, but the investigation into the men started last year based on a tip from two bowhunters, who reported a man shooting a bull elk with a rifle during archery season in September 2025.

“Lawful hunters are some of the most passionate outdoorsmen and women in existence. They’re very quick to report wildlife crimes and violations they see in the field,” Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks game warden and lead investigator Diego O’Brien tells Outdoor Life. “These two individuals, in my opinion, went above and beyond reporting the violation. They were very proactive with assistance in an area that I didn’t know very well. They proved to be incredible resources for me.”

Based on information provided by the two bowhunters, law enforcement located Billings resident Michael Letasky through a traffic stop. He matched the description of the man shooting the bull in the Little Belt Mountains, but he didn’t have the rack or any game meat. The bull was left to waste. (The two witnesses knew exactly where the dead animal was, but by then it was too late for wardens to salvage the meat.)

“The hunters that witnessed this trophy bull elk unlawfully shot during archery season were rightfully upset and immediately reported the crime to authorities,” O’Brien said in a statement. “Their quick and accurate reporting and assistance in locating evidence were crucial to this investigation. They sacrificed their own hunting trip to ensure justice was served.”

The poached 6×6 bull met the state’s trophy standards. By state code, restitution for the illegal killing and possession or waste of trophy elk is $8,000. The only animal with a higher restitution than a 6×6 bull is a bighorn ram with at least three-fourths curl, which earns a penalty of $30,000.

In addition to the poached bull, Letasky also shot a raghorn with a firearm during the 2023 archery season, and he had an unreported black bear. During the investigation, wardens also found evidence against Letasky’s son, Kolton, of Austin, Texas.

Kolton Letasky killed a Montana buck in 2024 and a Montana bull in 2022 without the proper permits. He pled guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game and two counts of hunting without a license. His penalties include more than $3,000 in fines and no hunting for four years.

Read Next: YouTuber Poaching Bust Was a Case of ‘Wildlife Commercialization with a Modern Twist,’ Says Investigating Warden

The elder Letasky’s penalties are more severe. Michael Letasky plead guilty to two counts of unlawful possession of game, two counts of hunting during a closed season and one count of wasting game. He owes more than $12,000 in fines and can’t hunt for 20 years.

Kris Millgate is a multimedia journalist based in eastern Idaho. She’s a fly fisher, a bird hunter and an avid seeker of awkward moments. Read and watch more of her work at tightlinemedia.com

#8354. Secrets for Deer Hunting the Big Woods, According to a North Country Expert

Published Nov 3, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Hunting whitetails in the North Country forests of New England and the Upper Midwest is an undeniably challenging pursuit. Up there the landscapes are massive, think tens of thousands of acres of forest. Food sources and deer sign are more subtle. There are no edges of agricultural fields to target, and there might not even be stands of oaks dropping acorns. Lastly, deer densities are low, with some areas having maybe five deer per square mile.

It’s within this environment that Brett Joy, a member of the Just Hunt Club, has made a name for himself. Using a mix of old-school and modern hunting strategies, Joy has found success killing mature big woods bucks season after season.

I sat down with him for the most recent episode of the Outdoor Life podcast to learn his strategies for targeting mature bucks in the northwoods. Even if you don’t hunt big woods deer yourself, you can learn from Joy’s tactics and experience.

Joy uses digital maps to identify areas where two or three types of habitat converge.

“Whitetails, whether they’re in a cornfield in Iowa or on a mountain in New Hampshire, are edge habitat creatures,” Joy says. “They live on the edges, but those edges can look a lot different depending on where you are in the whitetails’ range.”

In the big woods, look for edges between hardwoods and softwoods, swamps and mature timber, mature timber and early successional growth (recently logged areas). Once you’ve identified these spots, scout them in person. Ideally, you’ll be a mile or more away from any road.

Joy believes that because the habitat is so vast in the big woods, bucks tend to have larger home ranges and core areas. They also have a variety of bedding areas — even in the early season. Whereas in the agricultural country, mature bucks tend to have only a couple woodlots and thickets where they like to bed.

“Our deer could bed on any different point of a mountain in any cut, in a swamp on any given day,” Joy says. “[Those bedding areas] could be miles apart day to day. They’re almost more of a nomadic deer … but they do have areas that they come back to year after year.”

The key is that even if you’re in a buck’s core zone, you might not see him for a week or more.

Like everywhere else in whitetail country, during the rut big woods bucks will travel between doe groups searching for does in estrus.

“But here, you may have only three does that live within 500 acres,” Joy says. So bucks have to cover more ground and do more checking. And this need to travel long distances makes rutting bucks more vulnerable.

“I like to hunt them during the rut and really focus on those areas they frequent when they’re traveling from A to B, or I hunt near one of those doe groups … and if you can find a big primary scrape or pinch point within the core area of those does, you can catch bucks going through there semi-consistently.”

Trail cameras are a critical component of Joy’s strategy because there’s essentially no visibility in the areas that he hunts. In other words, there are not places to glass from in the big woods.

“If I cared less about what buck I was targeting, I could hunt sign and not use cameras and be successful, but I really do rely on them heavily for my strategy,” he says.

Joy positions most of his cameras on large community scrapes because they serve as social gathering spots that will attract deer in vast landscapes. On top of that, Joy focuses on secluded, high-elevation areas that bucks tend to prefer.

Joy aims to run cameras from about October 15 through December 15, which gives him the full range of rut activity.

When you’re hunting the rut in the big woods, you need to have a good understanding of peak rut activity dates.

“What dictates everything is does coming into estrus,” Joy says. “And those bucks absolutely know those dates in this landscape and they will show up checking those doe groups on the same few days year after year.”

Joy conducted an in-depth trail camera survey using several years worth of his trail camera photos, plus his buddy’s photos to identify peak deer activity during the rut. He found that peak activity in his area was November 19th.

He then paired his trail cam data data with a biologist’s data on fawn conception dates in New Hampshire and he found that the peak conception date was November 19 as well.

“If I had to pick five or seven days, I’d put November 19th right in the middle of it,” Joy says.

Joy adds that he hasn’t witnessed a shutdown in activity due to lockdown. Bucks are covering the most ground during daylight during peak breeding dates.

But peak activity is different throughout whitetail country. You must examine your own trail camera photos and examine historical data to nail down the key dates where you hunt.

Read Next: North Woods Legend Hal Blood on Snow Tracking Bucks

“Now to kill deer in these landscapes you can’t just expect to hunt one weekend,” Joy says. You need probably a week of hunting and you need to hunt for the entire week, dark to dark, he says.

Joy will set up different stands within an area for different wind directions, but once he picks an area he sticks with it and does not jump around from spot to spot — even if he’s not seeing deer right away.

“Sometimes I don’t make a decision about where I’m going to sit until the day before … I’ll wait until I have all the information on a particular spot, but once I decide to [hunt there], that’s it. There’s no deviating. Once you start to doubt and jump around, you’re done,” Joy says. “The day you’re not there is the day he’ll come by.”

If you have good trail camera data and historical data on a spot, it makes it easier to commit to it for a week of hunting. Other keys to staying in the hunt long-term are: efficient access to your stand, good clothing to keep you warm, quality food to eat throughout the week, plenty of rest at night, and staying hydrated. Most importantly, you’ve got to keep the faith.

“Sitting in the cold for 11 or 12 hours a day, day after day, it really does wear on you and you start to doubt yourself and doubt your spot. You start to become negative, and once that stuff compounds … you’re not going to be there when that buck comes by.”

If you are able to stay patient and stick it out, there’s a good chance that an old northwoods buck will eventually walk by. And no matter how big his rack is, he’ll be a true trophy whitetail.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.
