#8353. Winter Hiking Boots FAQ

If you plan to hike this winter, buy insulated, waterproof winter hiking boots to protect your feet and keep them warm. Regular hiking boots intended for three-season conditions, mids, or trail runners lack enough insulation and may not stay waterproof in wet snow, puddles, or slush. Even regular leather hiking boots treated with waterproofing products can absorb moisture, becoming cold and potentially freezing during a long outing. This can lead to discomfort, frostnip, or frostbite in severe conditions.

Insulated winter hiking boots are a much better option because they have waterproof construction, rubber or waterproof synthetic lowers, and insulation that helps retain warmth even if moisture enters from above or accumulates from perspiration. While waterproof membranes such as Gore-Tex can reduce water entry, they cannot prevent dampness from sweating or the chilling effect foot perspiration can cause in cold winter weather. When that happens, insulation remains the most important factor. A damp insulated boot can still retain warmth better than an uninsulated boot that has absorbed water and begun to freeze.

When choosing insulated winter hiking boots, you’ll want boots for the temperatures you expect to encounter, usually between -10°F and 35°F, although you may encounter even colder temperatures. People with cold feet may want to get more heavily insulated boots to stay warm. The temperature ratings that winter hiking boots come with assume active use, so it pays to get a boot that is even warmer if you have to stop and stand around for a while. Say, for instance, a companion is injured. You’ll want boots with enough foot insulation to stay with them until help arrives.

Winter boots generally fall into three categories:

Each type is designed for different conditions and activities, from winter hiking and snowshoeing to ice climbing, snowmobiling, and ice fishing. The best choice depends on how much you walk, how cold and wet the conditions are, and whether you need to use traction devices such as microspikes, snowshoes, or crampons.

The waterproof/breathable liners, like Gore-Tex, built into cold-weather boots usually do a good job of keeping moisture out, especially when the boots are new. But it doesn’t hurt to add extra waterproofing, like Sno-Seal, to the outside of the boots, especially along the seams, for added protection. Waterproof/breathable liners do break down with use, and it’s good to have a backup strategy. These liners also provide poor breathability in winter, and your socks will likely get damp from perspiration if you’re active. While not ideal, this is normal, and the added insulation will keep your feet warm.

If you plan to hike or snowshoe in winter, you’ll want insulated, waterproof boots designed primarily for walking, not more technical activities like mountain climbing or ice-climbing, or sedentary activities like snowmobiling or ice fishing.

Winter hiking boots look like regular hiking boots, mid-height boots, or even boots with coverage above the ankle, but they’re all waterproof and insulated. For most winter hiking and snowshoeing, boots that extend just above the ankle are the most comfortable and practical. The more calf coverage you have, the warmer your feet will remain.

Winter hiking boots should have laces instead of slip-on designs or zippers so you can tighten the fit. When walking on snow or ice, lug depth and rubber type matter less than your ability to use traction aids like microspikes or snowshoes, which bite into the surface and keep you from slipping. For instance, anti-slip rubber soles designed to prevent slipping on urban sidewalks are virtually worthless if you need to wear microspikes for traction most of the time.

Synthetic insulated boots are usually lighter and more water-resistant than leather boots. The insulation will be built into the boot and not removable, which keeps the weight down and makes the boots easier to walk in. The amount of insulation you need depends on the temperature, how active you will be, and whether you will walk continuously or stand still for long periods.

Winter boots are commonly offered with 200-gram or 400-gram Thinsulate insulation, although PrimaLoft or Aerogel insulation is also used and provides the same level of warmth retention. The 200g and 400g quantities refer to the insulation’s thickness or density, not its weight inside your boots.

As a general guide, 200-gram insulation suits active use in temperatures around 0 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit, while 400-gram insulation is better suited to temperatures between approximately -20 and -40 degrees Fahrenheit. These estimates assume that you are walking rather than standing around. Individual experiences vary considerably.

We recommend the following insulated 200-gram and 400-gram winter hiking boots:

Regardless of insulation level, check that your boots work properly with your microspikes, snowshoes, or crampons. Traction devices should not create excessive pressure on your toes or the front of your boots, since this can cause discomfort and blisters. This is often the case with lighter-weight winter hiking boots or mids that have soft uppers.

Mountaineering boots are designed for steep, technical terrain and ice climbing. They have rigid soles that support crampons and allow climbers to stand on small edges of ice or rock. They are also generally heavier, less flexible, and less comfortable for ordinary hiking than insulated winter boots. They can also be quite bulky and may not be compatible with microspikes or even snowshoe bindings. Mountaineering boots I recommend.

Mountaineering boots are available in single-layer and double-layer designs. Single-layer boots, like those listed above, are intended primarily for day trips in exposed alpine terrain. Double-layer boots have a removable liner and are best for overnight trips because you can remove a damp liner and sleep with it, preventing it from freezing overnight.  They’ve largely fallen out of use, but if you’re going someplace where you need them, you can often rent them from mountain guides, especially if you’ve hired a guide service.

If you need a full crampon compatible with the flexible soles of insulated winter hiking boots, look for one with a “flexible leaf spring or center bar,” like the Camp Stalker Universal Crampon. This flexible center bar connects the front spikes to the rear spike assembly. The flexible bar prevents the crampon from snapping in half when used with boots that have more flexible soles.

Pac boots usually have a rubber lower section, a leather or synthetic upper, and a removable felt liner. They are designed for very cold, wet conditions, but their warmth comes with several hiking disadvantages. Pac boots are heavy, bulky, extend well above the ankle, and provide limited ankle support.

They suit activities that require little walking, such as ice fishing and snowmobiling.

Their large size can also make it difficult to fit with microspikes, crampons, and most snowshoes. For active winter hiking, insulated hiking boots are usually a better choice.

Boot warmth ratings are useful for comparing products, but they are not standardized. Manufacturers may test their boots differently, and a rating cannot account for every person or condition.

Your experience will depend on factors such as:

Read customer reviews and look for boots that have been sold for several seasons. Recommendations from experienced hikers and people you trust can also be useful.

Beyond insulation and waterproofing, several design details can improve comfort and performance.

A manufacturer’s temperature rating provides a rough indication of warmth, but it should not be treated as a guarantee.

A sturdy toe cap protects your feet and helps prevent the front of the boot from collapsing under tight-fitting microspikes or crampons. A collapsed toe box can cause pressure and blisters.

A gusseted tongue is attached along its sides to the inside of the boot. It helps keep water from entering through the laces when you step into deep snow or puddles.

The cuff is the upper edge of the boot around your lower leg. A soft, comfortable cuff helps retain heat and prevents snow from entering when you walk through deep snow.

Deep, well-spaced lugs provide traction on packed and loose snow. Rubber compounds and tread patterns vary, but a durable sole such as Vibram can provide reliable grip. On ice, you will generally need microspikes or crampons in addition to the boot tread.

A gaiter ring near the toe allows you to attach the front hook of your gaiters. If your boots do not have one, you can often attach gaiters to the laces instead.

Winter boots should not be tight. A cramped boot restricts circulation and can make your feet colder. Your toes should have enough room to move, but your foot should not slide excessively from side to side. Your heel should remain secure when the boot is fully laced.

Try on winter boots with the socks you plan to wear. If you wear thick winter socks, try them on during the fitting process. When between sizes, it is usually safer to choose the larger size. You can fill a small amount of extra space with thicker socks or higher-volume insoles, such as Superfeet. You can’t make a boot that’s too small larger.

#8352. Fractals in the Dirt

A dusty exploration of the least-appreciated geology on the Colorado Plateau.

Not long ago, I drove six hours with the Mancos Shale riding shotgun. That isn’t a buddy’s quirky nickname, as in: Yo, my man Mancos, my Shaley bro, hand me the Doritos and Sour Patch Kids, would ya please? It is in fact a geologic formation, a remarkably friable gray-blue-brown mudstone deposited in the Late Cretaceous, some ninety million years before present, when much of what we today call the American West was inundated by a vast inland sea. To an unsuspecting bystander, a turkey vulture or big-rig trucker, I must have seemed to be a lone soul on a desert road trip, only the radio’s pop divas, evangelical preachers, and static for company. Wrong. Mile after mile, the Mancos was at my side, catching the corner of my eye, whispering sweet nothings in my ear, keeping me intrigued and entertained.

#8351. The FN Mauser Is the Best Deer Rifle that History Forgot

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:01 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Hunting rifles come and go and sometimes even good ones don’t stay around. The decades following World War II saw a boom in hunters and a voracious appetite for new rifles and cartridges. This was the heyday of the Pre-64 Model 70 and the Winchester Magnums, but we no longer hear much about the many Mauser sporting rifles made by FN and imported from Belgium.

I recently got my mitts on one of these rifles, which belonged to my great grandfather, chambered in .270 Win. While this gun undoubtedly rode around in the rifle rack of Grandpa Curtis’s truck when I was a youngster, I’m looking at it anew. According to my dad and uncle, Grandpa’s brother was a gunsmith and built the rifle for him. This was after he’d raised a family in a log cabin in Colorado during the Depression and developed a taste for July mule deer. He used this rifle to shoot a lot of deer and elk.

A family heirloom like this gives me a perspective on what a quality hunting rifle looked like in the 1950s, and an idea of how well it’s held up over time. It’s also fun to compare it to the rifles we have today.

It’s common to hear or read about the many sporterized military rifles that post-war hunters adopted. These would typically be either 1903 Springfields or remnant military Mauser rifles. But these FN Mausers weren’t sporterized — they were manufactured for a couple decades as sporting-specific guns. Many, including this rifle, were imported by Firearms International Corp. and marked as such on the receivers.

They were brought in and sold by various companies and in numerous formats. An ad in the November, 1951 Issue of Outdoor Life displays the JC Higgins Model 50 — which was simply an FN Mauser and sold at Sears, Roebuck. They had the chrome vanadium steel barrel and even came with a 2.5-power scope, for $135. Another ad, from the September, 1952 issue, for the Parker-Whelen Gun Catalog, lists .30/06 and .270 FN Mausers for $137.50 without a receiver-mounted rear sight. That would cost you another ten bucks. This could be a clue to the specific origin of this .270, as the front of the barrel has markings that appear to be where a front sight was once mounted, but there is no evidence of a barrel-mounted rear sight like you’ll see on Pre-64 Model 70 rifles and others like the Remington Model 721.

Ultimately, lots of these guns were imported in various forms and were sold by companies like Weatherby, Harrington & Richardson, and Colt. Complete FN rifles, according to what little I could find, had a specific pearl edge to the checkering on the grips, but it’s likely that not all of them did. Barrelled actions were also imported and built into custom hunting rifles.

This particular rifle appears to be either one that showed up as a barrelled action — possibly with a front sight. The barrel and receiver both bear the appropriate stampings for a matched pair that left the factory in Belgium. But the 22-inch barrel appears to have been cut down and re-crowned — as these were generally 24-inch barrels. It’s stamped with the year “1951” and bears matching 2837 serial numbers.

The stock has a handsome grain and good ergonomics. It lacks any checkering, but the fore-end has a nice belly and is capped with an ivory-colored plastic cap. The grip is capped with a similar plastic cap and its vertical orientation provides a wonderful balance of trigger reach and allows a crisp perpendicular squeeze. The raised comb is, in part, made from a separate block of wood. It’s pinned atop the buttstock and shaped to match, but the seams are still visible.

The floorplate isn’t hinged on this rifle. Rather, it’s detachable and retained by a spring-loaded button at the rear and retaining lip at the front. The fitting of the stock is very precise and, despite being bedded from the tang to the cap on the fore-end, very little bedding material is visible alongside the metal. Pillars around the action screws also help create an incompressible bridge between the bottom metal and action. The precise fit of metal and wood are things we’ll only see today on custom rifles and the highest-end production guns. Factory stocks — both wood and synthetic — are either CNC-milled or molded with baked-in tolerances rather than hand fit. The workmanship on my 1954 Model 70 is good, but not to the same level.

The barrel is a pretty standard sporter taper, finishing at .635 inches. I assume it has been cut down from 24 inches to 22. It’s a heavier barrel than you’ll see on classics like the M70 featherweight and contributes to the rifle’s roughly 9.5-pound overall weight.

The action and barrel share all matching and appropriate proof marks, and remain in good shape, with the bolt sliding like glass down the slick raceways. The bottom of the bolt handle is flattened and knurled for a better grip, and is generally smoother to operate than my previously mentioned M70. The safety switch is textured on both sides. It appears to be pitting because of its irregularity, but no other parts show similar signs of corrosion.

The receiver is topped with a one-piece Redfield mount and Bear Cub 2 ¾-power scope that uses a post-style reticle. In the early days of magnified optics, this gave a sight picture similar to that of a front post iron sight — to which most shooters would be accustomed. It was fitted with a Canjar trigger — a premium aftermarket upgrade, that breaks at 3 pounds, 7 ounces as set.

To test the rifle for accuracy, I fired four five-shot groups with several different types of contemporary .270 ammo. Where we would normally aggregate these five-shot groups into a single 20-shot group for each type of ammo, It was apparent that the system was limited, in part, by the optic, so I’m just sticking with the group size averages.

I believe the rifle is certainly capable of better accuracy than this but, considering the vintage scope, it proved itself perfectly capable of hitting a deer or elk cleanly out to 200 to 300 yards. Frankly, it’s not uncommon for us to test modern rifles with high-magnification scopes that average worse. A low-power optic itself doesn’t prevent a rifle from shooting accurately either, but this style of reticle requires the correct-sized target and a lot of concentration to maintain a consistent hold. The post covers about four inches of a 100-yard target. When the barrel warmed, mirage definitely affected sight picture too. I tried both a six-o’clock hold and a navy hold (dead center), and saw some vertical stringing with both methods.

Read Next: 10 Classic Hunting Rifles Every Hunter Should Own

For as much as we hear about classic rifles like the Savage 99 and Winchester Model 70, I’m surprised that Mausers like this haven’t carried a similar reputation. So many rifles, including the Winchester, were derived from the Mauser action itself. The rifles even commanded a higher price than Model 70s at the time. While precision manufacturing, materials, and coatings have gotten better, a rifle like this one could still hold its own today.

#8350. Where Did the Midweight Ski Touring Boot Go?

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The men's Tecnica Zero G Decoy Pro, staged and ready to go for a backcountry adventure in Cooke City, Montana. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: Midweight ski touring boots, historically three buckles and 1,300 to 1,500 grams, can handle the whole range of backcountry skis, yet the class has stagnated while lightweight and crossover boots got most of the industry’s R&D. Writer Bergen Tjossem, a former ski-shop employee, argues the next big touring breakthrough should come from the midweight category.

It’s 4 a.m. and the biting cold plunges into the open garage as I stuff my partner’s idling Forester with gear. But I stall, hovering over my collection of ski touring boots. Big boots or little boots? Neither seems right for the day. I throw my thrashed 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots over my shoulder, snap on my headlamp, and lug my skis to the car. I don’t know why I still hesitate at the start of every backcountry ski day—I end up picking the workhorse boot over the specialists most of the time.

Why, then, is the industry trying to squash this midweight ski touring boot class? Even the Maestrale RS, my beloved midweight archetype, is graduating toward the next class up this season, with a fourth buckle and more heft.

Owning a quiver of boots and skis is fun; it gives you options. But if you already own a pair of alpine boots like most skiers do, one dedicated touring boot could accomplish the vast majority of your needs. Yet where backcountry skis fall on a neat bell curve of dimension and weight, the boots we can buy to pilot them are bimodally distributed: ski shapes cluster in the middle, touring boots at the extremes. The evolution of midweight ski touring boots—the ones that best serve the majority of backcountry skiers—has stagnated compared to their cousins at the ends. It’s the “missing middle” problem every ski town knows from housing.

There’s no rule or buckle count dividing touring boot classes, but allow me to split them for the sake of the rant: lightweight boots typically have two buckles and top out around 1,200 grams, like the La Sportiva Kilo. Midweight boots historically use three buckles and weigh 1,300 to 1,500 grams. Then there are crossover boots that blend touring and alpine: four buckles, around 1,500 grams, typically with a GripWalk sole compatible with tech and alpine bindings, like the Dynafit Tigard.

Ski touring dogma says the optimum backcountry quiver is two pairs of ski touring boots and two pairs of skis: one lightweight and distance-oriented, the other beefy and fun. But here’s the catch—lightweight boots struggle with big skis, especially in poor snow, because they lack progressive flex and damping. And the opposite is also true. Crossover boots are a real drag on lightweight skis. Aside from the cumbersome ROM, the added stiffness, high cuff, and heft quickly overpower lightweight skis. Yet midweights can handle the whole ski spectrum.

When I worked in ski shops in the early 2010s as ski touring took off, midweight boots were the benchmark. Dynafit’s Vulcan and the Scarpa Maestrale were the choice for skiers who wanted to climb efficiently without giving up too much on the descent. What followed that workhorse boot era was an explosion of lightweight options, as almost every company in the business invested in svelter chassis while skis got lighter and less demanding. The rise of resort uphilling and Skimo racing only fueled the growth. Lately, lightweight boots such as La Sportiva’s Kilo XTR have been beefed up to claim more of that middle segment without overtaking it completely. But lightweight two-buckle designs with sturdier components still come up short on the leverage and suspension big skis demand.

Crossovers got the next round of R&D in the name of capturing the massive resort-hybrid buyer. Scarpa’s 1,500 gram 4-Quattro XT with a legit 61 degree range of motion (ROM) revolutionized the segment in 2022. All of a sudden, boots with alpine-like skiing capability unlocked a bigger ROM, while better materials and design brought weights down to 1,500 grams per boot or less. It also introduced freaky new levels of “quiver overlap” for skiers who already own alpine boots with a walk mode.

Smooshed between the crossover and the lightweight segments is that increasingly scant boot group, the midweights. It’s not that these midweight boots don’t exist—the Scott Cosmos Pro and Fischer Transalp prove they do—but rather that they’ve gotten the shaft on R&D over the last decade. Most of the remaining midweights are just stale, longing for a refresh, a trickle-down of new tech, and a burst of innovation.

A radical solution would be to have fewer skis, and I can’t believe you’d even suggest that. I’ve got a better idea: Give me one boot that can cover the entire ski quiver: three buckles, a camming power strap, over 65 degrees of ROM, under 1,400 grams, and minimal fiddle factor. Oops, I just mostly described the Scarpa Maestrale that’s been around for sixteen years. That’s because the industry is barely competing to refine that basic formula into its state-of-the-art form.

As a skier of many setups, I can say there’s a mismatch between the boots I want and those available. Lightweights and crossovers have had their run. My hunch is that the next big touring breakthrough will be, and should be, in the missing middle. Until then, you’ll catch me clinging to my 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots like the gear troll I am.

#8349. A Veteran Bowhunter Finds Two Bucks Locked Together Deep Into Public Land. Should He Shoot Them?

Published Nov 3, 2026 2:09 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Robert Denninger was in a tree saddle the afternoon of October 23 when he spotted a deer in a creek bed about 75 yards away. He’d accessed the Oklahoma public hunting area by kayak, paddling up a creek to a remote spot that he’d pinpointed the previous day.

“I decided to slide down quietly with my bow and get a better look at the deer in the creek,” Denninger tells Outdoor Life. “When I got close to the creek I spotted two big mature bucks fighting and they were locked up tight by their antlers.”

He knew he was witnessing an epic outdoor event and he shot video of the fight on his phone.

“The bucks were plowing into each other and into the creek bank,” says Denninger, a 42-year-old retiree from Dallas. “Mud was flying everywhere. My mind was racing – would attempting to harvest these bucks be a hunter’s gift or a violation of fair chase?”

It was clear the bucks were not able to separate their antlers. Denninger struggled with what to do and pondered if it would be ethical and legal to shoot the larger of the two bucks, which was a 12-pointer with a typical rack. He recalled a friend telling him a story of once finding a pair of locked-antler bucks dead in a pond. They had been killed and half eaten by coyotes.

Before deciding what to do, Denninger called a game warden.

“I spoke with a local [Oklahoma] Game Warden who assured me he didn’t have any on-call vet who could have come out to sedate the animals and attempt a safe unlocking,” Denninger says.

“The thought of letting ‘nature run its course’ and coming back in the following days to spook a pack of coyotes off two rotten carcasses or trying my best to put an ethical kill on these animals were what I believed my choices were,” he explains. “I decided to shoot the 12-pointer.”

His first arrow was deflected by brush. But his second arrow found the deer’s heart, and it quickly died.

“I watched to see if the eight point could free himself, but he only struggled more, barely able to move the weight of the harvested 12-pointer,” the bowhunter says.

Denninger had no way of freeing the deer, so he decided to shoot the second buck with his bow. Even when both deer were dead, it was impossible to unlock their antlers.

That’s when he called a couple younger buddies, who eventually arrived with a wheeled wagon.

“We tried to unlock their racks many times, and were unable to,” Denninger says. “We field dressed them. But it was a rugged haul to get the two bucks out, taking well over three hours to get them to a truck and out of the woods. It was almost midnight [by the time we were done].”

He called his Texas friend and taxidermist Dustin Moon and told him about the locked-antler bucks and his hunting tale.

“Dustin and his wife Stephanie of New Story Taxidermy drove five hours (on their sixth wedding anniversary) to where I was so they could see the bucks and help my deer processor get their antlers unlocked.”

Eventually they succeeded and the deer were separated. They will be mounted, though Denninger doesn’t know if he’ll have them in a locked-horn mount or separate mounts.

The 12-pointer is believed to be 7.5 years old and has a rough green score of 152 inches. It’s the biggest buck Denninger has taken during his dedicated bowhunting career. The 8-pointer is thought to be 5.5 years old and scores 132 inches. Both bucks have typical racks.

“I think what I did was the most ethical thing I could have done with my two Oklahoma buck tags, especially considering the alternative of having them suffer and die in their struggle, or have coyotes kill them.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8348. Forest Troop

Lessons in primate behavior on my first women’s surf trip.

Baboons are assholes. After leaving his birth troop at around age seven, a male will find a new one and spend his prime years trying to fang his way up the hierarchy. Once he’s gained a modicum of status, he devotes his days to terrorizing lower-ranking males and females, who only grow to half his size. Gashes, puncture wounds, and missing ears are not uncommon among baboons.

In the mid-1980s, Dr. Robert M. Sapolsky, a primatologist living in Kenya, documented an unprecedented cultural shift when he noticed that the alpha males of a baboon population suddenly vanished. The alphas had come upon a garbage dump near a tourist lodge, and they defended their spoils furiously from low-ranking males and females, who were relegated to leaves, seeds, and insects on the forest floor. One day, in the East African heat, the alphas were exposed to tainted meat at the dump, infecting them with bovine tuberculosis. They died soon after. Left behind were sixty-two baboons. The

#8346. How to Mount a Riflescope Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

When mounting a riflescope, you’re dealing with the most fragile and failure-prone point on your gun—so it pays to do it right. The process isn’t complicated, but it does require an attention to detail and some basic equipment. So in part one of our seven-part series on mastering the use of precision riflescopes and shooting to your rifle’s full potential, I’m going to dive in to how to actually get one of these bad boys mounted properly.

To correctly mount a riflescope, these conditions must be satisfied: The reticle needs to be level with the rifle. The scope must be positioned at the correct height above the bore. The proper eye relief needs to be established. And the fasteners in the rings and bases need to be tightened the right way. Before we get into detail on each of these points, here’s a basic outline of the process.

• Clamp the barrel in the padded jaws of a bench vise. If you don’t have a bench vise, you’ll need a solid gun cradle that will hold the rifle steady.

• Use a bubble level to level the rifle action. The flat on top of the Picatinny rail works. With some actions you can remove the bolt and have enough clearance on the tang (assuming it is flat) to set a bubble level as well. As a last resort you can attach the bottom half of a scope ring to the scope base and rest the level on it.

• Set the scope in the rings and lightly tighten the fasteners so that the scope will stay put but can be rotated and moved by hand. If your scope has a flat spot on the elevation turret, place the bubble level on it to level the reticle.

• An alternate method to level the reticle is to look through the scope on your leveled rifle at a plumb bob and orient the vertical crosshair with the string.

• Once the reticle is level, remove the rifle from vise and check your eye relief. Make adjustments as needed. Do this by placing the rifle back in the vise, making sure it is level, and then moving the scope.

• Tighten the fasteners to the correct torque levels with a torque wrench.

The depth of the scope rings controls how far above the bore the scope sits. The primary concern is that both ends of the scope have adequate clearance above the rifle. Having the objective end of the scope in contact with the barrel is an obvious no-no, but you want to make sure the eyepiece isn’t cramped either. Rings that are too low can limit the horizontal travel of the scope in the rings making it more difficult to get the right eye relief.

If your scope is too high, you’ll have a hard time lining up behind the rifle when shooting prone, though a stock with an adjustable cheek piece can mitigate this.

Ultimately, this is a Goldilocks situation where the scope should neither be too high, nor too low. As a rule of thumb, a gap between the objective bell and the barrel of .25 to .5 inches should be just right—but the profile of your barreled action and stock might dictate otherwise.

With proper eye relief the shooter is able to look through the scope without any part of the image being blacked out. The way to test whether eye relief (and scope height) are correct is to get set up behind the rifle in the prone position, close your eyes, rest your check firmly on the stock by taking the tension out of your neck, then opening your eyes.

You should be looking right down the center of the riflescope and have a clear view of the reticle and image without needing to move your head.

Fortunately, many long-range rifles make fine tuning this easier by have adjustable lengths of pull and cheek piece height. Rifles equipped with Picatinny rails—which most precision rifles are—provide greater flexibility with the forward and aft placement of the scope to establish good eye relief.

Read Next: The Best Scope Rings of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

Some manufacturers provide values for the fasteners in their scope rings. Many don’t. As a rule of thumb, you can tighten the screws on scope rings to about 20 inch-pounds and be good to go.

It always makes sense to check the screws on your Pic rail or scope base as well. They tend to be beefier, so you can torque them to about 30 inch-pounds without worry.

You can use a torque wrench with preset fittings, like Fix-It Sticks or the Wheeler Fat Wrench, or one with an indicator dial like this one from Seekonk Precision Tools.

Before tightening the screws, you should consider doing one of two things. Either use a sparing amount of blue Loctite on the treads—a single small drop will do—or spray the screws with some degreaser. These will help the screws acquire a more secure hold.

Tighten the screws as you would lug nuts on a truck tire. Tighten one a bit, go to a screw on the other side of the ring and tighten that a bit, and repeat as you work your way through all the fasteners.

Tighten them gradually so that the rings are applying an even clamping force to the scope tube. When done correctly, the gap on either side of the rings should be even. That’s a good sign that whoever put the scope on the rifle knew their stuff.

#8345. First Lite Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket, Tested and Reviewed

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:36 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

It’s not often that you get to hunt in an area that is the namesake for the jacket you’re wearing, but this fall, I did just that. The Uncompahgre National Forest covers almost a million acres of high-elevation backcountry in Colorado. At, and over, 10,000 feet, the wind and weather can be unpredictable. So your clothing needs to be versatile and ready for whatever Mother Nature might throw your way.

After wearing the Uncompahgre Foundry Jacket during my first-rifle elk hunt with fluctuating temperatures, driving rain, and even a healthy dose of snowfall, I will be the first to tell you that this jacket earned its name. It’s surprisingly packable, offers zippered ventilation around the triceps, and is incredibly warm. Since my elk hunt, it’s earned a spot in my treestand layering system as well. Here’s everything you need to know about this must-have outer layer.

As I mentioned above, the weather on my elk hunt was unpredictable at best. From driving rain for multiple days on end, to rapidly dropping temperatures bringing snow into the high country, I got to experience the full spectrum of temperatures and conditions. The Uncompahgre Foundry jacket was one piece of my kit that I wouldn’t have wanted to live without.

It remained durable after hiking through oak brush, deadfall, and large conifer stands, but more importantly, it kept me dry. Since I was living in a tent, my biggest fear was getting wet, and thus, staying wet with no way to really dry off given the conditions. Thankfully, this jacket both figuratively and literally had my back.

Upon returning home, I tested the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket throughout an October cold front here in Pennsylvania as well. While the conditions were drastically improved compared to the backcountry in Colorado, this jacket still fit into my kit wonderfully. Rather than wear it the entire walk to the stand, I simply packed it up into a ball and tossed it in my pack. After climbing in, I’d throw it on and enjoy my sit. It keeps me warm and surprisingly doesn’t make a ton of noise when you’re moving to grab your bow and draw back.

While I do really like this jacket, there’s always room for improvement. The first thing I noticed was the pocket design and layout. On the front of the jacket are four pockets. Two magnetic dump pockets, and just above those, two zippered hand warmer pockets featuring a warm tricot lining. Both are quite handy for different things, but I often found myself digging around in the wrong pocket due to their layout and close proximity to each other. If it were up to me, I’d leave the dump pockets where they are, and move the hand warmer pockets to a more traditional, hip-centric location.

I also had an issue, that was certainly in part user error, where the hand warmer pockets got wet during a popup rain shower. I had accidentally left the zipper open, but due to the design, the rain ran down the front of the jacket and right into those pockets. When the zippers were closed, no water intrusion occurred. User error aside, I’d argue it’s another reason to relocate the hand warmer pockets.

Where the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket shines truly is in its versatility. I was able to wear it in temperatures ranging from 20 degrees, all the way up to 50 degrees. Admittedly, 50 degrees might have been right on the edge of too hot for this jacket, it really did a nice job of ventilating when I opened up the tricep vents.

It’s incredibly windproof, waterproof, durable, and warm. Honestly, it’s an outer layer I didn’t even know I needed until I had it. And now that I have it, it’ll be accompanying me on every hunt for the remainder of the fall and winter.

As an avid hunter, I came to the realization years ago that you get what you pay for when purchasing hunting clothing. I hate being cold, and I hate being wet. Thankfully, the Uncompahgre Foundry jacket does a wonderful job of eliminating both of those concerns. If you’re hunting for a new outer layer to get you through the rut, rifle, and late season, look no further.

#8343. There Are Over 40 Resorts Planning To Open In November—Here’s Where Experts Say Conditions Will Be Best

Mammoth Mountain opening day 2025 (Photo: Courtesy of Mammoth Mountain)

Some folks may think skiing in November is crazy: the snow is rarely good, and the mere thrill of lifts spinning often attracts crowds larger than downhill capacity should allow.

It can be difficult to know where, if anywhere, it is worth skiing in November. While resorts are making snow around the clock, the decision to open boils down to weather.

For Colorado skiers, the weather may finally be on your side. According to Open Snow meteorologist Joel Gratz, November is set to start with a “bang.” He predicts a storm arriving Sunday will drop 6 to 12 inches on nearly all mountains, with some spots seeing up to 20. Did someone say powder day?!

Several Colorado resorts are opening their lifts before Halloween is over. Arapahoe Basin opened Oct. 28, Keystone follows on Oct. 30, and Wolf Creek on Oct. 31. Snow is thin at all three for now, but their high elevations should set them up for a stronger start to November.

Breckenridge and Copper Mountain are planning to open on Nov. 6, and if the snow comes in like Gratz is predicting, their opening days could feature more than just a white ribbon of death.

A little later into the month, Vail and Eldora are both planning Nov. 13 opening dates. It’s too early to tell if temperatures will preserve the snow from earlier storms, but as long as cold air remains, these are resorts to keep on your radar for potentially decent skiing.

Neighboring Utah resorts aren’t expected to receive as fruitful a snow bounty. They’ll see the same storm as Colorado, with the highest accumulations on Sunday, says Open Snow forecaster Evan Thayer. “Cooler air will eventually lower snow levels, with some decent accumulations possible up high.”

As of the time of publishing, Brian Head is planning on opening on Nov. 6. If Thayer’s prediction is accurate, the Southern Utah resort could see “decent accumulations” on its highest peaks. Alta, Park City, and Solitude are all planning on opening on Nov. 20. It’s too early to say how these resorts will fare, but cold temperatures will be the biggest asset.

California skiers will have to wait a bit longer. Open Snow forecaster Bryan Alleretto predicts the Tahoe region’s snowy start will likely come after Nov. 10, which could be good timing for Mammoth Mountain, set to open Nov. 20. Mammoth isn’t a Tahoe resort, but it tends to share weather patterns with those to the north.

The East Coast has had a warm fall, but that could change. There’s no official snow report yet, but Maine’s Sugarloaf plans to reopen Nov. 20, likely making it the region’s first resort to welcome skiers back. Vermont’s Sugarbush follows on Nov. 21, while nearby Killington, which often opens early, hasn’t announced a date as of press time.

#8342. His Bow Exploded When He Tried to Arrow His Target Buck — But He Still Got the Deer

Published Nov 4, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Oklahoma bowhunter Max Wynn was sitting in a ground blind with his wife Hartley, not far from a big river bottom in central Oklahoma the evening of October 17. Eventually, he spotted a nice 8-point buck (which was his target deer) and it walked to within just 10 yards of his blind.

“I wanted to take a close [shot at the] buck with my recurve bow, but as I started to draw it, the buck spooked a bit and moved out to 25 yards,” the 24-year-old archer tells Outdoor Life. “I set the recurve bow down, picked up my 75-pound draw weight compound bow, drew it, and released an arrow.

“When I did, it sounded like a cannon went off inside my blind. I set the bow down and saw the string serving was split, the bow string was slack, and both bow cams were bent.”

The arrow that Wynn loosed only flew about 8 yards and hit the dirt. The lighted nock  flew farther than the arrow that it was on.

The bow essentially exploded in his hands, bruising his wrist. Otherwise he was unscathed, though he said he was lucky the broken bow limbs didn’t hit his face.

“The bow limb could have hit the top of my ground blind when I shot my arrow, and that may have caused the bow to explode like it did,” says Wynn, a compression therapist and waterfowl guide for Tine Flies Outfitters. “I was done for the evening and immediately went to Cabela’s and bought a Bear Archery compound bow setup.”

Wynn rigged his Bear bow and sighted it in on targets at home in the truck headlights. The next morning he was back in his ground blind, and shortly a doe came into range at 28 yards. He took the deer with a well-placed arrow.

“That gave me confidence in using that Bear bow, and I went back to the same ground blind that evening with my brother-in-law Maddox Allbright,” Wynn says. “He’s 17 and wanted a doe for the youth deer season. But he decided to wait before taking a doe to see if the 8-point buck I was after came back into the area.”

Indeed, the big buck did come back – following another smaller buck.

“He walked in on the same trail where the doe came that morning, but when he got to where I shot her, he skirted the spot and went a little wider from my blind,” Wynn says. “But he offered a 30-yard quartering away shot. It was a good hit, and he only traveled 35 yards before falling.”

They got the 186-pound 8-pointer out of the woods, and Wynn started processing the buck.

Read Next: Do Deer Really ‘Jump the String?’ Here’s What All Bowhunters Should Know

“I was working my knife on the deer near the ribs by its shoulder and felt something sharp,” Wynn says. “I dug around and pulled out a Slick Trick broadhead that was buried in its chest cavity.

“There were no marks on the outside of the buck’s hide from an arrow wound. The tissue all around the broadhead was healed. The deer looked perfectly healthy before I shot it. Just shows how tough whitetails are.”

Wynn says he was lucky in dressing his 8-pointer that he didn’t cut his hands on the broadhead buried in the deer.

“I think I used up a lot of my deer hunting luck during those two days in the ground blind, and then dressing the buck with another broadhead inside,” he says lightheartedly.

#8341. How Two Bored Belgians Broke the Backyard Ultra World Record

Trail Runner contributing photographer Jacob Zocherman drove 15 hours from his home in Sweden to document the Belgian team at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship in Retie, Belgium. Unlike a typical race with a predetermined finish and a predictable narrative arc within it, backyard ultras only end when there is one runner left. Zocherman spent the five days and four hours of what ended up being a world-record-breaking run on the course, sleeping in a camper van when he could. He spoke with managing editor Abby Levene during and shortly after the race.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts had been running for 98 hours at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, and they were bored. Never mind they had each run over 400 miles on the same 4.167-mile course. Never mind they hadn’t gotten more than a few minutes of sleep at once in over four days. They looked fresh, the nights were long, and blah blah blah, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports. But with the 100th lap on the horizon, something clicked.

“You could see something happen to them, like a spring flower waiting through winter,” Zocherman tells Trail Runner. “Suddenly the sun comes and nothing happens, nothing happens, and then in a specific moment everything happens and the flower comes out in bloom. That’s what I saw in them—suddenly they were happy to be there, cheering with the audience, laughing with each other and joking.”

It was like colleagues going out to the bar on a Friday afternoon: They’ve found their happy place, Zocherman says. Except in this case, their happy place was a park in Retie, Belgium, aka the middle of nowhere.

“It’s very touching to see, because they are so humble and so easy to like,” Zocherman says. “At that point, I felt like the race would go on forever. But it also feels very fragile—when there are only two runners left, there is no room for error.”

Per backyard ultra rules, runners must run the 4.167-mile lap on the hour, every hour, until only one runner remains and is declared the winner. In case that isn’t nutty enough, the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is an even nuttier spinoff of this format: Each participating country (of which this year there were 67) simultaneously conducts its own backyard race with 15 participants, and the country with the most cumulative laps wins. This backyard team world championship now alternates every other year with the individual championship, held on the original backyard ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Team USA would go on to win the team world title, with Mark Dowdle leading the stars and stripes to a collective 1,120 laps, also known as “yards,” for its second world title in six years. Australia took second, 51 yards behind, and Belgium took third, 11 yards off of them. While the team competition inherently shaped the dynamic of the race, with runners sacrificing their own best interests to slow down and pull teammates along, Steyaert and Geerts had several additional goals on their minds.

They’d each run over 100 laps multiple times—four times for Steyaert and six for Geerts. But neither had ever run through a fifth night. Belgium’s fourth-place runner Kenneth Vanthuyne was long gone after hallucinating that he was at work when Steyaert and Geerts put on their headlamps for the fifth time.

“That was the critical moment,” Zocherman says. “It was the one thing they had always wanted to do.”

As the sun rose over the dewy fields surrounding the dirt road of the race course, they both looked unscathed.

“I was like, ‘OK, nothing can stop them,” Zocherman says. They turned their attention to the Belgium national backyard ultra record of 115 laps, held by Jan Vandekerckhove. They checked that off and reset the goal to the world record of 119 laps, set by Australia’s Phil Gore at Dead Cow Gully in Queensland last year. That, too, proved to be seemingly no problem.

At 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 22—over five days after they started running—Zocherman heard rumors that Steyaert and Geerts were setting out on their final lap.

“I think they could have continued. They looked fresh, they looked really good,” Zocherman says. “But I also know they wanted to finish together. And the longer you go, the smaller the margins are that something will happen and one will finish over the other. And they wanted to avoid that. But they wanted to finish together.”

Sure enough, when the pair returned to the start/finish arch at 5:57 p.m., they did not go back out when the clock reached the top of the hour. Instead, the two friends, standing side-by-side in matching red shirts, grinned to the crowd of cheering onlookers, each raising a hand and joining them together over their heads in the shape of a heart.

Together, they had accomplished what no one had done before: Run 124 laps of a 4.167-mile course every hour, on the hour, for a total of 516.7 miles and a new backyard ultra individual world record.

“They are like brothers and have run many times as the two remaining runners,” Zochermans says. “So to them, it is not a competition that late in the race. They are doing it together. And they want it to remain like that. It’s kind of beautiful. It’s poetry.”

From the start at 2 p.m. local time on Saturday, October 17, until Steyaert and Geerts concluded their record-breaking run five days and four hours later, Zocherman was on the ground to document it all. It’s a stroke of good fortune that of the 67 backyard ultra team competitions happening around the world, Zocherman—who lives in his native Sweden—chose to go to Belgium. It’s also not a coincidence.

In fact, Zocherman almost didn’t make the 15 hour drive to Retie after his mother was unexpectedly diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer two weeks before the race. The only reason he did go, Zocherman tells Trail Runner, is because that random campground in a foreign country is like home. Zocherman had been at the same course in April for the Legends Backyard Ultra, and the mini-universe environment of these events bring people together in a special way that’s hard to describe.

“It was an emotional rollercoaster and a logistical battle,” Zocherman says. “I wouldn’t have gone if it wasn’t this backyard ultra. It was a personal reason to be among people I know and like. I didn’t think it would be the crazy result that it was.”

Zocherman made the trek with his dog Balou, who he says keeps him grounded at these events with no predetermined end, or even rhythm. (She’s now witnessed three world records and could not be less impressed.) They did two laps of the course every day and got a decent amount of sleep for the first few nights before squeezing in 20 minutes at a time between loops by the end.

“I also know it will be a very long race and I have to drive home for 15 hours after so I can’t be crazy wasted,” he says. “Although you become crazy wasted anyway.”

Here’s how this world-record-setting run unfolded, through Zocherman’s eyes and words.

The first out of 372 whistles marks the start for the team world championships, by whistler Eilis Lanclus.

Matthias Pelgrims, one of the top runners the Belgian team is preserving his energy during the first loops of the competition.

Never a dull moment for the crews in between the loops. Always something to worry about.

The hula skirt. Once in a while there is a loop with someone wearing a hula skirt in order to break the monotony.

Resting runners in-between the loops with the watcher waiting to collect.

The puzzle. Whatever brings joy to the table and something to do during the early days is welcomed.

Approaching camp on day three. It’s a misty and cool morning after a very wet and challenging second night of the race.

The runners don’t fear the rain so much during the race, they say. It’s the wind ripping over the exposed night loop that they worry about.

Willem De Troyer is suffering from pain in his legs and is screaming out in pain at every step during what would be his last loop before timing out.

The emotions are rising as the race continues.

Jelle Tielemans is having a hard time during day three, moments before he quits. After 45 hours of racing, only 13 runners of the 990 who started in 67 countries remain.

As the race goes on, usually runners move closer to the start area in order to save time in between the loops.

Bert Verbist on his way back to the camp after yet another successful loop.

Common duties by different hands. Although the race is repetitive, the things that need to be done are endless and carried out by volunteers throughout all the hours of the day and night.

The remains of a celebration for Merijn Geerts, who turned 52 during the race.

Evariest Callens gets a massage on his throbbing legs after 69 hours of running.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

The intersection of the two loops. The night loop is more open and exposed, while the day loop is more sheltered but also a bit more technical in the forest.

Merijn Geerts takes a micro-nap in between loops.

Tanja Steyaert crews her husband Ivo throughout the race.

The control center with the camera feeds from different parts of the loops, as well as the race broadcast and other tracking sites.

A tense wait for the remaining runners to finish their loops and go out for another.

Sleep is grabbed when you can and where you can. Nothing is certain in a backyard ultra, other than knowing you will get little sleep.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts run through the fifth night. They are the only remaining runners of the 15 who started for Team Belgium.

The party is getting real in the Belgian countryside.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert’s backyard ultra world record is celebrated with the power cutting out (and the start/finish arch falling down) after heavy rain broke the electric circuits. But nothing, seemingly, can stop their progress.

The remains of the previous days. A lot of food, drinks, and beer.

Ultimately, Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert ran 124 loops—and set a new world record—before stopping.

In running and in life: Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts celebrate with their wives as well as crews after setting the world record.

#8339. The Best Laser Rangefinders for Hunting and Shooting, Tested and Reviewed

Published Nov 4, 2026 10:29 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Most of us judge a laser rangefinder by its obvious attributes. When we peer through the lens and press the ranging button, does it deliver an accurate and consistent distance to the target. Done and done. But when it comes to sorting out the best rangefinders for hunting, we need to dig a bit deeper.

A few curious members of our community navigate the mode commands, and learn that their range-u-lator can also measure incline, temperature, elevation, and altitude and apply a prodigious amount of ballistic calculation to make us more lethal hunters.

Ours is a test of these multidimensional monoculars, those that carry ballistic software, ranging reticles, and even navigation capability. Because not every hunter and shooter needs or wants that capability, we include a few point-and-shoot units fully worth your attention. This year’s field was among the most exciting we’ve seen with both high value and the latest technology. Here are our picks for best rangefinders for hunting from our 2026 optics test.

Garmin’s entry into the laser rangefinding market has had such a seismic effect on the category that once you use the L60i, LRF monoculars that simply measure distance and spit out a ballistic solution are so two-dimensional. By adding an augmented reality display that leverages Garmin’s extensive digital mapping services, the rangefinder becomes a first-rate wayfinder.

It’s impossible to overstate the ambition of this device. Garmin has managed to pack so much mapping horsepower in this handheld unit that it is being used by search-and-rescue agencies to locate wayward folks, by explorers who want to see what’s on the other side of a blind ridge, and by hunters who want step-by-step navigation to the spot they sighted that cross-canyon buck, even if they approach from the opposite direction.

The L60i communicates its mapping capabilities via a see-through overlay inside the display that seems at times like it’s an alternative-reality headset. You can see the real world of terrain through the glass of the optical system, but the display drops over the seen landscape a digital veil of landmarks, distances, navigation arrows, and waypoints. Operationally, this means you can find waypoints from any direction. Practically, it means the Garmin’s distance isn’t limited by its laser beam but by its optical gaze. If you can see a landmark, even 20 miles away, you can drop a waypoint on it using Garmin’s onboard map.

But the unit is also a first-rate laser rangefinder. Garmin rates its ranging capabilities in two very different conditions: full sunlight and optimal conditions. Those of us who have used laser rangefinders in full daylight know that the laser bounces off all sorts of reflective objects, limiting its precision. To get the best distance readings, you want to laze objects under cloudy skies or just after the sun has set. Garmin claims the L60i can range reflective targets out to 7,500 yards in optimum conditions, or to 5,500 yards in full sunlight. We got nearly those readings in our testing.

The Garmin also has a first-rate ballistics solver onboard, thanks to its long relationship with and now ownership of Applied Ballistics. It leverages the integrated AB Elite software or AB Quantum software via the Garmin app to provide not only ballistic groupings but the specific performance of custom loads out of your particular rifle. It links to Kestrel wind meters. It includes an archery mode and an extended-range ballistics mode for ranging out to nearly 8,000 yards. But it also links to the universe of Garmin devices, from dozens of smart watches to the company’s myriad GPS devices.

The unit is among the largest and heaviest (13.6 ounces with twin AAA batteries on board) LRF monoculars we’ve tested, but that heft settles nicely in hand. To get the best out of the unit’s extended range, mount it to a tripod via the threaded adapter on the underside of the monocular. But hand-holding the unit is the best way to enjoy its mapping features, because the heads-up overlay moves seamlessly with the landscape as you pan. The Garmin is at its best with both the rangefinding and mapping features employed. Laze a distant target, acquire the ballistic solution to make a shot (or not), then drop a waypoint on the target location. Now, employ the unit’s graphic overlay to not only “see” the waypoint on a topo map, but actually navigate to it, even if you approach from a different direction. Highlighted prompts give you step-by-step directions to the waypoint. The effect is surreal, as though you are watching yourself from the perspective of an eagle. Or a satellite.

This out-of-body experience is not only useful for the pedestrian tasks of hitting targets and retrieving game, but also for exploring your world both in your boots and from far above. By harnessing the best attributes of Garmin’s mapping library, applying an excellent ballistics package to the task, and then connecting both through devices, apps, and digital ecosystems, Garmin has elevated the LRF monocular to something that approaches the first do-everything handheld device on the market.

Outdoor Life’s testers approached the Garmin L60i with a dose of skepticism. Could an LRF monocular really drop waypoints 20 miles or more away? Could its heads-up display really be visible enough to be useful? And wasn’t that $2,500 price tag simply too precious? By the end of our test, every question had been resolved to our satisfaction, excepting the cliff-hanger: Whatever in the world will Garmin dream up next?

For its astonishing capabilities, its ability to perform as a ballistics-solving LRF at a high level, and the audacious ambition of the device, the Garmin L60i is the consensus winner of Editor’s Choice as the standout LRF monocular of the year.

An 850-yard rangefinder for under $100? That’s not only about 12 cents per yard, it’s a crazy value for a starter monocular or for hunters and shooters who don’t often shoot over a quarter mile.

The Triumph HD 850 continues Vortex’s product line that provides good performance and amazing value, with full warranty coverage. The Triumph line announced itself with the very good 10×42 binocular that has a real-world street price of about $100. Like the binocular, the HD 850 will get the job done, assuming the job is mid-distance ranging, without a lot of extraneous features or particularly good optics.

Vortex claims a range of 850 yards on reflective targets and 350 yards on game. We actually got pretty close, ranging metallic targets out to 680 yards and deer at 325 yards. The LRF has the typical modes: normal, first, and last target modes and line-of-sight and angle-adjusted ranging mode, along with a fairly sluggish scan mode.

The unit has a liquid crystal display that appears washed out against some backgrounds. The ranging engine is noticeably slower than the top LRFs in our test, but it’s just fine for most purposes. Note that the Triumph HD 850 doesn’t have a ballistic solver or location pinning or any of the features you might see in a unit that links to a phone app. But its angle-compensating mode and minimum ranging distance of 6 yards makes it a good choice for bowhunters. It’s also a good unit for shotgun hunters, straight-wall carbiners, and other hunters and shooters who shoot large-caliber bullets that drop quickly, and where knowing the specific yardage inside 300 yards is the difference between a clean miss and a killing shot.

The optics are pretty tough, and the plastic unit feels a little flimsy, but its 4.6-ounce weight and compact build make it a good choice for go-light hunters or a treestand hunter who doesn’t want, or need, a heavy ballistic-calculating rangefinder.

For all its remarkable value packed in a no-nonsense build and its ability to perform the basics we require of a laser rangefinding monocular, the Vortex Triumph HD 850 wins our Great Buy award as the great bargain of the year in laser rangefinders.

Bushnell has added some tasty updates to this workhorse LRF. The Broadhead 2 has Bushnell’s very good proprietary weatherproofing coatings that boost contrast and should make the unit more usable in drippy weather. Speaking of grubby conditions, the LRF’s Brush/Fog mode, which prioritizes farther targets, has a powerful update in this generation of the Broadhead. It’s a logic that discourages the laser from picking up reflections off water droplets, and Bushnell’s works quite well.

The second-generation Broadhead retains Bushnell’s ActiveSync display that sounds on the surface like a gimmick but is a very useful feature. Sensitive to light intensity, it runs black LCD in daylight conditions but automatically turns to a red illumination in twilight. It’s a clutch attribute that allows the display to pop against any background or light condition.

We really like the overbuilt VaultLite rangefinder pouch, which has useful hardware for belts, and we like the pistol grip of the unit. The protruding outline of the rearward battery compartment serves as a “hook” that grabs the hand, whether gloved or not, and helps stabilize the very light (6-ounce) monocular.

And we like the tripod mount on the belly of the unit. That’s a nice touch for those using the Broadhead at its most-distant ranges when precision is important.

The Broadhead 2 didn’t especially wow us with its optics, ranging horsepower, or menu navigation. All are fine, and just what you should expect from laser rangefinders at this price and ranging engine.

It may take users a bit of time to get used to Bushnell’s nomenclature. “Regular” mode is line-of-sight mode. “Bow” mode is the angle-compensating mode, which Bushnell calls its “ARC” feature. “Fog” mode is called “last target” by some manufacturers and Bushnell’s “Bullseye” mode is what most LRF users know as “first target” mode.

The Bushnell R5 Broadhead 2 is a great choice for bowhunters and rifle hunters and shooters who need to reach out to uncomfortable distances. The lack of a ballistic solver holds it back from being used by shooters who require more of an LRF than just range. But it’s a solid rangefinder in the middle of a very competitive pack.

The Gen II version of Sig’s excellent Kilo8K-ABS rangefinding monocular is more powerful, brighter, and connects to a larger galaxy of mapping and ballistics apps. In other words, it’s almost a brand-new laser rangefinder.

Its engine even got an upgrade. The Kilo8K-ABS Gen II runs on Sig’s new LightWave DSP, which returns four readings a second in scan mode, even out to a mile. Its return is snappy, precise, and confident, and new coatings and optics make the active-matrix display pop. The display is worth a few sentences. Some manufacturers are so busy crowding information in their display that the result is a confusing thicket of distance, ballistics solutions, angle, temperature, and mode. Sig has done a nice job of simplifying the display to just the elements needed to make a quick shot: the range, and the come-up and wind holds. In the field, it’s fast and simple.

The lazing power of the unit is simply stunning. In extended-range mode and strapped to a tripod, I was able to range grassy hillsides at 6,200 yards without much trouble. I worked on getting the claimed 8,000 yards out of the unit, but couldn’t quite get there. The impressive part to me isn’t the distance, it’s the speed of the DSP engine.

The onboard Applied Ballistics Elite software is similarly impressive. You can tack up the data by connecting to the AB Quantum app, but you don’t need to. The entire ballistics library is in the palm of your hand, almost quivering in the 7.5-ounce monocular that’s begging to be put to work. That the unit also connects to Sig’s BDX devices, including BDX-enabled riflescopes, gives this monocular even more utility.

There are a lot of choices on the market for ballistics-solving LRF monoculars. At first glance, the price of the 8K-ABS Gen II (just under $1,500) seems excessive, but when you consider its ability to quickly and precisely range, then deliver an equally fast and verified aiming solution out to 4.5 miles … I don’t know that I’d call the Sig a bargain, but it’s a very good deal for hunters and shooters who intend to take it to its impressive limits.

We’ve seen Leupold’s RX-5000 before. Two years ago, we gushed about its ability to remotely drop onX pins just by lazing a distant spot and then pinning the location to the digital map on your phone. It’s a useful feature, but Leupold’s competitors have made it standard on so many LRF monoculars and binoculars that it’s no longer novel.

But a lot has changed with this little handheld marvel since then. Its ballistics solvers are now powered by Hornady’s excellent 4DOF software, its bow mode borrows from Precision Cut Archery software, and its mapping feature is not limited to onX Hunt. You can drop pins on maps from Deercast, HuntStand, and both Apple and Google maps. Those updates are enough to include it in this roundup of new LRF monoculars because, while the form factor and operation are pretty much the same, the guts of the RX-5000 are new and galaxies more powerful and useful than the original.

That form factor is worth mentioning. While many sub-$400 LRF monoculars feel flimsy, the Leupold has a tight, metallic heft that settles nicely in hand. We wish the unit had a tripod adapter built in, but the tripod “saddle” that Leupold ships is a good addition, and it’s necessary to get the most out of the RX-5000’s long-range chops. With the unit stabilized on a tripod, we were able to get ranges very nearly to 5,000 yards, and when you add Hornady’s 4DOF ballistic solver to that extended distance, it’s both imaginable and possible to hit targets at that extreme distance.

The optics in the Leupold are excellent. The 8-power magnification combined with the relatively large 30mm objective make this a pretty good glassing unit. But the value proposition, of course, is the ballistics paired with the fast and precise ranging engine. Given the huge amount of ballistic computations, the powerful laser, the excellent Leupold Control app, and generally clear and intuitive navigation, you could make the case that the 799RX-5000issotalentedthatitcouldundercuttheequallyimpressivebutpricey(3,900) BX-6 Range HD, Leupold’s new LRF binocular.

With this do-everything long-range LRF monocular, Leica has regained its standing at the head of the rangefinding line. The Rangemaster CRF Max not only compares favorably to peers from Sig and Leupold, but its build and optics borrow from its extensive history in the category.

But it’s the electronic guts of the Rangemaster CRF Max, introduced in 2025 but hitting retailers’ shelves now, that elevate the device. Leica has stuffed the monocular with a best-in-class ballistics solver (Applied Ballistics Elite), an interesting should-I-or-shouldn’t-I shot-probability calculator that gives you the odds of making extra-long shots, a location feature to drop waypoints on digital maps, and a tracking tool that guides shooters from the place they took the shot to the location of the target.

For just under $1,500, that’s a lot of performance packed in a tight, elegant build. The flat dark earth colorway is a giveaway to its talents. Leica has started to use device color to define its place in the brand pantheon. The base Rangemaster CRF is onyx black, the mid-level Rangemaster CRF Pro is forest green, and the top-of-the-line Rangemaster CRF Max has this handsome FDE exterior.

The unit has all the ranging features you’d expect, including three target modes, the ability to input wind direction and intensity or connect to an external anemometer, and the ability to use either onboard ballistics or import custom ballistic data from Leica’s excellent mobile app.

The 3,700-yard maximum range for the device may not compete with Sig’s 8,000-yard model or Leupold’s 5,000-yard monocular, but it’s plenty powerful for nearly any long-range hunting or shooting situation. We managed to get very nearly that distance when ranging hillsides and reflective signs.

The laser return is fast, the display is clear and bright and customizable, so you can include only the data you need to make quick, confident shots. And the glass and coatings are superior, as you’d expect from an optics company with the performance expectations of Leica.

If Bushnell’s Broadhead 2 is purpose-built for bowhunters, the 2000 AB version is similarly configured for rifle hunters. To have baked-in Applied Ballistics’ solver in a $250 rangefinder is pretty extraordinary.

The value proposition of this new R5 rangefinder is pretty appealing. Once you build a ballistic profile for your rifle load in the Bushnell Ballistics mobile app, then connect via Bluetooth, the rangefinder will give you a distance-informed hold in MOA or MIL. Note that the Ultralite version of Applied Ballistics is valid only out to 800 yards, but that’s plenty enough horsepower for most hunters and long-range shooters.

The pros and cons that we discussed in the Broadhead 2 all apply to the 2000 AB, with the exception of the display. While the archery R5 contains Bushnell’s excellent ActiveSync display, the rifle version has only a black LCD. We also note that the 2000 AB is powered by a single CR2 lithium battery. We’d like to see a CR123-sized powerplant for extended use given the amount of data the little unit has to crunch.

The R5 2000 AB retails for $250, but you can expect to see that price come down as the unit wins more fans and as more customers learn about the crazy amount of performance in such a simple and affordable rangefinding monocular.

Manufacturers’ ranging claims are as spurious as a camouflage company’s promise to elude. Most take their best distances, not their average, and discount target size and orientation. They don’t always report what we found, some inconsistent ranging on a wide variety of surfaces, from gravel to grass to 3D archery targets to trees. We test the maximum and minimum range, and use every targeting mode and menu option. We’ve provided the max and minimum ranges we were able to achieve on non-reflective targets to give you an idea of real-world capabilities.

We mount monoculars on tripods to get rock-solid ranging, and we take the units in the field, deploying them both methodically and rapidly at targets of various sizes and distances. And then we pair them to a slave rifle and a ballistic app and judge their ability to improve our shooting accuracy.

We break our 10-point scoring into four general categories: ranging performance, display and optics, features, and value. The average of these categories is the basis of our grades, detailed below.

Ranging performance includes both the maximum and minimum distances the unit is capable of ranging, but also ranging precision and ability to repeatedly range objects of various sizes and textures. The performance score also considers various targeting modes. Display and optics assesses how well the unit “sees” targets, how useful and adjustable the display is to each users’ eyesight and different light conditions, and reticle utility. The feature grade assesses whether the unit connects to a mobile app, or contains a ballistic library, or has on-board sensors. Lastly, our value grade is a measure of whether the unit is worth its price, and considers its peer group, warranty, and amenities like a lanyard or carrying case.

The laser rangefinder that gets the highest overall score wins our Editor’s Choice award for the best in the category; the optic with the highest price/value score wins our Great Buy recognition. We also assigned other awards for specific noteworthy attributes.

Our 10-point evaluation adds up to a total numeric score, but we translate those to grades for each submission. The ranging Performance grade combines the scores from ranging, accuracy, sensitivity, and processor speed. Our Display/Optics grade aggregates both display and optics scores. The Features grade considers amenities, connectivity, and versatility. And then the Price/Value grade is our assessment of whether a rangefinder is worth the money, which also considers durability.

To earn an “Excellent” grade, the average of that category must be 9 or higher, which is extremely hard to achieve. “Very Good” is an average score of 7 to 9. A “Good” grade is 5 to 7. Our “Fair” grade is 3 to 5, and “Poor” is anything under 3. This scoring system gives us a great comparative tool for the best rangefinders for hunting.

As you can deduce from the wide variety of capabilities in submission to this year’s LRF test, you can spend over $1,000 for a gee-whiz rangefinder, or you can spend $200 for a basic unit that will range your target even if it doesn’t make you breakfast.

It’s up to you to determine what you want out of a rangefinding monocular. Do you want a hand-held ballistic calculator that will give you precise ranging out to 2 miles for your pet load? Or are you satisfied with a basic unit that provides line-of-sight and angle-adjusted ranging and little else?

Of course, there are plenty of units that reside between those two poles, but the biggest differentiator for LRFs in this year’s test are those that borrow from a mobile app to provide very specific customized aiming solutions, and those that don’t allow for many inputs and instead spit out ranges for a few basic hunting and shooting scenarios.

The price between those two capabilities is immense, with Bluetooth-connected units selling for close to $1,000 and bare-bones LRFs retailing for under $300.

Beyond those basics, if you are mainly a bowhunter who wants archery-specific ranging data, look for those units that have arrow-flight dynamics baked into their software. Similarly, suppose you’re an ultra-long-distance target shooter. In that case, you’re going to want a unit with precise, situation-informed ranging results based around the specific bullet dynamics you’ve measured and plugged into the ranging software.

Check out the display of a rangefinder you’re interested in in a wide variety of light conditions. Some units have blazingly bright OLED displays while others have black LCD displays that can get lost against a cluttered background or low-light situations.

Lastly, consider the warranty. Unlike the lifetime, fully transferable warranty that has become an industry standard for non-electronic optics like binoculars and rifle scopes, most companies offer a limited warranty for electronics like rangefinders. But there’s such a wide range of protection on the market that it pays to take a close look at the details.

There are a lot of great rangefinders for hunting. To find the best one for you, you need to consider how, where, and what you hunt.

Bushnell rangefinders are popular, especially because they are affordable. But there are also other options that are better in some ways.

Yes, a rangefinder is an incredibly valuable tool for hunting.

That depends. Cheap rangefinders can work great if you only need to range shorter distances under 200 yards or so, and you won’t be subjecting them to bad weather or too much moisture. For some hunters, they will get the job done.

Most of us use only a single laser rangefinder button—the ranging button—and as long as we get fast, reliable range dope, we’re happy. That’s actually how we started our assessment, simply by punching the range button and recording the results.

But the cool thing about the best rangefinders for hunting is that they are so adaptive. The most sophisticated have on-board or off-board ballistics solvers that can guide a bullet well beyond reasonable ranges. The best units have environmental sensors and sensitive angle and directional intelligence that can inform a shot whether you’re connected to your phone, or not. And the expectation of a LRF these days is that it must have both line-of-sight and angle-adjusted ranging along with ballistically informed ranging.

If you don’t need the full-on connected unit, make sure the unconnected unit performs the basics well, with an intensity adjusted display, an ergonomic body, and enough features to enable ranging a buck deer standing behind a screen of branches. The only downside to this crop of capable rangefinders is that they’re removing our last excuse for missing that must-hit shot.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.
