#8274. The Best Ice Climbing Gear of 2027: Boots, Tools, Crampons, and More

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The author, Anthony Walsh, heads up 'Nightmare on Wolfstreet' (WI6 M7+) on B.C.'s famed Stanley Headwall. (Photo: Sebastian Pelletti)

Overview: The best ice climbing gear of 2027 includes Petzl Dart crampons, La Sportiva Olympus Mons Pro boots, Black Diamond Viper ice tool, the Blue Ice Choucas Pro harness, and the Mountain Equipment Xenith jacket, plus proven picks like the La Sportiva G-Summit boots. Our testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 from the Canadian Rockies to the Patagonian Andes, in temperatures down to -30°F.

Ice climbing is a high-stakes sport. Do it right, and you’re in for a meditative cruise with just the right level of spice. Do it wrong, and you’ll be left spooked, shivering—or worse. The difference often boils down to your experience level. But right after that comes your ice climbing gear. When you’re 100 feet off the ground, pinned to a silvery ribbon of ice by nothing but four blades of steel, you need absolute trust in your equipment. But how can you tell which products to rely on? That’s our job.

This season, our team of testers tried out 15 pieces of ice climbing gear that are either new for 2026-’27 or came out partway through last winter. Some turned out to be overengineered, overpriced, or poorly built. Others proved thoughtfully designed and dependable in a range of winter conditions. Over thousands of vertical feet of testing everywhere from the Patagonian Andes to the Canadian Rockies, we sorted out the bad from the good. Below: nothing but the best ice climbing gear available this season.

Weight: 11.3 oz (men’s medium) / 9.9 oz (women’s medium)

Pros and Cons + Novel and effective baffle design + Two-way zipper with bottom hem snap + Low-profile, elasticated cuffs + Impressive warmth-to-weight ratio – No way to tighten hood – Gimmicky and impractical hexagonal stuff sack

Mountain Equipment’s all-new Xenith is the big experiment in winter insulation this year. After a research paper suggested hexagons might be the most thermally efficient shape, the brand built the jacket with hexagonal baffles. (These weirdly shaped baffles also seem to limit down migration.)

Our testers found it extremely warm for 11.3 ounces (with 4.3 ounces of 800-fill hydrophobic goose down)—making it the ideal midlayer on -30°F days and nearly unnoticeable clipped to a harness on warmer ones. The Xenith’s low weight comes from its spare design. It has two hand-warming pockets, elasticated cuffs, a two-way zipper, internal drop pockets, a hem-cinch cord, and a hood. Downside: The hood can’t be cinched at all. Without a helmet to fill it, you’ll feel like a kid wearing your parent’s oversized clothes.

Weight: 8.5 oz Sizes: men’s XXS-XXL (the women’s counterpart is the M10 Storm Bib)

Pros and Cons + Surprising stretch and durability + Superior range of motion – No women’s-specific version

The M10 Storm Hardshell offers hands-down the best range of motion we’ve ever experienced in an alpine climbing pant. Thanks to a roomy fit, gusseted crotch, and slightly stretchy fabric—a mix of ripstop nylon, proprietary waterproof laminate, and a slick jersey backer—we were able to step high and wide without feeling constricted—a refreshing departure from the Euro-style, slim-fit trousers that have taken over the market in recent years.

“While transitioning from a panel of limestone to a hanging ice dagger, I stemmed my legs as far as I could between the two mediums and felt zero resistance,” reported Climbing senior editor Anthony Walsh. Some testers reported doing a full split just to test out the mobility. No torn crotches yet.

The rest of the layout is smart but simple. The thigh pocket, big enough to fit a smartphone, and fly are both positioned to remain accessible even with a harness on. “The zipper is on a diagonal rather than vertically-oriented like most other pants, so you can relieve yourself without a harness’s tie-in points or belay loop getting in the way,” Walsh reports. Elasticized cuffs keep moisture out—something we appreciated when spring conditions left our ice pitches streaming with water.

We loved how waterproof the M10s were, too. “I tested the M10s on some of the wettest pitches of my entire season,” said Walsh. “My ‘waterproof’ gloves soon wetted out, and my face had a steady drip of water coming off my nose, but under the M10 pants, I stayed 100 percent dry.” Credit goes to a lightweight, breathable, proprietary membrane and a PFCs-free DWR (durable water repellent) that boasted best-in-test longevity. After eight straight days of fighting up scrappy mixed lines in the Canadian Rockies, both the waterproofing and the fabric remained intact.

Pros and Cons + Legitimately waterproof + Decently breathable + Cuff closure keeps out loose snow – Not very warm

These insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

The Temres is not exceedingly warm, but for temps hovering around freezing (or those with excellent circulation) these are a fantastic, cheap option. Otherwise, buy a larger size and add a thin liner glove for deep-winter leads. A note on sizing: Showa gloves run small, so size one up from your typical ice glove.

Pros and Cons + Warmest technical mountaineering boot made + Easy adjustment with BOA system + Surprisingly nimble and lightweight – Expensive – Unnecessarily tall gaiter

Knee-height mountain boots are no longer just for guided Himalayan climbers. La Sportiva’s new Olympus Mons Pro—a 4-pound-4-ounce pair of “8,000-meter boots”—is a game changer for ice and mixed climbers who need serious warmth without sacrificing performance.

Our tester wore them on Field of Dreams (WI5; 250ft), Mixed Master (WI4 M5; 1,000ft), and M7 cragging. “I have generally cold feet yet I was sweating standing around in -5°F in these boots,” he said. “Despite all the insulation, these are plenty nimble for WI5 and M5.” The Olympus Mons Pro might be a couple ounces heavier than La Sportiva’s G-Summit boot, but it is drastically warmer and just as comfortable. Unbelievably, it’s also 7 ounces lighter per pair than the brand’s flagship leather single boot, the Nepal EVO, thanks to Primaloft Gold Aerogel insulation.

The one gripe: an unnecessarily tall gaiter. “With such a long zipper to get in and out of the boot, I’m less likely to adjust the Velcro power strap when I need to,” said one tester. Thankfully the external BOA allows a climber to adjust some of the fit on the fly.

Weight: 1 lb 13 oz (per boot) Sizes: 37-48 (half sizes)

Pros and Cons + Easy to adjust with gloves on + Highly versatile + Ideal fit for small and low-volume feet – Not as durable as they should be for the price

The G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.

“I loved the BOA system for quick tightening mid-pitch and for equally quick loosening when I arrived at the next belay and needed blood to rush into my feet,” said Climbing Senior Editor Anthony Walsh, who was able to operate the dial easily with gloves on. The system eliminated heel-lift, both on-route and off. “I’ve front-pointed 10,000 feet in these boots and walked many horizontal miles. I haven’t received one blister, and yet I can still climb WI6 and M7 in them,” Walsh said.

Our female testers raved about the fit, calling it a serious game-changer in a world dominated by men’s boots. “Not only does this accommodate lower-volume feet, but the BOA ratchets tight enough to keep my heel down,” said one woman. “That allows me to climb a lot harder, for a lot longer.”

The boot isn’t totally waterproof, but its TPU coating, weather-resistant zipper, and water-repellant finishes kept our feet dry after dozens of days on ice and snow. “Lots of approaches in the Rockies have semi-frozen rivers at the base,” said one tester. “I punched through multiple, and never felt humidity or wetness.”

But while the weather resistance easily survives hard use, some of the plastic parts may not. One tester noted a sticky zipper and a peeling toe cap. Another reported that the toe welt quickly shows signs of wear and had to order a replacement after just a few weeks of testing. The toe welts on her second pair have held up fine. Still, if you’re hoping for a boot that will last you for years, you might want to get some reassurances from La Sportiva’s warranty department first.

Pros and Cons + Top-tier durability + Technical aptitude + Out-of-the-box comfort – Not quite warm enough for extreme-altitude objectives

Scarpa’s fan-favorite Phantom Tech HD offers the same climbing precision as the old Phantom Tech, with more warmth, durability, and comfort at just a 2.5-ounce penalty. Body-mapped insulation—micropile, aerogel, and PrimaLoft Gold Eco—kept our feet frostbite-free at -22°F (with vapor barrier socks) near Field, British Columbia, but we wouldn’t quite trust it on Denali. “The rockered outsole has a trail-runner-like feel,” said one tester. “I’ve hiked and skied many miles in ice climbing boots over the years, and the Phantom Tech HD is without a doubt the most comfortable I’ve used.” After a full season, our pair shows no wear or delamination.

Pros and Cons + Packable + Superlight + Five gear loops – Uncomfortable to hang in – Ice clipper locations reduce usability of gear loops

For multi-pitch ice, where hanging belays are rare, our testers gravitate to a minimalist harness like the updated Blue Ice Choucas Pro. Its UHMWPE construction is surprisingly durable for 5.1 ounces, and it’s fully featured: gear loops, a haul loop, four ice clipper slots, and leg loops that open for skis or crampons.

Unfortunately, Blue Ice sewed the clipper slots over the gear loops, so loop real estate feels a bit scarce. Nevertheless, it easily held a full rack of screws on Murchison Falls (WI4+; 600ft), but our tester noticed the unpadded leg loops on the free-hanging 100-foot rappel.

Skip it for cragging or steep terrain; it thrives on big days in the alpine—where a harness’s weight and packability make a real difference.

Pros and Cons + IP56 water resistance + Low operating limit (-20°F) + Invaluable for anchors and belay-station communication – Expensive

An IP56 water-resistance rating and a -20°F lower operating limit make the Rocky Talkies as well suited to ice as to the mountains they’re named for. We found them invaluable for setting up anchors in Ouray Ice Park and for communicating between multi-pitch belay stations. The only knock is the price, though most testers found the durability worth it.

Pros and Cons + Long-lasting dry treatment + Easy handling – No middle mark

If you’re the kind of person who prefers the safety and flexibility of a half/twin rope setup, you’d be hard-pressed to do better than the DYAD 7.7. Our testers used these ropes on everything from Bridal Veil Falls to ice park laps over a full season in Ouray, Colorado, and not even the wettest pitches iced them up or wetted them out. Cons: There’s no middle mark, and the ropes are pricey.

Pros and Cons + Many accessories for specific customization + High-performance ice pick – Shaft shape and handle is not suited for sustained vertical or overhanging pitches

Gently curved ice tools have fallen out of favor for the flashier, radically shaped Black Diamond Hydra, but the updated Viper still has a home in our quiver. Its 2.5-millimeter pick is incredible in ice, but the tool’s standout feature is its customization: it comes with modular headweights, a long alpine spike for snow plunging, a micro spike, a full-size alpine hammer, a micro hammer, and an adze. One tester, an ACMG apprentice alpine guide, found the mellow shape natural for sniffing out thin hooks on slabby, traddy mixed up to M7, versus an aggressive tool like the C.A.M.P. X-Dream. The knuckle-bashing shape isn’t ideal for overhanging mixed or WI5, but it’s a great option for moderate and big-mountain routes.

Weight: 1 lb 9 oz (per pair, with monopoint setup) Sizes: 34-44; 38-49 with extension bar (sold separately)

+ Extremely light + Solid climbing performance + Surprisingly durable + Wide range of adjustability – Aluminum heel doesn’t penetrate dense ice well

With razor-sharp points and a modular design, the Petzl Dart has been our favorite technical crampon for years. Its new aluminum rear section and linking bar save 4 ounces per pair and eliminate the need to jerry-rig fit with Petzl’s Cord-Tec Kit.

Testers climbed up to WI5+ and M7 with zero flex or shifting. Like the all-steel Dart, it’s simple to switch between mono- and dual-point layouts, and interchangeable toe bails customize the Dart for any boot, welts or not. Testers used these ‘pons on everything from Bridalveil Falls (WI5+) in Telluride and hard mixed cragging to big Canadian Rockies north faces, including Mount Robson and Mount Temple.

The geometry of the front point is just downturned enough to hook securely into ice, but not so aggressive that you have to adjust your technique to get a solid stick. In fact, most testers found they hardly had to double-kick at all to get a quick, reliable bite.

“The secondary points are far enough back that they don’t get in your way when you just want to use your front point, but forward enough to engage when you want them to,” said one tester, who wore them on more than 100 pitches this winter. He also found them blessedly intuitive to walk in: “Even when hiking up and down the Ouray Ice Park trails or navigating a mixture of rocks and ice between backcountry pitches, the Darts kept me secure and balanced.”

Cons: Honestly, not many. One climber found the newly slimmed-down heel lever tough to operate with thick gloves on. Another found the metal buckle fussy—though Petzl’s sold-separately Elastic Strap ($26) fixes that issue with a surprisingly durable plastic buckle.

Pros and Cons + Triple-grip handle + Flexibility and reach in steep terrain – Too aggressive for pure ice – Handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as other triple-grip models

One climbing coach and U.S. Ice Climbing Team member used the X-Dream Total Dry on hard mixed routes in Ouray and D14 king lines in the Italian Dolomites. The first widely available commercial tool with a triple-grip handle, it gives you tons of flexibility and reach in steep terrain. But it’s too aggressive for pure ice, and the handle isn’t as ergonomically contoured as on other triple-grip models. Thankfully, the X-Dream’s all-around handle is available separately.

Pros and Cons + Modular head weights + Ultra-sharp picks + Adjustable handle size – Geometry isn’t aggressive enough for seriously overhung terrain

An impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. “I certainly appreciated being able to adjust the handle size to accommodate the difference,” said one tester, who swapped between thin dry-tooling gloves and thick, three-finger mitts. The geometry isn’t aggressive enough for overhung mixed, though, like the crux ice-dagger transfer on Dark Nature (WI5+ M5/6).

Pros and Cons + Lightweight + Durable steel + Seamless rotation + Easy to place – Spring-loaded crank knobs are sometimes overeager

We occasionally steer clear of aluminum screws because we find they bind up in plasticky ice. But the featherweight, all-steel Blue Ice Aeros are easily the next best thing. The lightest steel screw on the market, the Aeros are easy to start, easy to clean, and rack neatly on a harness. The three-tooth design seems to bite more reliably than four-toothed models, and we found the Aeros never bound up, even in warm, snowy conditions in Colorado’s Ouray Ice Park.

Ease of racking was another fan-favorite perk. You can fit six screws on a single clipper as opposed to Black Diamond or Petzl’s four to five. Credit goes to the low-profile aluminum hangers, which Blue Ice managed to trim down without sacrificing the size of the crank knob or the length of the hanger.

“The hangers are long enough to provide plenty of torque to easily turn the screw, and they’re simple to manipulate with gloves,” said one Colorado-based tester after a season of backcountry ascents in the San Juans.

The Aeros also offer a larger barrel diameter than any other screw we’ve tried, which means you can thread them into old screw holes in a pinch and still get a tight, reliable placement. The larger diameter also came in handy while setting up rappels.

“V-threading was a breeze with the Aero, providing a wide window of ice to thread the rope and get it back out with my V-thread tool,” reported one tester.

The only thing we didn’t like was the spring-loaded crank knobs. While some testers loved that they snap back into the screw automatically, others found that the snapping sometimes occurred prematurely, pinching their fingers or gloves in the process.

Buy in this order: boots, layers, gloves, then a big belay parka. Crampons, ice tools, and screws are easy to rent or borrow while you’re learning. Boots and apparel aren’t, and they matter most to your comfort on the ice.

Start with boots, because fit is everything.

You can find used boots for $200 to $300, but buy new if that’s what it takes to get a perfect fit. Visit a local climbing shop, tell the sales associate about your objectives and experience level, and let them guide you.

Layer for the conditions, and keep your insulation adjustable.

Carry two to three pairs. Wet hands are cold hands, so the number-one tip for staying comfortable is keeping your mitts dry. You’ll need:

As with boots, buy your gloves new if that’s what it takes to get the fit right.

Yes, eventually. Make it the last piece of your kit. A two-way zipper and interior drop pockets are nice, but warmth matters most. Standing around belaying in the snow can be downright frigid, and the bigger and warmer your belay puffy, the happier you’ll be.

Rent or borrow these until you know what you like:

Yes, but upgrade as you get more into the sport.

Buy safety essentials new. That means ropes, harnesses, and helmets. It’s hard to tell if used gear has been compromised, and trustworthy safety gear is the cheapest insurance policy you’ll ever buy.

For most other items, shopping secondhand can help you figure out what you like before you shell out for a spendy new kit. Try MountainProject.com, GearTrade.com, and eBay, or Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace if you live in an outdoorsy town.

Gear reviews are highly subjective, but we do our best to combat that by taking a slightly more scientific approach to testing ice climbing gear. At the beginning of each season, we wade through sheaves of PR requests, consider the specs and promise of each one, and then carefully select the gear we deem fit to test. Then, we do our utmost to get each piece in the hands of as many testers as we can—and in as varied conditions as the team can manage.

This year, testers picked and kicked their way up everything from steep ice in Colorado’s San Juans to long mixed lines on Mount Robson. Samples traveled from Denali to the Italian Dolomites to the Patagonian Andes and back again. We belayed through blizzards, swung into bullet-hard ice, whooped over perfect sticks, and cursed through some of the wettest pitches of our lives. At the end of the year, we compared notes and selected only the best ice climbing gear to review. Those are the products you’ll see here.

Anthony Walsh is a senior editor at Climbing. Based in the Canadian Rockies, he does it all—from steep ice to long alpine routes to rowdy mixed climbs. All those pitches have helped him hone two unmatched talents: suffering honorably in Arctic conditions, and complaining about poorly constructed gear in the most eloquent way possible.

Corey Buhay is a freelance writer and editor based in Boulder, Colorado. She is a current member of the U.S. Ice Climbing Team and has redpointed up to WI5, M12-, and D14 around the Colorado Rockies and beyond. She is a coach and board member at The Ice Coop, Colorado’s only dedicated ice-climbing gym.

Emilie Grenier is a regular contributor to Climbing who actually prefers climbing ice to rock. As a result, Emilie is hunting for frozen smears come September each year, and you can’t drag her out of crampons until at least May.

#8273. These 6 Nordic-Cycle Cabins Make Recovery the Ultimate Focus

(Photo: Left: WestWind Cabins cold plunge tub/Brian Reid - WestWind Cabins Owner; Middle: Taking a dip in the cold plunge at Desert of Maine Campground & Unwind Nordic Spa/Ben Sarle; Right: Cool plunge at Frontcountry Salida/Daylene Wilson Photo; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva)

There’s something so invigorating about unwinding in a hot, dry sauna, then plunging into an ice-cold tub or pool. While such contrast therapy is offered at high-end spas and popular among wellness and outdoor enthusiasts, the practice has long been a staple of Nordic living and recovery.

To save you the search for the ultimate Nordic cycle retreat, I researched the most beautiful cabins in nature, decked out with saunas and cold plunges. Before sharing them with you, though, let’s take a beat to understand the scientific allure of contrast therapy—the risks associated with it.

“Nordic cycling improves circulation by shifting rapidly from heat to cold, flushing metabolic waste and lactic acid from your tired muscles,” Harry Pino, PhD, an exercise physiologist at Princeton Longevity Center, told Outside. Princeton Longevity Center offers comprehensive diagnostic health testing and preventative care. “It triggers a release of norepinephrine, dopamine, and endorphins, increasing alertness, focus, and a sense of well-being,” he said.

Additionally, Pino said cold exposure specifically suppresses inflammatory pathways, which is particularly beneficial for athletes and fitness enthusiasts because it speeds up recovery. Moreover, research has linked regular sauna routines to a lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease.

Although the Nordic cycle has a reputation for being wildly beneficial, it’s not without risk. Pino said potential sauna side effects may include intensified itching, heat discomfort, lightheadedness, and low blood pressure.  “It is also possible for blood pressure to rise or fall depending on the person’s cardiovascular health,” Pino said. Cold plunges, on the other hand, can cause cardiovascular stress, hypothermia with prolonged exposure, and cold shock, which can be deadly. “It is advised for people with pre-existing health conditions to consult a doctor before taking the plunge,” he said.

If you’re ready for the ultimate recovery experience, keep reading for six stunning sauna-and-cold plunge cabins worth booking to explore the wellness trend for yourself.

You’ll feel immersed in nature, even though you’re five minutes from downtown and ten minutes from the world-renowned Homer Spit (a.k.a., the halibut fishing capital of the world), in one of four architecturally unique cabins that sleep four to six guests. On the grounds, enjoy the inclusive spa, where a six-person hot tub, cedar-clad wood-fired sauna, and cold plunge tub await you and your adventure buddies. For a taste of Alaskan adventure, wander around Kachemak Bay. The cabins overlook the famed waterway, known for world-class recreation from running trails and paddle sports to fishing opportunities and whale watching.

Enjoy front-row access to some of Colorado’s most exhilarating mountain recreation in Salida. Suitable for two to four guests, these thoughtfully designed wellness cabins make returning from nearby Monarch Mountain just as enjoyable as the slopeside adventures themselves. Each cabin, called a boutique micro-cabin, includes a private cedar barrel sauna, cold plunge, outdoor stargazing canopy, and fire pit, making it ideal for winter après-ski. You’ll also be able to relax after hiking, climbing, and mountain biking, or paddling, rafting, and fly fishing along the neighboring Arkansas Headwaters Recreation Area, which is also in Salida and just a 20-minute drive away. A word to the wise: pack layers; temperatures can vary greatly between highs and lows, with fall and winter weather dipping into the teens and rising into the mid-seventies.

Idaho is an under-the-radar playground for outdoor enthusiasts, often getting overlooked for Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado. One stay at these cabins, which boast Japanese-inspired beds and accommodate up to six people, and are just a short 30-minute drive from Yellowstone National Park’s West entrance, and you’ll want to return to explore the area again and again. In addition to private wood-fired hot tubs at each cabin, the retreat offers a communal Nordic spa, complete with a sauna and cold plunges. When you’re not cycling between contrast therapies or cedar-soaking beneath the galaxy, consider a scenic stroll or top-notch fly fishing along Henry’s Fork of the Snake River. If dry adventure is more your thing, head over to Harriman State Park, where more than 22 miles of hiking, biking, horseback riding, and Nordic skiing trails are at your disposal.

Hidden in a pocket of lush New England forest, this woodsy retreat feels miles from civilization. In reality, it sits mere minutes from downtown Freeport, Maine, and 20 minutes from Portland. The campground’s A-frame cabins and stargazing domes (sleeping two to six guests) offer the best of both worlds: full immersion in nature and easy access to the area’s best recreation, shopping, and dining. You’ll also be just ten minutes from L.L. Bean’s flagship store, where you can watch live fish swim in the indoor ponds and take a photo next to the iconic duck boot sculpture, which stands roughly 17 feet tall. The on-site Unwind Nordic Spa (featuring a sauna, invigorating cold plunge—never more than 60 degrees Fahrenheit—with a waterfall, and a salt-water stone hot tub that hits 104 degrees Fahrenheit) draws wellness lovers to unwind beneath the Northern Pines. You can plan your stay at the campground, and you can book spa appointments now.

The adjacent but separate tourist attraction, also called Desert of Maine, lures visitors with its intriguing sand dunes and gemstone mining for kids. Though this tourist attraction is closed for the season, it reopens in May 2027, so you can start planning your next spring adventure now. For a more mountainous excursion, meander over to Hedgehog Mountain Trailhead or Bradbury Mountain State Park to explore miles of multi-use trails. Or, if you have a bit more time to spare and are craving an unforgettable coastal climb, Acadia National Park is just under three hours away.

Planning a Glacier National Park getaway? This forested retreat, with cabins sleeping up to four guests, is about an hour from the West Glacier entrance and offers wellness amenities that make the drive well worth it. Beyond the cozy, vintage-inspired Montana cabin decor, this Western woodland escape boasts a unique Nordic circuit, with a custom-built, forest-view Finnish cedar sauna and a natural, spring-fed stone group cold plunge pool. Just beware: local trout call the plunge pond home. Outside of camp, nature is calling. Nearby Flathead Lake is a popular spot for kayaking, paddleboarding, and swimming, while Blacktail Mountain Ski Area is great for intermediate to advanced skiers (only roughly 15 percent of slopes are greens).

There’s so much to see and do in Shenandoah National Park that booking an overnight seems only obvious. This hidden, Scandi-style A-frame, suitable for up to four people and located just over an hour from Washington, D.C., invites guests to relax and recharge among the forest, then sweat and plunge beneath the stars. A few can’t-miss sights (and flavors) in the area include White Oak Canyon, with its six waterfalls ranging from 25 to 86 feet; Old Rag, Shenandoah’s most popular and strenuous hike; and The Apple House, a Linden institution frying up the most delicious apple butter cinnamon donuts you’ve ever had. (No, really: the roadside restaurant has drawn crowds since 1963, and three generations of my family have been loyalists—it’s that good.)

#8271. 4 Speed Records and Free Solos That Went Down in the Last 2 Weeks

Becca Droz (left) and Kate Kelleghan (right) set a new female speed record on the classic 'Naked Edge' in Boulder's Eldorado Canyon on October 26. (Photo: COROS)

Maybe it’s the erratic weather pressures of El Niño, or perhaps there’s just a particularly competitive spirit in the air right now. In the past two weeks, several climbers have broken records, made improbable repeats, and soloed terrain that would make many of us squirm.

Last week, we looked into the culture of free solo speed climbing in Boulder, Colorado, speaking with several athletes about the risks and influences they carry in their high-stakes sport. On the heels of this deep dive, two of the athletes who spoke to us went on to break additional records of their own within the past few days. This includes a new FKT on Half Dome and a fresh women’s speed record on Eldorado’s most famous route.

More broadly, we’ve seen a few historic achievements in the past couple weeks by free soloists and speed athletes alike. Here are four record-breakers we’ve been watching lately, in chronological order.

Just a few weeks ago, Alex Honnold told Adrian Ballinger that he thought someone would likely repeat his free solo of El Capitan before anyone dared to repeat his insanely hard linkup of peaks and scrambles in Red Rock. Back in 2022, he dubbed that linkup the Honnold Ultimate Red Rock Traverse (aka the HURT).

Honnold will have to eat his words, because on October 19, Nevada climbing guide Nik Mirhashemi put down the world’s second HURT, with slight modifications. Friends have been calling his revised route the NURT: Nik’s Ultimate Red Rock Traverse.

For the NURT, the 36-year-old skipped four non-technical summits, including Goodman, Buffalo Wall, Sandstone North, and Limestone North. Instead he traversed from White Rock Peak to ascend the seven-pitch Frigid Air Buttress (5.9+; 800ft). He then continued to the top of Icebox Peak. “Basically, I had to choose between adding Frigid Air or sticking with the OG route, where those nontechnical peaks are,” Mirhashemi said. “I didn’t want to skip Frigid Air as it is quite classic.” He also called the section he swapped in one of the traverse’s “routefinding cruxes.”

Despite the variations, Mirhashemi doesn’t think there’s a significant difference in effort level. He said that though his traverse is slightly shorter, he added more technical terrain, making the difference essentially a wash. “Nice to add a little personal flair to these things I suppose,” Mirhashemi said.

“I wanted to try the HURT for similar reasons to Alex,” Mirhashemi told Climbing. “Super long days of soloing moderate terrain is one of my favorite things to do. I’ve been coming out to Red Rock for many years and just moved here a year ago. I’m always looking for new ways to challenge myself and it just made sense as a goal right in my backyard.”

Last spring, Mirhashemi made his first HURT attempt, then completed several “scoping missions”  to prepare for his fall go. “I was never sure if I could pull it off,” he said. “Stoked it’s not haunting me anymore!”

Kate Kelleghan has been busy breaking her own record again, shaving minutes and seconds off the female fastest known time on The Naked Edge (5.11b), a classic multi-pitch in Colorado’s Eldorado Canyon.

Kelleghan, along with her French partner Laura Pineau, already held the record for the route’s women’s speed record of 37 minutes and eight seconds, which was 32 seconds faster than Kelleghan’s previous go in 2021 with Becca Droz, a Boulder-based climbing guide.

In late October, Kelleghan began working the route again with Droz. And on October 26, the athletes set a new record of 36 minutes, 26 seconds, shaving 42 seconds off the previous record.

“Becca and I were the team that started the women’s record, so taking it back together feels full circle for our friendship and our community,” Kelleghan said. Droz added that being able to track splits, as well as time out the approach, actual climb, and descent with their COROS watches “was a game changer”; both women are COROS athletes.

The men’s record is held by John Ebers and Ben Wilbur at 24 minutes and 14 seconds.

Just a couple months after smashing the speed record on the First Flatiron in Boulder, 32-year-old American climber Michael Reese established a fastest known time on Yosemite’s Half Dome on October 28. In so doing, he broke an 11-year FKT set by the late Dean Potter. Reese climbed the 2,000-foot batholith from the Mist Trailhead to its summit in 1 hour, 12 minutes, and 58 seconds. He followed Potter’s original line up Grizzly Gully, then free soloed Snake Dike (5.7 R; 800ft). He broke Potter’s previous record set on May 3, 2015 by about six minutes.

A few days after his Half Dome lap, our reporter Holly Chen, who also reported on his Flatiron speed record, caught up with Reese.

“In 2021, one of Dean Potter’s good friends told me about this as a potential record to try. He became one of my main climbing partners,” Reese told Chen. Since then, Reese has made 16 attempts and several scouting missions before his record-breaking attempt in late October.

“Records are made to be broken. I’m not gonna be surprised if it’s broken one day,” Reese said.

In the second-hardest free solo by a woman, Aleksandra “Ola” Taistra climbed a seven-pitch, 720-foot route in Sardinia, Italy on October 29. The line in question is Margarites (7a+/5.12a) up the limestone cliffs of Monte Oddeu. Established in 1998 by Andrea Calvo and Lorenzo Nadali, the route has become one of Sardinia’s “most sought-after lines,” according to Taistra. It includes a bouldery 7a+/5.12a crux pitch high off the deck; two 7a/5.11d pitches; and four additional pitches graded 6c+/5.11c, 6b+/5.11a, 6a+/5.10c, and 5c/5.10a, in order of descending difficulty.

“Climbing Margarites for the first time I thought that climbing it without a rope was impossible for me,” Taistra shared with Climbing, “and that’s exactly how the plan was born—first get to know the route, and then properly assess my skills.” Taistra says that when she finished free soloing Margarites, she thought: “Oh, that’s it?”

Taistra already put down one of the hardest female free solos in history in May, when she climbed Alfredo Alfredo (5.11d/7a) ropeless. Now, the only known harder female free solo belongs to French legend Catherine Destivelle, who climbed an unnamed route in Mali without a rope that she said maxed out at 7b or 5.12a/b.

In May, 44-year-old Taistra told Climbing that free soloing gives her “so much peace” and feels less stressful than climbing with a rope. The 44-year-old climber rehearses her routes on toprope until she feels confident in the moves.

#8270. Avoid California’s Crowded Trails With These 5 Quiet Coastline Hikes

There’s no shortage of spectacular hiking in California. Big Sur, Yosemite, and Redwoods have achieved international renown––and for good reason. But if you want to escape the crowds, the less congested San Luis Obispo coast offers scores of trails, uncrowded wilderness, and stellar vistas along Highway 1.

These routes invite you to hike on hills turned gold by spring flowers, spot seals in coastal reserves, and explore both long and short routes near cozy coastal towns—all without fighting for a parking spot at the trailhead. Integrate these hikes into a road trip along the iconic Highway 1, or just visit for an active getaway. San Luis Obispo’s landscapes are beautiful, the food is delicious, and, for the nights you’re not camping, there’s great lodging.

Named for the abundant yellow wildflowers that paint the hills gold every spring—namely bright yellow poppies, Deerbrush, and wild mustard—this unique park along the Morro Bay estuary is home to riparian environments, coastal scrub, and pines.

Scores of trails weave across 8,000 acres of wilderness and offer views of Morro Bay. But for epic views of the coast and a solid taste of all the park has to offer, start at the Hazard Peak Trailhead on Pecho Valley Road and hike out on Hazard Trail to the peak. From there, you can retrace your steps back to the junction with Canyon View Trail. Take that and descend a series of short switchbacks to Islay Creek Road, which will spit you out just down the street from the Hazard Peak Trailhead. You can also extend the hike by doing the full Hazard Peak loop, which is about 11 miles.

Located in the Lopez Lake Recreation Area outside Arroyo Grande, this trail climbs up and along the western ridge of the county park. Wildlife sightings of deer, birds, even black bears, aren’t uncommon. The last section of trail involves a steep climb to the peak, but the 360-degree views of the Oceano Dunes and coast to the west and surrounding Santa Lucia, Caliente, and Sierra Madre Mountains are worth the effort.

Start on Wittenberg Trail at the end of Lopez Dr. and branch off onto Duna Vista Loop Trail. Duna Vista Spur Trail will lead you to the peak. Hike directly back on the southernmost part of the loop for a slightly shorter route (8 miles) or split off onto the northern section for the full 8.8-mile trek. A day-use fee of $12 per vehicle is required.

This beautiful coastal walk isn’t a challenging one, but give yourself plenty of time to complete it: You’ll want to stop and soak in the wide ocean views, sea stacks, and wetlands. Most of the hike is along bluffs, but opportunities to descend and explore intertidal areas at low tide abound. Expect to see plenty of sea lions and bring your binoculars to try to spot an endangered snowy plover.

Start at the North Ocean parking lot on the edge of Cayucos and take Estero Bluffs Trail along the coast to the end of the park and back.

There’s more to this hike than classic California coastal scrub. In fact, as you climb over rolling hills, you’ll score views of Morro Bay and jagged Morro Rock, a volcanic plug in the estuary, and even drop into shady live oak groves. Volcanic peaks pepper the periphery, and opportunities to spot wildlife abound, including any of hundreds of bird species that follow the Pacific Flyway.

The state park’s trail system is extensive, but this route is a nice loop that touches a lot of the trails on the east side. Start at the parking lot on S Bay Blvd. and take Quarry Trail to Canet Trail, followed by Chumash, Crespi, Park Ridge, and Live Oak Trails. That leads you right back to the parking lot you started in. You can customize the length by combining various side trails, including to the top of Portola Trail, a small summit, which adds about a mile. A state park pass or $8 day-use fee is required.

This rugged trail leads into the Santa Lucia Wilderness within Los Padres National Forest, finally reaching an 80-foot waterfall that streams into an azure pool. Much of the trail slowly climbs through the woods alongside a creek and lush riparian zone in Big Falls Canyon. However, if you continue onward past the trio of falls, your efforts will be rewarded with sunny views of the surrounding Coast Ranges.

Start at Big Falls Trailhead on Upper Lopez Canyon Road and hike to the junction with Hi Mountain Trail. Return the same way. The last section of Lopez Canyon Road to the trailhead can be rough, so 4WD is recommended.

Eat: Gardens of Avila, located within Sycamore Mineral Springs Resort and Spa in San Luis Obispo, offers elegant dining, homegrown ingredients, and garden paths for after-dinner strolls.

Sip: Wineries abound. Oenophiles who appreciate organic and regenerative farming should visit Chamisal Vineyards in Edna Valley.

Explore Town: Los Osos offers welcoming coffee shops, local art galleries, and fine boutiques. Avila Beach is worth exploring for sunny waterfront vibes. Cayucos is home to classic seaside tourist scenes complete with souvenir shops and antique stores.

Campgrounds are in no short supply along Highway 1, and the San Luis Obispo area is no exception. Most of the state parks, like Montaña de Oro, Morro Bay, and Estero Bluffs, have their own developed campgrounds. Morro Beach also has a campground along the coast. Those can be booked online or in person, but they fill up quickly, especially on weekends. During the winter, these campgrounds are closed, so you’ll need to seek out dispersed camping or other lodging options.

Dispersed camping is strictly prohibited along Highway 1. However, some nearby mountain areas allow it. Check out TV Tower Road, Carrizo Plain National Monument, or Williams Hill Recreation Area.

Want to break up your nights outside? You have options. San Luis Obispo and nearby towns have plenty of hotels, BnB’s, and more luxurious accommodations. For a splurge, check out La Lomita Ranch, a chic and colorful former stable with painted tiles, terracotta, and horses in San Luis Obispo.

#8269. Take a Break this Winter. Warren Miller’s ‘Days Off’ Is Coming to a City Near You.

After 77 years of iconic ski films, Warren Miller is asking a question never posed before: What do the world’s greatest skiers and snowboarders do on a day off?

Days Off celebrates skiing for skiing’s sake. This fall, Warren Miller’s new narrator and host, Katie Burrell, is taking audiences from backcountry laps to heli drops and the après in between with the world’s best to find out what they do when they slow down and rediscover the art of the day off.

Tickets are on sale now and run throughout North America until late December. Find a screening near you here.

Marty Shaffer, founder of backcountry ski company CaPow, knows how to take a day off. The film features his annual trip to Blanket Park Chalet in Revelstoke, British Columbia. Shaffer’s parents bought the helicopter-access-only A-frame cabin in 1986, a month before he was born.

“Back then, it was a bunch of granola munchers,” Shaffer told Outside. “For years growing up, it was hard to get people to ski with me.”

Now, he and his wife run guide-curated backcountry ski trips with their two young boys. Burrell was also Shaffer’s first employee, and bringing her back to the chalet held a special place in the film.

“The story and the segment are super meaningful for my family because we filmed, and then ten days later, we had our second kid,” Shaffer said. “It’s special to me because it’s a story that we were able to tell at a very specific time in our life, and the magic of our family.”

Shaffer invited Burrell on the friends-and-family trip, and when she accepted the Warren Miller hosting position, she asked if she could bring a film crew

“It’s a special time for us to be up there with family,” Shaffer said. “Working as a guide and having a small business, this is one of our only times to really enjoy Blanket with our family and away from all the chaos.”

Shaffer has been watching Warren Miller films for ages, and said this year’s film reflects on the importance of relationships, slowing down, taking time off, and getting outside.

The film includes seven other segments shot across three continents, taking audiences from the remote heli-skiing terrain of Alaska and high-alpine mountaineering of Chamonix, France, to legendary powder of Hokkaido, Japan, and the pristine slopes of Deer Valley, Utah. The journey continues through the heart of Canada’s best ski destinations—Whistler, Pemberton, and Banff—capturing the sport’s raw spirit through backcountry snowmobiling, skijoring, and endless alpine pursuit.

Burrell joins athletes and industry professionals on their days off—unscripted runs, backcountry lodges, and local traditions that live just beneath the ski industry’s surface.

Hundreds of showings are still on deck, spanning the U.S. and Canada. Some events will feature giveaways, others will have surprise guests, and all will build community and stoke excitement around our favorite season: winter

Other featured athletes include Sam Kuch, Craig Murray, Jess Kimura, Marie-France Roy, Christina Lustenberger, Guillaume “Gee” Pierrel, Craig McMorris, Sebastian Judge, Mark Sollors, Truth Smith, Court “Blackbird” Larabee, Mason Mashon, Kaylin Richardson, Ted Ligety, Chuck and Claudia Mumford, Pep Fujas, Sam Mitchell, Marty Schaffer, Kate VanHee, and Himari Takamori, Hinano Sakamoto, Shizuku Hanada, among others.

Warren Miller’s Days Off is presented with support from Mammut, Deer Valley, Brooks, REI Co-op, Swany, Silverton Mountain, DryBrew, and in production with Outside Studios.

#8268. Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia, Leaving Officials to Look for Answers

A young grizzly in British Columbia (Photo: Colleen Gara / Getty Images)

Two hikers are dead after a suspected bear attack on Indigenous lands in British Columbia, provincial wildlife officials say. The incident comes just a year after a bear encounter in the same area left four people seriously injured.

Rescuers discovered one body on the afternoon of Nov. 2 near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, leading to a search for a second, missing victim.

That search concluded late Tuesday night when searchers found the second hiker dead. Officials with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) believe both were attacked by a grizzly bear, and efforts are ongoing to locate and trap any bears in the area for assessment.

Authorities and family members have since identified the pair as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter, 20-year-old Selah Reed.

“It is not yet clear whether more than one bear was involved,” BCCOS Investigator Jeff Tyre told Backpacker. “Any captured bear will be assessed. If it is determined to have been involved in the attack, it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety.”

Family members first reported Balcarras and Reed overdue on Sunday, Nov. 1. Police and SAR operators found the first human remains on Monday afternoon, and called BCCOS due to evidence that suggested an animal was involved.

The victims’ remains have since been returned to their families, and the Snooka West Trail remains closed.

In the wake of the deaths, tribal authorities of the Nuxalk Nation, the First Nations people who live in the Bella Coola valley, expressed their support. Samuel Schooner, elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said in a statement that the tribe understands firsthand the trauma this incident will inflict on the victims’ family members and on the survivors of last year’s attack.

That incident occurred near Highway 20 on Nov. 20, 2025, when a grizzly attacked a local school group taking a lunch break. Adults were able to repel the animal with bear spray and a bear banger, but not before it severely injured four people, including three children. The four individuals were rushed to the hospital in varying conditions, and seven others required care at the scene.

No one died, and investigators continued to search for grizzlies in the area, eventually determining three bears could have been involved. Over the following two weeks, officers captured eight adult and juvenile grizzlies for forensic testing. All eight animals were eventually collared and relocated after they could not be forensically connected with the attack.

A total of 24 officers were involved in the response to that attack. Some reportedly drove 14 hours overnight to hand-deliver samples to the Alberta Wildlife Forensic Laboratory. BCCOS described both the response and the incident as extraordinary.

“In my 34 years of experience, I have not seen an attack like this with a large group of people,” Kevin Van Damme, with BCCOS, told Global News at the time. “So this is extremely rare and I think the public needs to understand that part.”

As 2025 field operations concluded, the Conservation Office reported decreasing bear sightings and pointed out that grizzlies in the area typically transition from hyperphagia to denning in or around December.

It’s unclear how long the current search will continue. A spokesperson for BCCOS said investigators were unavailable for comment due to heightened field activity.

“Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time,” the agency said. “We are in contact with the family to offer any support we can as we continue to investigate this incident.”

Landscape experts reveal how to recreate the striking, sculptural cactus display at Mandy Moore’s former Pasadena home – wherever you garden.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Mandy Moore put her Pasadena house on the market, most people looked at the interiors. But what stopped me was her living room’s floor-to-ceiling windows, which looked directly onto a patch of massive cacti. In effect, it made her garden look like a living piece of wall art. Architectural, barely any maintenance, and just impossibly cool.

Growing cacti outdoors is much more achievable than you might think, and you don’t have to live in Southern California to do it. I consulted a couple of experts on how you can get this look, too.

Many plants can be quite finicky, and you have to care for them like you would a child or pet. You plant them, water them, tend to them, and eventually, if you’re lucky and the weather cooperates, they reward you with flowers. But, only for a few weeks before they go back to looking like a stick in the ground. Cacti are quite different, fortunately.

Swipe to image 8 to see Mandy's statement cacti:

A post shared by Mandy Moore (@mandymooremm)

Marta Pawlik, Co-Founder and Director of luxury property management company Laik, has used statement cacti across over 50 premium properties and knows exactly what they do to a space: "Cacti serve as great focal points because they fill up the space they occupy without any effort. While most plants ask you to wait for blooms, growth, and seasons, cacti have presence from day one."

Noé Lerma, landscape architect at GreenMex, agrees: "It has forms that are really easy to appreciate on their own. You don't need many to make it look nice. It's a species that doesn't need to be accompanied by other plants."

One plant, one corner, and you’re done. Easy, peasy, organic lemon squeezy.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Mandy Moore is likely growing Euphorbia ammak, which is typically suited for USDA Hardiness Zones 9b through 11b. But the variety you pick should be matched to both your garden size and the visual effect you want to go for.

Pawlik has a clear framework for this: "Golden Barrel cacti (available here on Amazon) work well for small gardens because they group together nicely and allow you to create an intentional look. They tolerate temperatures as low as 20°F (-6°F). Prickly Pear cacti add unique texture to mid-sized gardens and depth where flowering shrubs won't work. Cold-hardy varieties, like Opuntia humifusa (eastern prickly pear), tolerate cold winters down to USDA zone 4. You can order prickly pear at Walmart. For larger properties, Blue Columnar cacti, available on Amazon, are the ones that guests typically capture in photos uninvited."

Lerma's list leans more towards the dramatic, telling me, "Organs, barrel cacti, and Pachycereus are often the most ideal choices for creating a strong visual impact in the landscape."

If you prefer Mandy Moore’s look specifically, columnar varieties are your best bet. Cereus peruvianus, available from Walmart, and Blue Myrtle cactus, from Amazon, both have that striking vertical look that photographs so beautifully and looks super architectural when viewed from indoors.

Often, our first instinct with a dramatic plant is to surround it with other dramatic plants, but this is a mistake.

Lerma is direct on this, telling me, "Avoid placing too many large cacti close to each other. This creates a visual competition between them, rather than allowing each species to stand out on its own." His suggested companions for smaller species: "Natal plum, purple ruellia, fountain grass, and desert rose. And some elements for the soil, such as crushed stone."

A bag of YISZM decorative gravel pebbles (available on Amazon) spread around the base of your cacti pulls double duty. It improves drainage while giving that desert landscape look that ties the whole aesthetic together.

Pawlik shares her most successful pairing to illustrate this point: "Last year I used blue fescue grass with a columnar cactus against dark wooden elements, and all of the guests mentioned this space in their reviews, without prompting."

The formula: one statement cactus, one or two soft companions, and a textured ground cover; resist anything else!

Scale blindness is the most common error. Pawlik has seen it happen, saying, "Recently, one owner traveled two hours to purchase a six-foot Saguaro cactus for his yard, but the cactus appeared unfeasible, and instead of judging the owner's decision, everyone assumed it was an issue." You can buy a smaller specimen from The Cactus Outlet Store via Amazon.

Lerma's advice for avoiding it: "Make sure not to use them too close together. Most of the time, the main objective of a cactus is to be a protagonist element. You can use elements like other desert or xeriscape plants and sculptural stones, but keep in mind to embrace the cactus."

This is the question most people have, and the answer is more encouraging than you'd expect. Pawlik operates properties year-round in the North of England, which is not exactly the Sonoran Desert, with statement cacti: "Hardy Opuntias can withstand harsh winters when the drainage is properly installed and maintained. I have comfortably operated properties with statement cacti year-round with zero maintenance required."

Lerma's approach for cooler climates is equally practical. He tells me, "What we always recommend is to first investigate which type of desert garden you like, then search for species that have a similar look but at the same time can be developed appropriately to your space, and finally make a match between those species. But you should always investigate before planting."

When growing cacti, drainage is non-negotiable, no matter the climate. Cacti will survive cold far better than they'll survive waterlogged roots. Get the soil right – gritty, fast-draining, and ideally amended with horticultural grit or a cactus mix – and the rest will take care of itself. Which, let’s be real, is the whole appeal.

Bonsai Jack's Gritty Mix, available on Amazon, is the easiest way to get that drainage right straight out of the bag. It's specifically formulated to dry out fast between waterings, which is exactly what cacti need and what standard potting compost can never give them.

#8266. Even When Everything Goes Right, the Backcountry Can Turn Fatal. What College Recreation Clubs Are Doing About It.

Search-and-rescue responders with the Chaffee County Sheriff's Office search for two missing Colorado ice climbers (Photo: Courtesy of CCSO)

The small Colorado Mountain College community in Leadville is in mourning after two of its students—19-year-old Kaden Matsuda and 20-year-old Jackson Donlon—died in late October when their climbing anchor failed during their descent of West Apostle Mountain.

While investigators emphasized that the pair took extensive safety precautions, their deaths come amid a string of recent high-profile outdoor accidents involving college students.

A 21-year-old with the University of Cincinnati’s Mountaineering Club was found dead on October 12 after he slipped while crossing a stream during a trip in West Virginia. A 19-year-old wrestler at a California community college also fell to his death while hiking on September 20 in Yosemite National Park. In Kentucky, nine college students from Indiana and Illinois called search-and-rescue officials after they became stranded on a trail called Indian Staircase on August 15. That same month, four college students from New Jersey were rescued in New Hampshire after departing late and getting caught by nightfall. In January, a helicopter rescued three college-aged hikers from Utah’s Mount Olympus.

Andy Millick owns Sharp End Rescue, a search-and-rescue training company in northern Vermont. He told Outside that many outdoor hobbies have a learning curve—from mastering basics like what to bring or how to pack a backpack to developing map-reading and weather-monitoring skills.

“A lot of people grow up in a world that doesn’t have access to those experiences,” he said.

Younger people sometimes venture into the backcountry without adequate preparation, the proper equipment, or familiarity with the terrain, he said. They may also lack the experience and judgment to recognize and avoid unnecessary risks. As Millick noted, they don’t always fully understand the prep work that it will require.

“There’s [sometimes] a miss in all the preparation it takes to really have fun,” he said. “That’s where people start getting into trouble.”

On October 18, Millick helped rescue a 19-year-old hypothermic college student in the middle of the night on a remote section of the Long Trail in Vermont. The hiker was on a student-led club outing, and when trouble hit, the group acted quickly.

“[They] got him in a sleeping bag with more layers, got another student in that sleeping bag as well to share some body heat, put sleeping pads underneath him to keep him off the ground,” Millick said.

“[They did] all the right things at that point,” Millick said. “Unfortunately, the tricky thing with hypothermia is once somebody starts to get cold, it takes a long time to get them warm again.”

The group contacted a faculty advisor for additional help and called 911 as the sick student went in and out of consciousness. When first responders arrived in the early morning hours, they continued warming the student with additional measures, including a heated blanket. By morning, the student had improved enough to walk out with the rescue team’s help.

Millick said it made a huge difference that the trip leader had a Wilderness First Responder certification, an 80-hour course that teaches backcountry survival skills.

“They learned so much more coming away from that and utilizing the skills that they had been taught and seeing, ‘Hey, this stuff is real, and it does work,’” he said.

College outdoor recreation clubs expose young people to the outdoors and usually center on activities such as hiking, backpacking, or adventure sports like kayaking. Some of these, such as the hiking club at the University of Colorado, Boulder, and the Dartmouth Outing Club, are more than 100 years old. Historically, many of these groups are student-run, organized, and often have a faculty advisor.

“It’s an opportunity to introduce people to outdoor programming that maybe they’ve never been introduced to [and] to step outside their comfort zone,” Jan Hackett, who ran outdoor programs at Duke University in the late ‘90s and early 2000s, told Outside.

Hackett now owns Wilderness Education and Medicine of Texas, a company that offers wilderness education classes. Outdoor clubs let more experienced students build the skills needed to lead an outing. Proper training, Hackett says, is imperative to that leadership. At a minimum, Hackett believes a trip leader should be required to have wilderness first aid certification, which teaches individuals how to handle serious injuries or heat- and cold-related emergencies, including hypothermia.

“The instructor is probably going to mix in some stories–some real disasters–that happen to drive home the point: this is why we do this,” Hackett told Outside. “It’s about risk management, having you prepared in the event a disaster happens.”

The goal of this training is not to scare students or dampen their enthusiasm, he says, but to teach that assessing risks can help combat any feelings of invincibility that may accompany youth.

“Safety is your judgment,” Hackett said. “Even if they are 22 years old, sometimes they haven’t had as much experience, so how do [they] get some of that judgment? It’s through training.”

Zach Waksmonski, 19, is the president of the student-run Penn State Outing Club at State College, Pennsylvania. A college junior, Waksmonski told Outside that his group helps build a sense of community around a shared passion for hiking and backpacking.

It’s also taught him to be more vigilant about anticipating the unexpected.

“Even if it says that there’s no chance of rain for a given weekend, if you’re going on a backpacking trip, you’re definitely still going to want to have some sort of rain protection,” he said.

Penn State temporarily shut down the program in 2018 because it deemed it too risky. After the school faced a backlash, the club was reinstated with new safety guidelines. Now trips require a certain number of students to either be Wilderness First Aid or responder certified.

Waksmonski says some members miss activities that they could have done in the past, such as climbing expeditions. But he said the standardized tools now in place help set students up for success. For example, participants must fill out a detailed planning document that lists how they’ll manage any potential hazards, and it undergoes peer review.

“Those give us a framework where if something unexpected arises, we can more effectively deal with it,” Waksmonski said. “It goes from being a day-ruining event to a minor inconvenience.”

Students also submit post-trip reports where they can identify teachable moments. One recent example? A student wore shorts on a trail with overgrown, thorny vegetation. The takeaway: pants are advisable.

Safety and enjoyment in the outdoors come down to proper preparation. Millick advises groups to check the functionality of any equipment they’re using before setting out and to understand the terrain and weather in the area they’re targeting.

“Stuff absolutely happens, [but] it’s how you react to it in the moment,” he said.

Always tell other people about your plans, he adds, and assess the group’s knowledge base, including map-reading skills and first-aid capabilities. Millick also says to thoroughly run through what-if scenarios and develop contingency plans for being out longer than expected.

“If we run out of water, what are we going to do for a water source? Do we have the ability to treat or filter water? Millick said. “Do we have multiple ways to build a fire or heat source?”

Whether you are looking to extend the flowering season of your fall favorites or encourage the strongest plants through winter, these tasks are key to years of gorgeous mum blooms

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What would fall be without chrysanthemums? As traditional garden favorites, mums (Chrysanthemum spp.) offer a welcome burst of rich color in autumn, when many other flowering annuals and perennials have faded for the year. From fiery bronzes and golds to lush purples and crisp whites, mums are celebrated globally as symbols of joy, optimism, and longevity.

While growing mums is pretty straightforward, keeping these fall beauties blooming for longer and ensuring their long-term survival requires more effort. Mums fall into two categories: hardy garden mums (C. × morifolium) which can survive winter outdoors in zones 4-9, and florist mums which are grown as temporary decorative annuals. Regardless of which variety adorn your porch or backyard beds, October care determines whether your plants fade fast or stay vibrant into late autumn.

Fortunately, mums are tough, resilient plants. With a few simple steps this month, you can nearly double the time your mums light up the fall garden. Following these 5 essential October tasks ensures a spectacular seasonal finale, while safeguarding your plants for a triumphant return next spring. Here’s how to keep these happy flowers blooming for as long as possible both this year and the next…

It’s important to know what you can and can’t do for chrysanthemums this month. Depending on your USDA hardiness zone and local weather, different mum varieties sit at varying stages of growth mid-autumn. Early-blooming cushion mums may already be finishing their first flower flush, while late-blooming heirloom varieties like Hillside Sheffield Pink or Clara Curtis are just starting to open their daisy-like blooms.

Managing in-ground plantings and container mums requires a clear understanding of what not to do in October. While it is tempting to plant potted nursery mums into garden beds during autumn sales, October is too late in most northern regions for roots to establish before the ground freezes. Unless you live in a mild southern climate where the first hard freeze is at least 6 weeks away, keep any late-purchased potted mums in their containers rather than risking root death in frozen soil.

Similarly, October is not the time to divide mum clumps: doing this now would be the equivalent of a death sentence. Splitting root crowns in autumn would disrupt the plant's winter survival mechanisms. This month, put a note on the refrigerator to divide mums in early spring when green shoots appear. Dividing in spring every few years helps to keep clumps healthy and vigorous. As for what you can do to help your mums now, these tasks below are really easy to do and won’t take long at all.

Keep an eye on flower and stem quality, water management, container essentials, and crown insulation. If you need to check soil condition before carrying out these tasks, grab a soil meter. The Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter from Amazon is perfect for getting a solid read on soil quality. Then try these easy mum secrets to guarantee a gorgeous flowering display that lasts longer and comes back even stronger.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Deadheading is often viewed as a way to encourage fresh flower buds. But that’s not the only reason for deadheading mums. While snipping off spent blooms now may not force a new flush of blooms, it stops the plant from expending energy on seed production. By regularly snapping or snipping off brown, wilting flower heads just above the nearest leaf junction, you force the plant to redirect all its energy downward into root growth and crown development.

Building a robust root system now is key to helping garden mums survive winter freezes and break dormancy in spring. Make deadheading a quick weekly routine for the next few weeks. Pinch off faded blooms with your fingers. Alternatively, remove them with snips or spring-action blades like Fiskars Micro-Tip Pruning Snips, available from Amazon which are great for clean cuts that won’t tug or damage stems. Keeping spent flowers removed also improves airflow around remaining buds and prevents gray mold (botrytis) from taking hold in damp fall rain.

Consistent moisture is essential for keeping mums hydrated and blooming through October. While fall weather brings cooler temperatures and frequent rain, seasonal rainfall may not be sufficient to meet the needs of dense, heavily budded mums, especially container-grown specimens. Container mums have tightly packed roots that dry out rapidly in fall. Check potted soil daily by inserting a finger an inch (2.5cm) into the pot. If it feels dry, water thoroughly until fluid runs from the drainage holes. For ground-planted mums, check soil moisture every couple of days.

Your job as a mum mom is to check frequently. When watering, direct it to the base of the plant rather than overhead. Keeping foliage and open petals dry prevents fungal pathogens like powdery mildew, rust, and leaf spot from ruining your fall display. Every couple of weeks, add a diluted seaweed or kelp drench. GS Plant Foods Organic Liquid Kelp, available from Walmart, adds a light mineral boost to help stressed mums maintain vibrant flower color for longer. Once the soil freezes solid, stop watering in-ground plants.

October is not the time to do a hard pruning of your mums. You should snip off any diseased or rotting foliage. Cut off yellow foliage and leaves close to the base of the plant that are likely to harbor fungal diseases. If you need a comfortable set, Corona Dual Link ComfortGel Bypass Pruners from Lowe’s are excellent value and highly efficient. However, leave the main stems intact. Performing a hard prune in fall is one of the most common reasons garden mums fail to return in spring.

Allow the woody stems to stand uncut through the fall and even the winter. These stems trap snow that helps to insulate the roots and protect the crown. Furthermore, standing stems provide valuable winter habitat for beneficial garden insects. Wait until early spring, when green shoots peek through the soil, to cut the old, woody stems back to ground level.

In-ground garden mums planted in the ground can survive much colder weather than container mums. Potted mums, however, face a bit more of a challenge. Soil in above-ground pots can freeze solid quickly, subjecting pots to freeze-thaw cycles. If you want your potted mums to survive winter, protect them before hard freezes arrive. In mild regions (zones 7-9), move your containers to a sheltered spot against a warm, south-facing house wall and wrap the pots in burlap or bubble wrap.

In colder northern regions (zones 3-6), transition dormant potted mums into an unheated garage or shed once night temperatures drop consistently below freezing. Use the excellent Bloem 12-Inch Heavy Duty Terracotta Plant Caddies, available from Walmart, to move heavier mum containers for overwintering. Their caster wheels make light work of moving heavy pots. The goal is to keep the soil cold and dormant (around 32-40°F / 0-4°C) without exposing roots to sub-zero winds. Water your stored pots lightly once a month to prevent roots from drying out completely.

Applying a protective blanket of mulch over garden mums is an essential fall task, but timing is everything. Applying mulch too early in October, while soil is still warm, can trap heat and moisture against the crown of the plant, encouraging fungal rot and encouraging pests to nest. Wait until after the first hard freeze has killed off top growth and the ground begins to cool significantly before adding your mulch.

Spread a 2-4-inch (5-10cm) layer of loose, airy organic material (such as clean straw, evergreen boughs, or pine needles) around the base of each plant. You can also use an organic wood mulch. Our team loves Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon for a dye-free bark mulch that insulates crowns against freeze-thaw cycles and helps prevent frost heave. Loose materials insulate the crown without packing down into a heavy, waterlogged mat. Just don’t use heavy packed leaves which can suffocate the plant.

Taking a little time to care for your mums this month pays massive dividends now and next year. By maintaining consistent moisture, deadheading spent blooms, leaving main stems intact, and applying a protective layer of mulch after the first hard frost, you maintain strong, healthy plants for seasons to come. Give your mums the attention they deserve this month, and enjoy their lush blooms year after year.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#8264. What’s Your Hiking EDC? Backpacker’s Editors Share Their ‘Every Day Carry’ Gear

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Associate Editor Will Brendza's EDC requires three to four pockets, but prepares him with tools, fire-starter, light, and his favorite pair of sunglasses. (Photo: Will Brendza)

It seems like everywhere online people are sharing photos of their “Every Day Carry” (EDC) kits. Watches, pocket knives, key fobs, and other day-to-day, on-your-person gear are photographed in a spread and posted to socials with a quippy caption. Often, it’s tactical bros who just want to show off their knives and handguns. For others, it’s an opportunity to flash a Rolex or humble brag about their expensive whip. It’s an internet trend that’s exploded among gear nerds, collectors, survivalists, and preppers.

But what about hikers? We’ve all got a dedicated list of gear we wouldn’t hit the trail without. How would the EDC trend look if you shook people down on the trail to find out what was in their pockets?

We wanted to know. So we’re starting with Backpacker’s editors—to see what our trail EDC looks like and how it’s different from person to person. We’re curious what others’ might look like, too. Tag @backpackermag in a photo of your hiker EDC on Instagram, and we’ll check it out.

Here’s what our team is never leaving the house without. #hikerEDC

The most important piece of gear I keep on me is my Ombraz Armless Sunglasses. I’ve got sensitive eyes and a penchant for losing things—these dandies solve both of those problems. They stay tethered to my neck or head, even when I’m underwater or upside down, and offer fully polarized eye protection. Next is my Knives of Alaska folding knife, which is big enough for most camp tasks and still fits in a pocket. I also always keep a bandana handy, because it’s the single most versatile tool a backpacker can carry (serving as a headband, handkerchief, surface cleaner, hot mitt, face mask, etc.).

If you follow Backpacker’s Editor’s Gear Picks, you’ll recognize my Nocs Zero Tube Monocular, which is one of my favorite backpacking tools. For scoping routes, spotting wildlife, or just enhancing the details of a view, it’s an incredible companion. My no-frills Petzl headlamp is getting old, but still serves me well when I get caught on the trail after dark.

Then I usually keep tissues for when I get sniffly, a pen and paper for taking notes, my ID and money, the sunscreen and chapstick I apply on the go, and, of course, a lighter (preferably one with a recognizable graphic so people are less likely to “accidentally” snatch it).

Not pictured: My dog, a compass, and my Coros Pace 4 Pro watch.

I’m on a never-ending quest to see how many essential items I can cram into a waist pack, but one thing I usually leave at home during non-working hours is my smartphone; I’ve found that the more I disconnect, the happier I am. Instead, I’m generally packing an AT&T Cingular Flex 2 flip phone, which cost me all of $15 and, besides texting and calling, can display rudimentary hiking maps with the O.map app. I supplement it with a button compass, which is enough for me to rough out directions, and my Life Camera S168, a tiny digital camera capable of taking better photos and videos than my Walmart phone.

A cheap space blanket has saved my bacon at least once, and I usually add a lighter wrapped in a twist of duct tape and a travel-size tube of sunscreen. My (sadly discontinued) Leatherman Tread multitool bracelet keeps a TSA- and security-friendly cutting tool and a host of screwdriver heads at hand, and for dayhikes where the possibility of being caught after dark is remote, I toss in my (also sadly discontinued) 40-lumen Black Diamond Ion Keychain Light. My wallet-size first aid kit has antibiotic ointment and a couple of adhesive bandages in kid-friendly patterns for the inevitable skinned knees and elbows that happen on family hikes.

I carry a waterproof notepad for jotting things down. My pen of choice is a Pilot Precise Varsity disposable fountain pen; it’s probably not the lightest scribbler out there, but it’s fun to write with. I usually bring cheap sunglasses so I don’t stress when I break them—these are from last year’s Outside Days in Denver. My choice of snacks is cheap, too: fruit snacks, granola bars, or whatever I most recently bought in bulk for my kids. And the toothbrush? I’ve just found my quality of life is way higher if I can brush my teeth whenever I want.

Most days, I walk out my front door and hit my local trails with very little in my pockets save for my iPhone and one or two dog poop bags (whatever brand was on sale last time I ran out). If I’m carrying any snacks, gummy candy is the first thing I reach for, and Nerds Gummy Clusters have never let me down. On long, difficult efforts, I like Honey Stinger Organic Energy Chews. My Garmin Instinct Solar watch is always on my wrist to track mileage or elevation gain, and of course, if I’m going far, I’ll pack my inReach to contact help in an emergency. Whether I’m hitting the trail or exploring a new city, my Nalgene is along for the ride, too.

Not pictured: My Kula cloth, avalanche transceiver for winter adventures, collapsible dog bowl, and some Leukotape wrapped around my sunscreen stick.
