#8263. The 7 Best Men’s Base Layers of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: Our team of expert testers wore 46 bottoms and tops made of natural and synthetic materials for skiing, running, and other winter activities. Their months of evaluation resulted in naming the Stellar Merino Base Top and Tights as the best overall base layer for men for its comfort and moisture management. Most versatile is the Flylow Hanmer Wool Baselayer Top for under $100.

The base layer (aka long underwear or thermals) is both the literal and metaphorical foundation of a proper layering system. A wrong choice makes the whole system fall apart. If you pick a layer that chafes or gets sweaty, you’re going to be miserable no matter how perfect your insulation or shell performs.

Even after testing them for over a decade, however, I’m still hesitant to crown a few as the best because base layers are highly personal. Someone skinning uphill in the damp Pacific Northwest needs something very different from a resort skier sitting on frozen chairlifts in Colorado. Your ideal fabric feel, insulating weight, shoulder fit, and myriad other variables may vary greatly from mine.

This year’s rough snow season in the western U.S. only reinforced how important versatility is in our gear. Due to inconsistent winter conditions, we found ourselves wearing these base layers not only while skiing and touring, but also during mountain bike rides, cold morning runs, gym workouts, and shoulder-season adventures where moisture management and mobility mattered just as much as warmth. After months of testing 46 bottoms and tops—because it is our job, after all—these are the best base layers that we believe will appeal to a variety of preferences.

Pros and Cons + Most comfortable wool layer in test + Best-in-class moisture management + Remarkable odor mitigation – No hood

Out of the 46 base layers we tested, the strongest pool we have ever drawn from, the Stellar Merino Base Top and Tights were the best base layering set in the widest variety of conditions. From 15-degree full-day ski tours in Colorado’s San Juan backcountry to 45-degree high-output mountain bike rides in Durango, the layers scored best in comfort, moisture management, fit, and odor mitigation. One tester put it simply: “Clear best in test.”

Sourced from Uruguay and produced in a family-owned factory in Portugal, the Stellar kit uses premium fine 19.5-micron merino wool fibers, which deliver both softness and stretch. The fit earned praise from our tester, who is 5’10” and 170 pounds, and extremely picky about how his base layers hug his body while he moves in the snow. “Both the top and bottoms were snug but never bunchy, with an ideal sleeve and leg length for unhindered movement,” he said.

Each layer features flatlock seams to reduce bulk, gusseted underarms for full range of motion, and an elongated back panel to block cold drafts. It moved moisture efficiently and transitioned from sweaty to completely dry in under 30 minutes. After a season’s worth of wear, odor buildup was minimal. “Still haven’t washed it!” said our tester, who cohabitates with his fiancée and hasn’t heard her complain. The only knock? No hood, which would’ve been nice to help the top transition to a standalone spring skiing piece.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: 100 percent recycled polyester

Pros and Cons + Silky smooth + Friction-free seams + Excellent mobility across multiple sports – Too lightweight for chronically cold skiers

Built with The North Face’s lightweight double-knit DOTKNIT polyester fabric, this shirt combines engineered holes in the face fabric and targeted yarn construction with a wider knit in high-heat areas like armpits. The marriage accelerates moisture transfer during movement, which testers appreciated during sweaty mountain bike rides, icy bump skiing in 45-degree weather, and early-morning runs in Ashland and Bend, Oregon. Despite weighing just 6.67 ounces, the double knit still delivered enough warmth for winter weather while drying quickly and remaining exceptionally breathable. No clamminess here.

Its standout feature was the construction. The low-profile merrow stitching (an overlock stitch that wraps the edges of fabric panels as it joins them) and slim athletic fit made the base layer almost completely disappear during repetitive movements like pedaling, skinning, and gym workouts. Thumb loops also prevented sleeves from bunching underneath outer layers during cold ski days and made transitions between activities seamless. While it kept us warm while we were moving, this is definitely not the thickest or toastiest layer in the test. Skiers who routinely run cold on frozen chairlifts will likely want a heavier option (read on for our recommendation).

Sizes: XS-3XL Key Material: 100 percent recycled polyester

Pros and Cons + Extremely breathable + Casual enough to wear anywhere – Minimal insulation in truly cold weather – Must be coupled with outer layer in wind

Patagonia has been making Capilene layers for over 40 years, and the new Capilene Lightweight Crew is proof that this signature fabric just keeps getting better. Made of 100 percent double-knit, recycled polyester, with HeiQ Mint odor control and a wicking finish, it weighs a scant 3.3 ounces. Those technical details translated directly into real-world performance during mountain bike rides, gym workouts, and early-morning runs where the layer consistently dumped heat and dried almost immediately. The odor mitigation worked so well that this top once went three full weeks of heavy use between trips to the washing machine.

Unlike heavier synthetic layers that can start to feel swampy once soaked, this one retained a dry, barely-there sensation even after sweaty intervals and long climbs. The fitted cut also helped the top transition comfortably between sports and life, and the stripes made it look more like a casual long-sleeve tee than a dedicated technical layer. We ended up wearing it so often that it became part mountain-bike layer, part workout shirt, and part accidental Zoom call uniform. Disclaimer: this is not a deep winter insulation monster. On truly cold days, it worked best underneath a shell and insulating layers, or alone only during high-output activities.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: 100 percent merino wool

Pros and Cons + Soft and comfortable + Fantastic warmth-to-breathability balance + Excellent mobility despite heavyweight feel – Too warm for spring touring

The Woolx Backcountry Leggings delivered some of the best next-to-skin comfort and thermoregulation this season. Built with heavyweight merino wool, they struck an impressive balance between warmth, stretch, and breathability that made them equally enjoyable during cold ski mornings, frigid dawn-patrol jogs, and recovery hangs at home.

Despite their thickness, the leggings moved exceptionally well during mountain bike rides and gym workouts. The fabric stretched naturally through deep squats, pedaling, and mobility work without ever feeling restrictive or bunchy under outer layers. While they didn’t dry as quickly as lightweight synthetics, they retained warmth even when damp. The fabric also resisted odor buildup during repeated workouts and back-to-back days of use—another advantage of merino wool in multisport layering systems. We’d recommend reserving these for the most frigid temps: during sunny spring ski days and warmer trail rides, testers overheated in them.

KUIU’s most advanced fleece to date, the Vital S3 Zip-T Hoodie is the base layer that can do it all. The soft-brushed fleece interior traps heat, wicks moisture, dries quickly, resists odors, and still gives you plenty of mobility on high-output cold weather hunts. Boosted by XLANCE®️ technology, the fleece is reinforced with an advanced polyolefin-based stretch yarn with built-in resistance to sweat, chemicals, heat, ozone, and UVA/UVB radiation. This means your hoodie retains elasticity and durability even across the most grueling treks—you’ll get the same fit and performance when you reach for it season after season.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: 100 percent merino wool

Pros and Cons + Remarkably breathable for its weight + Soft next-to-skin feel + Immediate warmth during cold starts and transitions – Too warm for sustained high-output efforts – Slightly bulkier under trim shells

The Ridge Merino Inversion Crew managed one of the hardest balancing acts: delivering substantial warmth without feeling stifling the second testers started moving. Made of 100 percent merino wool, it became a favorite during freezing dawn starts, snowy driveway shoveling, and post-ride recovery hangs. Superfine 18.5-micron fibers were impressively soft against the skin for such a warm piece—one tester wore it to sleep even after sweating in it during the day. Low-profile flatlock seams, raglan sleeves, thumb loops, and an extra-long cut minimized friction points underneath packs and outerwear, making it all the more cozy.

What surprised us most was how flexible and breathable the top remained despite its warmth. Heavyweight base layers often feel amazing when you’re standing still and miserable once your heart rate spikes, but the Inversion regulated temperature better than expected during moderate-output movement. This is still, however, fundamentally a cold-weather specialist. During hard uphill efforts and warmer spring conditions, it quickly became too much of a layer. It also felt a tad bulky when coupled with a very trim Rab shell—worth noting if you like tighter outer layers.

Sizes: S-XXL Key Material: Polyester/wool blend

Pros and Cons + Packs down to the size of a tangerine + Fast drying + Silky next to skin – Doesn’t work as a standalone layer in cold

Over ten days of skiing in the Japanese Alps, spinning lifts at Mount Ashland, and ski touring at Crater Lake, the Rab Syncrino Base LS Tee became one tester’s default when he knew he was going to get hot and sweat hard. Built with Rab’s lightweight Syncrino 125 fabric, it combines merino wool for insulation and moisture-wicking with polyester for strength, durability, and fast drying. We found this triad of attributes ideal for high-output touring, hut trips, and traveling in temps 40 degrees and below.

It packed down to the size of a tangerine, which one tester squeezed into his pack as a safety layer on hut trips and a two-week trip to Nozawa, Japan. He praised the next-to-skin comfort, saying it “felt like you didn’t even have it on,” and rated its mobility and sweat management highly. The single-jersey construction, low-bulk seams, drop tail, and set-in sleeves made it especially comfortable under other layers.

Even after sweaty skimo sessions and back-to-back cold days, it stayed fresh. “No matter how much I sweat, it [shone] in many environments,” our tester said. However, it was too lightweight to be a standalone layer during the winter months.

Sizes: S-XL Key Material: Merino wool/nylon blend

Pros and Cons + Wide temperature range + Highly breathable + Minimal friction during exercise – Fit is long for shorter users

The Flylow Hanmer Wool Baselayer Top was winter MVP for one tester after five big days of testing on his local ski hill, Mount Ashland. He not only appreciated the Hanmer’s incredible versatility in the mountains but also felt like he was wearing a normal, non-technical top around town thanks to its two-toned sleeves and casual style. “You could literally wear this every day in winter,” he said. Tested from zero to 40 degrees while skiing, running, and during three full-on nighttime skimo training sessions, the Hanmer consistently stood out for its ability to keep him warm and efficiently move his sweat at the same time—two attributes that often conflict with each other. “I would finish a skimo workout and rip off all of my other sweaty layers and keep the Hanmer top on and throw on my down jacket over it. It was amazing that it wasn’t soggy,” he said.

The Hanmer is woven from a blend of merino wool and nylon that Flylow claims is 50 percent stronger than comparable merino fabrics. While we weren’t able to confirm that number, we can confirm that it did not experience pilling after a full winter’s worth of testing. It proved warm, breathable, sweat-wicking, and also impressively odor-resistant even after days of heavy use. “It was noticeable how odorless it was; most of my other layers would carry a little stink after the same amount of use,” he said. Flatlock seams eliminate chafing, while a long cut makes layering easy. Thumb loops and a backpack-friendly raglan construction enhance usability during high-output movement. “The thumb holes are ingenious,” our tester said. With cozy skin feel and all-conditions reliability, the Hanmer is a layer that disappears in a good way.

Everybody is different, so dialing in the materials that feel the best against your skin is the most important part of the base-layer buying journey. In general, the best base layers are constructed of either polyester or merino wool, with spandex, elastane, or nylon spun into the fabric to increase stretch or durability. Polyester layers are usually cheaper and quicker to dry, while merino is more expensive, dries slower (but retains heat while wet), and is more odor-resistant.

Which is better comes down to personal preference: some love the soft hand of natural fibers, but even the most advanced, small-micron merino wool material can make someone with a wool intolerance miserable. If you can, try on any layer you want to buy. How it feels against your skin is paramount and differs per person. If something feels itchy in a dressing room, run from it, as it is only going to get more uncomfortable with prolonged use.

Once you land on a material that works for your skin, start looking into moisture management. If you sweat a ton, as many of the testers for this category do, look into lightweight synthetic base layers, as they have an excellent track record for moving moisture efficiently. If you don’t sweat much, then you can get away with thicker next-to-skin layers that will also be warmer when you’re not in motion.

In terms of design, base layers are pretty straightforward. To maximize comfort, look for upgrades like flatlock seams and raglan sleeves. These can prevent chafing, especially when wearing a pack.

When deciding what to avoid, we would suggest starting by looking at the label. Staying away from certain materials is a great way to minimize your chances of getting a bum base layer. Cotton is an obvious material to avoid for winter-specific base layers because it holds onto moisture and can become dangerously cold. Synthetics without some type of odor-mitigating technology might also not be your best bet for hut trips, winter backpacking, or high-output skinning because they can become unsavably stinky in one trip. If something is wool, check the micron number. A lower micron count (finer fibers) will be softer and more comfortable next to skin than a higher one.

We also suggest looking a little deeper at the wording of wool/synthetic blends. Purpose-built blends (which intentionally place wool and synthetics in different parts of the blend) can utilize the hydrophilic and hydrophobic natures of the fabrics to its advantage. An example of this is a material that has a hydrophilic synthetic next to your skin to grab moisture with a layer of a hydrophobic wool that will move that moisture away from you. If the blend is described as “intimate,” that means it weaves them together in a way that will deliver the worst of both worlds. An intimate blend creates a tug-of-war over that moisture that can leave you super clammy, so we recommend steering clear.

Due to the abysmal snowpack in the Pacific Northwest, category manager Joe Jackson had the most varied testing conditions for base layers he has experienced in more than a decade of testing the category. In addition to the ski days he eked out at Mount Bachelor and in the backcountry, he used these layers during more than 60 mountain bike rides, early-morning runs, and high-output workouts in his home gym. That broad mix of activities allowed him to evaluate not only warmth and next-to-skin comfort, but also mobility, moisture management, odor mitigation, and versatility transitioning between sports.

Skiing, however, remained a critical part of testing, as always. Testers used these layers during resort skiing, uphill touring, cold transitions in parking lots, and long days spent sweating under packs. We paid close attention to how quickly layers dried after high-output efforts, whether fabrics became clammy during sustained sweating, and how well the materials retained warmth after becoming damp. We also stress-tested mobility across all sports because the best modern base layers should disappear while you move instead of restricting you.

But this year’s low snow totals also created a more realistic picture for how today’s base layers are actually used by many outdoor athletes, as multisport layering pieces that need to perform just as well on trail runs and shoulder-season bike rides as they do under a ski shell.

Category manager Joe Jackson has been testing gear professionally as his main gig for over a decade. While he has tested everything from whitewater kayaks to sporks, base layers remain one of his all-time favorite categories. They can be absorbed into everyday life to get the type of testing reps needed to help tease out the nuance that makes a piece of gear truly special. They also don’t take up much space in his overburdened garage.

If you suffer from FOMO, do not follow Southern Oregon-based tester Yu Kuwabara on Strava—his output is absolutely bananas. He’s the kind of athlete who will climb and ski Mount Shasta (he has 37 summits) in the morning, then teaches a mountain biking clinic that afternoon on a casual day. The local race director and father of rippers logged hundreds upon hundreds of multisport miles and tens of thousands of vertical feet around Southern Oregon, as well as on a trip to Japan, to test the dickens out of these layers.

Durango, Colorado–based tester Ryan Pyles has enough energy to power a small city. He positively channeled said energy this winter with remote packrafting trips, dozens of days skiing in the backcountry around Durango and Red Mountain Pass, mountain biking, trail running, and skiing in his local resort of Purgatory. He worked as a science teacher while testing last winter and has also worked as an engineer. The two jobs arguably make him the perfect candidate to deliver solid feedback because of his ability to really get in the weeds with materials as well as distill that into understandable information.

#8261. 4 Quick Activities to Try If Your Kid Is Wired at Bedtime

As a parent, you probably know that bedtime can go two ways: one, your kid was so busy all day they’re exhausted and can’t wait to get that story and hit the pillow. Or two, they haven’t had a chance to expel the endless amounts of energy they store in their little bodies. The latter is where a normal nighttime routine can get tricky because that second wind is no joke. They’ll be jumping, singing, fidgeting, and doing everything they can to delay the inevitable “lights out” moment, meaning there’s even less time for you to binge a few episodes of your new favorite show.

If you’re dealing with a kid who’s wired at bedtime, there are a few things you can do to make the transition to dreamland easier. Mom and pediatric occupational therapist Courtney English recently shared a few of her favorite sensory activities that help kids calm down before bed, and they’re simple but effective. Her TikTok video shows what parents can do:

Dr. Megan Anna Neff writes for Neurodivergent Insights that “Proprioception plays a role in body awareness, self-regulation, coordination, posture, and the ability to focus.” Playing a short game of tag in their bedroom will allow kids to realize where they are at that very moment in time, helping them to center themselves and be present.

Massage is known to be a great way to receive proprioceptive input, and what English calls a sensory sandwich (putting your child between two pillows and pressing down) is a low-energy activity that’ll give their body what it needs to relax.

Vestibular input is another important factor for kids who are wired at bedtime. As Laura Petrix writes for the OT Butterfly, it’s “a network of parts in your inner ear that contribute to your sense of balance and coordination.” It allows our bodies to know when we’re falling, move in coordinated ways (like riding a bike), and know the right speed to walk around other people. The combination of singing and rocking helps to calm the vestibular system by providing auditory rhythm and linear movement.

This is another great type of massage or touch activity that provides proprioceptive input to the nervous system. Plus, it’s a great chance to get a few snuggles in there before they close their eyes.

These activities are no secret to occupational therapists, who use them often. In fact, English has offered other sensory activities that are appropriate for bedtime, including tossing around a weighted animal and doing the “clock move.” But they’re something we should all have in our back pockets next time we’ve got monkeys jumping on the bed.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8260. Appalachian Trail Threatened by ‘Uncommonly’ Large Wildfire in White Mountains

The Wild River Fire burns in the White Mountain National Forest (Photo: Courtesy USFS)

A wildfire that may be the largest in White Mountains history is currently burning just miles from the Appalachian Trail, and officials say a human may have caused it.

The Wild River Fire started on Tuesday, November 3, in Coos County, New Hampshire, and has grown to 865 acres as of this writing, with just 11 percent contained. While the Appalachian Trail (AT), roughly 10 miles from the blaze, currently remains open, the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) has closed numerous other trails and roads in the area.

Small brush fires and wildfires occur in White Mountains National Forest (WMNF) almost every year, but according to Gorham Fire Chief Philip Cloutier, who spoke with NHPR on Wednesday, a wildfire of this size is unusual. Both extended drought and extremely dry fall conditions have fuelled its speedy growth.

“That’s very uncommon in our area,” Cloutier said. “The largest wildfire that we can remember was just under 100 acres, and that was over 20 years ago.”

Officially, USFS is still investigating the wildfire’s source. Authorities have indicated that they believe it was human-caused, though they have released no further details about the origin.

While the Wild River Fire is burning roughly 10 miles east of the AT, no closures or evacuations have been issued for the trail yet. Still, other trails in the area (some of which connect with the AT) have been closed. Below is the USFS list of trail closures in WMNF.

We will update this article if more closures are announced.

In addition to these closures, Wild River Road is also closed in its entirety.

According to the USFS, the response to the Wild River Fire has been swift, and additional resources, including thje Cherokee Hotshot Crew and a smoke suppression module, have been sent to aid in the fight. The area’s steep, rocky terrain, remote location, and wet conditions have made it particularly challenging for firefighters. A USFS spokesperson told NHPR that firefighters had to cross the Wild River on foot to mount a direct attack.

However, the efforts seem to be paying off. On November 4, the fire swelled to 982 acres. That evening, it was reduced to 865 acres, where it remains currently.

“I am proud of the firefighters who responded quickly and continue to work tirelessly to contain the Wild River Fire,” noted Josh Sjostrom, District Ranger for the White Mountain National Forest’s Androscoggin Ranger District. “We will continue to work with our neighbors and local and state partners to contain this fire.”

Shorter days and indoor heating change the rules for jade plant care in fall. A few adjustments can prevent rot and keep your plant in top shape until spring.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By October, a jade plant (Crassula ovata) is heading into its slow season. Days are shorter, the sun rides lower in the sky, and the heat comes back on in many homes. Growth slows way down through winter, and the same routine that kept the plant plump all summer can start causing trouble if nothing changes.

Good jade plant care in fall is mostly about pulling back. Too much water is the most common problem, and the risk climbs as the weather cools, as soil in a cool room stays wet longer and a slow-growing plant takes up less of it. Fertilizer and big pruning jobs can wait too, while light is the one thing plants need more of.

There's a small reward for getting the season right, as jade plants do well with cooler nights. A mature plant given a cool, fairly dry rest sometimes produces clusters of small white or pale pink, star-shaped flowers in winter. Indoor blooms are fairly uncommon, but a plant kept in bright light with cool nights has a better chance than one kept warm all winter. Get these seven things right for healthy, happy plants.

A jade plant needs four or more hours of direct sun a day, and in October there's less of it to go around. Low light shows up in the stems – they stretch, the gaps between leaf pairs get longer, and the plant grows leggy and weak. Put the pot in a south- or west-facing window if you have one, but keep leaves off the cold glass at night, and well away from any radiator or heat vent.

If you don't have a good window, you'll need to use a grow light. The Sansi Clip-On Gooseneck LED Plant Light, available on Amazon, has the option of 1–4 flexible lights.

Let the potting mix dry all the way through, or close to it, before watering again. The surface dries well ahead of the soil around the roots, so a dry top inch (2.5 cm) doesn't prove much. Push a wooden chopstick to the bottom of the pot and pull it out. If damp soil clings to it, wait. Or use the probe on a soil moisture meter, like the XLUX moisture meter from Amazon, which gives a more definite reading.

When the mix is finally dry, soak the pot until water runs out the bottom, then let it fully drain. Soft, yellow leaves that fall at a touch mean the roots have stayed too wet; wrinkled, deflated-looking leaves mean the opposite.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fertilizer doesn't do a jade plant much good this time of year. The plant hardly grows from fall through late winter, and whatever the roots don't take up gets left in the potting mix as salt. That buildup can make it harder for the roots to pull in water, and in bad cases it burns the root tips. Hold off until you see fresh growth in spring. When you start again, use a targeted liquid feed that's suitable for jade plants and other succulents, like Miracle-Gro Succulent Plant Food.

Jade plants do best with nights around 50–55°F (10–13°C). A plant that summered outdoors can stay out through the first cool nights. Bring it inside once nights regularly drop below 50°F (10°C). Colder nights can damage the leaves, and temperatures much below 40°F (4°C) can kill the plant.

Indoors, place the plant in front of the sunniest window in the house. If it sits lower than the glass, use a plant stand to raise the height, like Walmart's Mainstays metal plant stand. Some leaves may drop after the move, but firm, green leaves that fall off now are usually a reaction to the change, not a sign of disease.

Jade stems bend toward the window, and in weak winter light the lean shows up faster. A plant left facing one way from now until March can end up noticeably lopsided. Turn the pot a quarter turn every time you water so a different side faces the glass. It won't pull a badly stretched plant back upright; it just keeps new growth from piling onto one side.

Old jade plants get heavy, too, and a hard lean can tip a light plastic pot right over. A wide clay or ceramic pot is steadier, but switching pots is a spring job.

Inspect the plant before bringing it inside, since outdoor pests spread quickly indoors. The most common culprits are mealybugs and scale. Start with the stems and leaf joints, then turn a few leaves over and check the undersides.

Heavy pruning and repotting are easier on a jade plant once it's actively growing again, so save both jobs for spring. There's rarely any rush – these plants can live happily in a snug, root-bound pot for years. Rot or a broken branch is the exception.

Cut soft or damaged stems back to healthy tissue with clean tools. Fiskars micro-tip pruning snips, available at Home Depot, have a narrow, curved blade that fits into tight branch forks. Come spring, a jade that needs a bigger home does well in a clay pot with a drainage hole, like this Vigoro terra cotta clay pot from Home Depot. Fill it with cactus mix, like Espoma Organic Cactus Mix from Walmart, for fast drainage.

By March, a jade plant that spent the winter dry and in good light should look a lot like it did in October. That's a good outcome. Every so often a mature plant does more than that and blooms, with small clusters of white or pale pink flowers opening at the branch tips after a run of cool nights for an even better show.

#8258. Lindsey Vonn Is Headed for Her 9th Surgery. She’s Still Thinking About Skiing.

Lndsey Vonn inspects the slope before the second official training for the women's downhill event at the Tofane Alpine Skiing Centre during Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games (Photo: Stefano Rellandini/AFP via Getty Images)

Lindsey Vonn is just days away from her ninth surgery in as many months, and the three-time Olympic medalist is still thinking about skiing.

On November 9, Vonn, 42, is heading into what’s slated to be the final surgery on her left leg following her severe crash during the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics in February. In an exclusive interview with Forbes, the alpine skier detailed her upcoming surgery.

“The plan is to remove all of the hardware, finally fix the ACL, and hopefully that’s my last surgery,” she told Forbes.

In February 2026, Vonn started the Olympic downhill race despite rupturing the ACL in her left knee just days earlier. After taking an aggressive line through the first few turns, Vonn clipped a gate just 13.4 seconds into her run, pushing her off course at the Tofane Alpine Skiing area.

The impact sent her spinning through the air before she crashed onto the icy surface, ending her race. Vonn was eventually airlifted to a hospital and diagnosed with complex fractures of the two bones in her lower left leg. Doctors put three plates and up to 20 screws in her leg, but couldn’t fix her ACL until her bones healed properly, she told Parade.

In the weeks following her initial surgery, Vonn shared that her injuries were so severe that she had to undergo an emergency fasciotomy, a procedure used to treat acute compartment syndrome. This potentially life-threatening condition occurs when pressure builds up around muscle groups, restricting blood flow or damaging muscles, tendons, and fascia. Colorado-based surgeon Dr. Tomas Hackett performed the complicated operation that saved her left leg from being amputated.

In a video shared to Instagram, the ski champion is sailing on a hydrofoil, writing that the event “was a big step in my recovery that made me incredibly happy. It may not have been snow but … it was one step closer to skiing.”

“I know I won’t be doing this, or much else, for quite some time after this next surgery, but I know I’ll get back to it,” she continued. “Eventually, I will.”

She said she expects to be on crutches for about four weeks and still has at least six months of rehabilitation in the works.

In 2010, Vonn became the first American woman to win Olympic gold in downhill skiing. Wherever she winds up, whether it’s slopeside or downhill, Vonn will always be our favorite comeback story.

#8257. The First-Time Experiences Kids Will Never Forget in Citrus County

There’s something magical about watching your child experience something for the very first time. The wide eyes. The nervous excitement. The inevitable “Can we do that again?” And the stories they tell anyone who will listen long after you’ve unpacked the suitcases. In Citrus County, Florida, those moments are practically everywhere.

Welcome to Crystal River, Homosassa, Inverness and Floral City—a refreshingly wild side of the Sunshine State where first-time adventures come naturally. Here, kids can swim alongside gentle manatees, search the Gulf for their own dinner, explore underwater worlds and discover that sometimes the best adventures don’t require a screen, a schedule or even a ticket. It’s outdoorsy without requiring your family to be expert adventurers, educational without feeling like school and relaxed enough that you don’t need a vacation from your vacation.

An easy road trip from many Florida cities and an unexpected nature escape for families traveling from farther away, Citrus County is where your next family vacation can become a collection of unforgettable firsts.

Imagine the look on your child’s face when a 1,000-pound manatee glides through the water nearby. It’s the kind of moment that makes even the too-cool-for-everything tween forget to play it cool.

Crystal River is known as the Manatee Capital of the World, and it’s one of the few places in North America where families can swim with these gentle giants in their natural habitat. Book a certified tour with an outfitter like Explorida, where guides teach families the importance of respectful wildlife viewing, including the all-important “Manatee Manners.” Tours operate year-round, but winter is prime time for seeing larger numbers of manatees as they gather in the area’s warm springs.

Not ready to snorkel? Explorida also offers manatee-viewing eco cruises, so younger kids, grandparents and anyone who prefers staying dry can still experience the magic.

Why they’ll remember it: Because seeing a manatee in a book or aquarium is one thing. Sharing the water with one in the wild? That’s a story they’ll be telling for years.

For little explorers (and grandparents) who aren’t ready to jump into the water, the next best thing might be watching nature unfold right beneath their feet.

At Three Sisters Springs, a boardwalk winds around the crystal-clear spring complex, offering an incredible vantage point for spotting manatees during the winter months. The surrounding wetlands are also home to birds and other wildlife, turning an ordinary walk into an impromptu nature safari.

Give your kids a challenge: How many manatees can they spot? Can they find a mother and calf? What other animals can they discover along the way?

It’s stroller-friendly, wonderfully unhurried and proof that you don’t have to get wet to make a splash.

Why they’ll remember it: The thrill of spotting their first wild manatee all on their own, and the pride of being the one who shouts, “I SEE ONE!”

Forget searching for seashells on the beach. In Citrus County, kids can head underwater on a real-life treasure hunt and bring home something delicious.

During summer scalloping season, families venture into the shallow Gulf waters off Crystal River and Homosassa, armed with snorkels, masks and mesh bags, to search the seagrass for bay scallops. Think Easter egg hunt, except underwater. And instead of chocolate, the reward might end up on your dinner plate.

Never tried scalloping? That’s part of the fun. Guided excursions with operators like Explorida help beginners learn the ropes, with equipment, guidance and plenty of encouragement along the way. And the moment your child spots that first scallop hiding in the grass? Pure victory.

Why they’ll remember it: There’s something incredibly satisfying about finding your own food. Just wait until they proudly announce at dinner, “I caught that!”

Tinybeans tip: Scalloping is seasonal, typically July through September. Check current dates, regulations and tour availability before planning your adventure.

For kids who’ve never tried kayaking and paddleboarding, Citrus County offers a pretty spectacular introduction. Imagine pushing off from shore, dipping a paddle into clear spring water and realizing that, for the first time, you’re helping steer the adventure.

At Hunter Springs Park in Crystal River, families will find a freshwater swimming area, kayak launch, waterfront boardwalk, picnic spots and a playground. The spring water stays around 72°F year-round, and during cooler months, there’s even a chance of spotting a manatee.

Bring your own paddle craft or book with a local outfitter. Younger kids can ride along with an adult, while older children can take a more active role in navigating.

The best part? There’s no rush to get anywhere. Stop to watch a bird, look for fish beneath the surface or simply float and take it all in.

Why they’ll remember it: That first feeling of independence. The realization that they can help navigate a kayak, explore somewhere new and discover what’s around the next bend.

What if your kids could explore an underwater world without ever putting on a swimsuit? At Ellie Schiller Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park, they can. The park’s famous Fish Bowl Underwater Observatory lets visitors descend beneath the surface of the spring to watch fish and, when present, manatees swim past the windows. For kids, it’s a little like stepping inside a nature documentary.

Back above water, shady, stroller-accessible boardwalks lead past native Florida wildlife, including black bears, alligators, red wolves and Florida panthers. Daily manatee programs offer another opportunity to learn about these remarkable animals and why protecting their habitat matters.

It’s an ideal first introduction to Florida’s wild side, especially for families with younger children or anyone who prefers wildlife encounters on dry land.

Why they’ll remember it: Because the first time you see the underwater world from a fish’s point of view, you never look at the water quite the same way again.

Remember the first time you rode your bike somewhere that wasn’t your driveway or neighborhood? The freedom. The excitement. The feeling that you could go anywhere? That’s what makes the Withlacoochee State Trail such a great family adventure.

Stretching approximately 47 paved miles through forests, lakes and charming small towns, the trail is flat, scenic and easy to explore in family-sized sections. No one expects your six-year-old to conquer all 47 miles.

Start in downtown Inverness, where the trail passes through the Depot District, and let your kids help choose how far to ride. Along the way, keep an eye out for birds, turtles and other wildlife. When everyone starts asking about snacks, make The Train Station part of your plan for pizza, pretzels and a well-earned break.

Why they’ll remember it: Their first real biking expedition, complete with the satisfaction of going farther than they thought they could. Bonus points if they proudly tell everyone how many miles they conquered.

You can tell your kids mermaids aren’t real. Or you can take them somewhere that might make them question everything.

At Mertailor’s Mermaid Aquarium Encounter in Lecanto, live mermaids perform underwater alongside fish, rays and other marine life, creating a magical experience that feels straight out of a storybook. But there’s more here than mermaid magic. The indoor aquarium features over 20 exhibits, interactive touch tanks, sharks, stingrays and freshwater animals, giving curious kids plenty to explore.

For children ages nine and up, the separate Discover Mermaid experience takes things a step further, with the chance to put on a mermaid tail and monofin and learn to swim like one. It’s also a great rainy-day adventure or a welcome break from the Florida sunshine.

Why they’ll remember it: Because watching a mermaid swim with sharks is pretty unforgettable. But getting to be a mermaid for the first time? That’s next-level vacation bragging rights.

Not every unforgettable first requires an adrenaline rush. Sometimes it’s the first time your kids experience what it feels like to slow down.

Head to Homosassa for a waterfront meal at Crumps’ Landing, where palm trees, water views and laid-back Florida charm set the scene for a different kind of family dinner. No rushing to make a reservation across town. No squeezing in one more attraction. Just good food, waterfront views and time to talk about everything you’ve done together. Let the kids recap their favorite adventures while you watch the sky change colors over the water.

Why they’ll remember it: It may not be the meal they remember years from now, but they’ll remember the feeling: salty air, sunset skies and everyone together with nowhere else they need to be.

Remember when simply staying in a hotel felt like the most exciting thing in the world? Now imagine staying somewhere that puts you right in the middle of the action.

Paddletail Waterfront Lodge sits on King’s Bay in Crystal River, giving families easy access to the area’s most memorable experiences. With paddlecraft activities, manatee excursions, waterfront dining, a pool and complimentary hot breakfast, the lodge makes it easy to spend less time coordinating logistics and more time having fun. Rooms with refrigerators and microwaves, and select kitchenette options also make traveling with kids a little easier.

Wake up knowing that another adventure is waiting just outside.

Why they’ll remember it: Because when the place you stay is part of the experience, even the moments between activities become vacation memories.

Here’s a first that might surprise you: What if you gave your kids an entire afternoon to decide what the family does? No packed itinerary. No racing from one attraction to another. No pressure to squeeze every last minute out of your vacation.

One of the best things about Citrus County is that it gives families room to explore at their own pace. Maybe your kids want another swim at Hunter Springs. Maybe they want to wander downtown Crystal River, go for another bike ride, find ice cream or sit by the water and watch for wildlife. Let them choose.

Because sometimes the most meaningful first isn’t swimming with a manatee or spotting a scallop. It’s the first time your child discovers that an adventure doesn’t need to be planned to be unforgettable.

Why they’ll remember it: Because they helped create the memory themselves. And those are often the moments that stick.

Someday, your kids might forget what they packed, what they ate for breakfast or how long the drive took. But they’ll remember the first manatee they saw. The first scallop they found. The first time they paddled across a spring or rode their bike farther than ever before. And you’ll remember the look on their faces when they did.

That’s the magic of Citrus County. It’s not just a place to visit. It’s a place to try something new, discover something extraordinary and make the kinds of memories that grow more meaningful with time.

#8256. It’s an All-Day Pool Day at Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort

An all-inclusive vacation with kids should make family time easier, not leave parents juggling restaurant reservations, activity schedules, and snack requests every few hours. At Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort, Spa & Casino in the Dominican Republic, families can explore a sprawling resort, splash in pools, and enjoy activities for all ages.

The resort is part of the Lopesan Costa Bávaro Resort, Spa & Casino complex in Punta Cana, a destination known for its white-sand beaches and turquoise Caribbean waters. With family accommodations, supervised kids’ activities, and options for teens who prefer to spend time away from their parents, Lopesan Caoba Lagoon offers a setup that makes multigenerational family trips or vacations with school-age kids easier to plan.

Whether your family wants to spend most of the day in the water or mix pool time with games, dining, and evening entertainment, there are plenty of ways to make the vacation your own.

The largest family accommodation configuration combines a Resort Junior Suite Connecting room with a Family Junior Suite Connecting room. Together, the rooms offer 1,179 square feet of space for up to seven guests, with one king bed, two queen beds, a sofa bed, and two bathrooms.

That layout is especially useful for families traveling with several children, grandparents, or another family member. Two bathrooms make getting ready for dinner much less chaotic, while connecting rooms let parents stay close to younger children without everyone sharing the same sleeping space.

Before booking, confirm the exact room configuration and occupancy with the resort. Connecting rooms can be a practical alternative to squeezing everyone into a single suite, especially on a multi-night trip.

Even on a family vacation, it’s nice to have a little time apart. Lopesan Caoba Lagoon offers a Mini Club for children ages 4 to 12 and a Teen Club for guests ages 13 to 17, giving kids time with peers while parents enjoy downtime.

The clubs operate from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with meal breaks to give families flexibility to plan around breakfast, lunch, pool time, or dinner. Parents can enjoy a quiet break, book a spa treatment, or simply spend a little time together while the kids have activities of their own.

For families with younger children who aren’t quite ready for a group kids’ club, babysitting is available 24 hours a day with advance arrangements at $20 per child per hour.

One of the highlights of Lopesan Caoba Resort is its water features. Families can ride the waves in the wave pool, let little ones splash around in the kiddie waterpark area, splash down on the waterslides, or find a spot in the shade to enjoy one of the lagoon pools.

My favorite was the cenote swimming pool, something I haven’t seen at other all-inclusive resorts. This tranquil area never got crowded when I visited, offering a respite from the lively swim-up bars and water aerobics sessions.

For those looking for beach time, the property is adding a beach club, and in the meantime, guests can visit the Lopesan Costa Bávaro Resort beach club. Keep in mind that seaweed can be an issue in the Dominican Republic, depending on when you visit.

One of the main advantages of an all-inclusive resort is not having to figure out every meal. You can plan meals around swimming and activities instead of interrupting the day to find an off-property restaurant. The breakfast buffet was massive, offering everything from fresh fruit smoothies to pastries and waffles made to your liking. They even had a whole section for kid-friendly options and Dominican favorites.

With eight traditional restaurants to choose from, you’ll find something for every taste, from deeply flavorful Indian dishes at Indra to upscale pasta, pizza, and more at Sotto Terra. If you decide to get a babysitter for the night, definitely book a meal at the adults-only steakhouse Brassa Nova.

Evenings can be a highlight of an all-inclusive vacation, especially when there’s entertainment close to your room. Instead of arranging transportation or trying to keep everyone awake for a late dinner in town, families can enjoy the resort’s evening offerings and return to their rooms when the kids are ready to wind down.

The Boulevard, which connects Lopesan Caoba to Lopesan Costa Bávaro Resort, offers a bowling alley, theater, ice cream shop, café, and casino for adults. We enjoyed live music performances and karaoke at the bars during our stay.

Families can fly into Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ), about 20–30 minutes from Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort, depending on traffic. Private airport transfers and transportation through the resort or a third-party provider make getting to the property easy, so you won’t need to rent a car. If it’s busy when you are departing, consider using the airport’s VIP Fast Track service.

Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort, Spa & Casino Online: lopesan.com

Editor’s note: This trip was paid for by Lopesan, but all opinions belong to the writer.

Raise handsome houseplants and cut-and-come-again crops from the fruit and vegetable waste you toss into the trash.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Turning fruit and vegetable seeds and peelings into new plants on your kitchen windowsill is such a satisfying process, for us adults as well as kids. Grow plants from lemon seeds and you could raise a citrus houseplant with glossy, aromatic leaves, or root a pineapple top for a striking pot of spiky foliage. Or how about growing a feast of fabulous foliage from an avocado stone? Seedlings grown from apple and pear seeds can be shaped into stylish bonsai trees, too.

If you like the idea of free food as well as free plants, then cabbage bases will grow a tasty supply of cut-and-come-again leaves for salads and stir-fries, while carrot tops produce herby foliage that’s so flavorful blended up into a pesto.

Propagating is a great way to get plants for free and, as well as creating garden plants with cuttings in October, a spot of indoor plant-baby-making is just the thing for rainy fall days. Got a little free space on a sunny kitchen windowsill? Then let's make a start on your soon-to-be-favorite gardening project…

Creating houseplants from citrus seeds is a relatively quick process and with the right care, a seed will grow into a foot-tall plant by its first birthday. While you'll have to wait a decade or so for fruit, citrus trees make beautiful foliage-first houseplants with glossy leaves that release a fresh, aromatic fragrance when rubbed. Lemon and lime plants will have pointy oval leaves, while orange and grapefruit foliage is rounder. All can be grown the same way so, if you've always dreamed of growing a lemon tree, why not try a whole citrus selection?

First wash the seed so it’s free of any citrus pulp. Carefully scratch off the outer shell with your fingernail to reveal the brown seed inside – though this step isn’t essential, it will speed germination. Sow the seed ⅓-inch deep in a small container of moist potting soil and use a clear cover to lock heat and moisture in.

You could use an old yoghurt pot with a drainage hole poked into the base and a clear plastic bag fixed over the rim with an elastic band, or make life easy with domed propagation pots like these 4" Nursery Pots from Amazon. Using a tailored potting mix like Gardenera Citrus Potting Soil, also available from Amazon, will support good germination and strong root growth. Stand the pot on your sunniest south-facing windowsill and remove the cover once you spot growth.

Growing an avocado stone into a tropical tree-let is straightforward, and fast growth makes this a great project if you're gardening with children, but it's fun for adults too. While you can absolutely let your avocado grow tall, it’s easy to keep smaller by pruning, and the 8-12-inch leaves mean this is a standout houseplant.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

First, clean the stone. It’s best to sprout avocado seeds in water rather than soil, with just the bottom, broader third sitting in the water. You can do this with a jam jar by pushing three or four toothpicks into the sides of the stone so it sits on the jar rim, or use a purpose-made avocado vase and skip the toothpicks.

Stand the jar in a bright spot with plenty of indirect sunlight – an east- or west-facing windowsill is ideal – in a warm room as avocados are tropical plants. Change the water every 2-5 days and wash the jar as needed, and keep levels topped up so the seed base remains wet and the top stays dry. Rainwater is best but tap water is fine, but do make sure it’s at room temperature so as not to shock the roots.

Once the stone has cracked open (this can happen very quickly, but be patient as it can sometimes take up to two months), there are a couple of inches of roots and you can see leaves forming on the top stem, move the plant into a pot of potting soil. Avocado plants need good drainage so use an all-purpose houseplant mix like Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix, available from Lowe's.

Your growing avocado will naturally form a single stem with a canopy of big leaves at the top – which gives a great architectural look. If you want a bushier, leafier houseplant however, simply prune off the top set of leaves once the stem reaches 6 inches high to force the plant to grow multiple branches.

An apple or pear tree grown from a seed can produce an attractive garden tree – but don’t expect to be eating its fruit! The genetics of apple and pear trees are complex and seeds almost always revert to a wild ancestor with small, acidic fruit. However, apple and pear trees make great candidates for bonsai trees as they have lots of small fibrous roots and flexible branches that are easy to wire. If you fancy a little long-term gardening project, growing a bonsai fruit tree for your garden is so rewarding, and the spring blossom is so pretty.

Drop the seeds into a jar or water and slosh them around to clean. Ignore any seeds that float to the surface – these won’t germinate – but save the plumpest ones that sink to the bottom. Wrap these in a just-damp piece of kitchen paper inside a sealed zip-lock bag and pop them in the fridge to mimic winter, which is essential for germination. Check the kitchen paper is just-damp every week and, by around the sixth week, you’ll likely spot a white root protruding from the seed.

Then fill small pots or old yoghurt pots with a seed-starting mix like Back to the Roots Organic 3-in-1 Seed Starting Mix, available from Amazon. Use your little finger to poke a ½-inch hole, pop in the sprouted seed with the root downwards and gently push the soil over to cover. Pop this on a warm, sunny windowsill, keep the compost just-damp and in a couple of weeks you’ll see a green shoot.

In a few months, you’ll need to snip off the taproot and move your tree into a bonsai starter pot like this from Walmart and begin pruning branches and wiring into shape with training wire like this, also from Walmart. You can keep your mini apple or pear tree indoors over its first spring or summer but by autumn, move it outdoors.

It’s a hoot to grow a plant from a pineapple top, and as they're part of the bromeliad family, pineapples make good-looking houseplants with striking leaves. It’s unlikely to fruit, but so exciting if it does!

Rather than slicing off the pineapple top, hold the fruit in one hand and the leaves in the other and twist firmly in opposite directions. The top stem should pop out cleanly. Strip off the lower 5-8 layers of leaves until you have around an inch of naked stem. Let this dry – just leave it on a kitchen counter top – for 3-5 days until the base scabs over.

Treat the stem like you would an avocado stone, using toothpicks and a jar, an avocado vase or even a large wine glass to submerge the bare stem in water but keep the leaves dry.

Place this set-up on a warm, sunny south-facing windowsill, change the water every 2-3 days and, within a month, you should see roots. When roots are 2-3 inches long, move into a pot of potting soil tailored for cacti like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from Amazon to grow your pineapple houseplant on.

Save the base of a cabbage and it’s easy to regrow fresh cut-and-come-again leaves to toss into salads and stir-fries. Slice the bottom 2-3 inches from a fresh cabbage and peel away outer leaves to expose the bare inner stem. Set this, cut side up, in a shallow bowl of water – or, if you want to make your cabbage crop into a fancy feature on a sunny kitchen windowsill, pop into margarita glasses like these from Amazon!

Keep the bottom edge of the cabbage base submerged and the top rim dry. It’s vital to change the water every day to prevent rotting, but you'll be well rewarded with new shoots that grow from the core within days. Crop only the outer leaves to prolong the harvest.

You can use the same method to grow leafy greens from carrot tops, which taste rather like parsley and are delicious as a herby garnish or blended into a pesto. Simply cut the top inch from the carrots, trimming any green stems off, then pop cut-side down into a shallow saucer of water. It’s vital that the water doesn’t cover the top of the carrot stub where the leaves emerge, and that you change the water every day.

Your kitchen windowsill will soon be full of all sorts of lovely leafy greens, and I hope you enjoy your plethora of new plants!

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

George Harrison’s $875 gardening jacket is a design lover’s dream. These alternatives capture the same relaxed, utility-inspired style for less.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

George Harrison may be best remembered as a Beatle, but away from the stage and recording studio, he found another creative outlet in the garden. His historic Friar Park estate in Henley-on-Thames became a lifelong labor of love, with its sprawling grounds offering a retreat from the outside world.

For Harrison, gardening was more than a hobby: it was a way of finding peace, getting his hands dirty and nurturing something over time. That passion is now inspiring a new wave of garden-inspired design, thanks to a collaboration between the Friar Park estate and Japanese gardening brand Niwaki, developed with Harrison’s son, Dhani.

The collection brings together gardening tools and accessories, but it’s the jacket that’s catching everyone's eye... and for good reason! It's taken things well beyond the normal realm of gardening clothes, in the best possible way.

The Friar Park and Niwaki Meditation Jacket (as seen above) is just stunning, isn't it? With its Japanese silhouette, chic denim material, oversized hood, relaxed cloak-like shape and thoughtful detailing, it’s the sort of jacket that makes pottering among the plants feel a lot more stylish.

Think practical workwear with a distinctly design-conscious twist – and it’s easy to imagine wearing it well beyond the garden, too.

There’s just one catch: it costs $875, which is a substantial investment for a jacket you might wear to prune roses, turn the compost or nip out to check on your seedlings. Thankfully, you don’t have to spend nearly a thousand dollars to capture some of that same style, as these alternatives offer different takes on the trend, from a traditional Japanese-style jacket to an everyday barn coat and a practical hooded layer.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A hanten is a traditional Japanese jacket style, and this one offers a more traditional silhouette rather than a direct copy of the long Niwaki design. Consider it a relaxed layer for pottering around the garden or throwing on over everyday clothes.

Practical, easy to layer and rooted in classic workwear, this longline style offers the utilitarian feel of the Harrison-inspired jacket, while the contrast collar and color-blocked details give it a slightly more fashion-led finish.

If the oversized hood and practical pockets are what caught your eye, this hooded cargo jacket is worth considering. It won’t replicate the original’s cloak-like shape, but it brings some of the same functional details into a more casual category.

If you love the George Harrison-inspired Meditation Jacket but can’t quite justify spending $875, Niwaki’s Engei Lightweight Garden Jacket is worth a look. It has the same garden-minded, Japanese-inspired sensibility, though at $320, it’s hardly an impulse buy either.

The beauty of the original Friar Park x Niwaki jacket is that it doesn’t look like conventional gardening gear. It’s practical, yes, but it also has a distinctive shape and enough style to wear well beyond the garden gate.

Of course, you don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars to give your gardening wardrobe a little more personality. Whether you go for a Japanese-inspired hanten, a classic barn jacket or a relaxed denim layer, there are plenty of ways to borrow the look without breaking the bank.

And as the Beatles once sang, money can’t buy you love – but it might just buy you a rather good gardening jacket.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Scale insects look more like bumps than bugs, making them easy to miss. A careful inspection and timely treatment can prevent them from spreading indoors.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Almost every year in my house, when the porch plants come inside in October, scale insects often come in with them. Adults don't move. Each one sits on a stem or the back of a leaf under a hard or waxy cover, and most people mistake them for rough spots on the bark until the leaves start to yellow.

The best time for controlling scale insects is before the pots come inside. Outdoors, cold nights slow scale down, and lady beetles and tiny wasps eat a share of it. Indoors, the pests have nothing to stop them. They just keep breeding through the winter on whatever plant they came in on.

An adult's waxy shell keeps most sprays from reaching it, making scale harder to get rid of than aphids or spider mites. Newly hatched crawlers have no shell yet. They're the stage sprays work best on, and new ones keep hatching, so treatments have to be repeated.

All scale insects feed through a thin, straw-like mouthpart sunk into a stem or leaf. Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) is rounded or slightly domed, and its covering is part of its body. Armored types such as fern scale (Pinnaspis aspidistrae) are smaller and flatter. Pry one up with a fingernail and the cover usually comes away by itself, leaving the insect behind.

Only the young get around. Crawlers are about the size of a speck of dust, usually yellow or orange, and they spend a day or two wandering before they settle down to feed. Indoors, they cross from pot to pot wherever leaves touch and ride along on hands and pruners. There isn't one hatch to wait out – new ones keep turning up all winter.

Look for small bumps on stems, along leaf veins, and on the undersides of leaves. They can be brown, tan, white, or black. Black scale (Saissetia oleae) is dark, while oleander scale (Aspidiotus nerii) has a pale, nearly round cover. Use a magnifying glass to check plants properly; Carson's TriView folding loupe, available on Amazon, magnifies up to 15x.

Soft scale leaves sticky honeydew on the leaves and on the table under the pot. Black sooty mold, a group of fungi that includes Capnodium species, often grows on it. Badly infested plants show yellowing leaves, leaf drop, and stunted growth. Dead scale can stay stuck for months – press a bump with a toothpick; if it leaves a wet smear, it's alive.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Citrus, jade plants, hibiscus, ficus, bay laurel, oleander, and orchids are some of the most common hosts. Plenty of other tropical houseplants get scale as well, from peace lilies and pothos to palms and snake plants.

Plants that spent the summer outside need the closest look, especially ones that sat close together on a deck or patio. Edible plants like citrus and bay laurel need extra care during treatment, since some products aren't labeled for anything you plan to eat.

An infested plant needs its own spot, starting the day you find scale on it. A spare room is ideal. Otherwise, a windowsill on the other side of the house will do. Wash your hands and tools after touching it.

Leave the plant on its own until several weekly checks in a row turn up nothing new. One crusted with scale from top to bottom is often better off in the trash.

If you only find a handful of scales, there's no need to spray. A cotton swab dipped in isopropyl alcohol loosens them as you rub, and cheap Equate 70% isopropyl alcohol from Walmart is fine for it. Stick with isopropyl, but test it on one leaf first and wait a day or two to see if it leaves marks.

Scale that won't budge usually gives way to a fingernail, a toothpick, or an old soft toothbrush. You can wipe tougher leaves with a soft cloth and a weak dish soap solution, which also removes the honeydew. The shells need to come off, not just get wet. Alcohol doesn't reach the eggs a female keeps under her cover.

Heavier infestations call for a spray. Horticultural oil smothers scale, and insecticidal soap kills the young on contact. Bonide's All Seasons horticultural oil, available on Amazon, comes ready to spray, and for soap, there's Garden Safe insecticidal soap. Coat every stem and both sides of the leaves.

Adults under a thick shell often survive a spray; crawlers don't. More eggs hatch after the first round, so one spray won't finish the job. A common schedule is two or three rounds spaced 10 to 16 days apart, though the label has the final word. Test any spray on a few leaves first, and skip soap on jade plants and ferns, which it can damage.

Broad-spectrum insecticides rarely need to come indoors. Hand removal followed by oil or soap is usually enough.

Keep checking all winter, once a week, and include plants that never had scale. Go slowly over new growth, the leaf joints, and the undersides of leaves. A strip of double-sided tape wrapped around a stem catches crawlers on the move. Under the loupe, they're easy to tell from dust.

Sticky traps won't tell you much about scale. The yellow cards target flying pests, whiteflies (Trialeurodes vaporariorum) and fungus gnats (Bradysia species), both of which turn up indoors in winter. These Safer Brand houseplant sticky stakes from Walmart push straight into the potting mix.

Start outside, before nights turn cold. Go over each plant with the loupe, and treat anything with scale while it's still outdoors. Mix Garden Safe neem oil extract concentrate from Home Depot at the label rate in a Chapin trigger sprayer.

Once plants are inside, keep the ones that summered outdoors apart from the rest for a few weeks. Leave enough space that leaves from different pots don't touch. Check any new plant before it joins the others, too.

Plants that went in clean in October should come out clean in spring. Any that needed treatment can go back outside once nights stay warm. Lady beetles and tiny parasitic wasps live out there, and both attack scale.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8249. 9 Things to Say About Yourself in Front of Your Kid

How many times have you looked in the mirror and frowned at the outfit you’re wearing, or thought twice about eating dessert because it’s a “bad food” (even though it’s not)? Definitely a few, because you’re human, after all. But it’s important to take stock of the things you say when the kids are around and do your best to present yourself as a strong, confident parent.

Kids learn about body positivity and self-confidence from their parents long before they internalize perceived ideals of how they should look on YouTube or social media. And if they have a strong foundation of self-esteem, those messages will have far less of an impact when they do, inevitably, encounter them. We rounded up 9 things to say—and believe!—about yourself in front of your kids so you can help them learn to take pride in who they are.

1. I look nice today. Say it when you’re tired, when you feel a cold coming on; say it even if you haven’t showered in a few days. Little ones learn by example; if they hear you speaking positively about yourself, it becomes second nature to do the same. Projecting self-confidence shows worthiness—despite the negative messaging that bombards us daily.

2. That was challenging, and I’m going to try again. Showing you are okay with failure helps kids develop the tools necessary for dealing with disappointment. It might help to have a list of people who failed before finding success on hand: think Albert Einstein, Michael Jordan, and Oprah.

3. I made a mistake. It might be one of the hardest things to do, but admitting when we are wrong is one of the best ways to show (and teach) personal responsibility. And that’s a life skill everyone needs.

5. I am proud of my job. Whether you’re a stay-at-home parent, work remotely, or head out to a job, show pride in what you do! Talking about what you do all day shows the kids that while you might be busy, it’s for a good reason—not because you don’t want to read Dragons Love Tacos for the 10th time.

6. I’m glad my body protects me and keeps me alive every day. We can kick a soccer ball, push a swing, and play a board game, and we can do it all without being the “right size.” Referring to your body as something you use as a tool for life is key to helping kids develop a positive self-image.

7. This outfit makes me feel beautiful. Raise your hand if you’ve found yourself cursing while trying on clothes because something doesn’t look quite right. Try focusing on things you like about what you’re wearing: this color complements my skin tone, these leggings are perfect for our park play date, and this hat makes me stand out in a crowd. Pointing out the good instead of the bad is a way to encourage self-love and confidence.

8. I enjoy exercising because it makes me feel strong. Moving our bodies is about so much more than losing weight. It’s about how exercise is good for our brain, helps us ward off illness, and prolongs our lifespan. In today’s tech-driven culture, driving home these ideas is more important than ever.

9. I believe every day is a new chance to start over. It’s easy to let negative thoughts rule our mindset. Yes, life is tough, but it’s also beautiful, and we only get one go at it. A wonderful gift (or tool) you can give your kids is the ability to look at the present and the future and understand that everything moves forward. We alone can make change for ourselves, even if it’s something as tiny as writing down notes of gratitude or as big as demanding the help you need.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8248. The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

The Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

The Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

The Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

Fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional issues to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

The National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

The Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

The National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

Established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is currently undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”
